The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 33
33. How did God create heaven and earth? — God created heaven and earth from nothing by His word only; that is, by a single act of His all-powerful will.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 34
34. Which are the chief creatures of God? — The chief creatures of God are angels and men.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 35
35. What are angels? — Angels are pure spirits without a body, created to adore and enjoy God in heaven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 36

36. Were the angels created for any other purpose? — The angels were also created to assist before the throne of God and to minister unto Him; they have often been sent as messengers from God to man; and are also appointed our guardians.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 37
37. Were the angels, as God created them, good and happy? — The angels, as God created them, were good and happy.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 4. On Creation · Q. 38
38. Did all the angels remain good and happy? — All the angels did not remain good and happy; many of them sinned and were cast into hell, and these are called devils or bad angels.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 39
39. Who were the first man and woman? — The first man and woman were Adam and Eve.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 40
40. Were Adam and Eve innocent and holy when they came from the hand of God? — Adam and Eve were innocent and holy when they came from the hand of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 41
41. Did God give any command to Adam and Eve? — To try their obedience God commanded Adam and Eve not to eat of a certain fruit which grew in the garden of Paradise.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 42

42. Which were the chief blessings intended for Adam and Eve had they remained faithful to God? — The chief blessings intended for Adam and Eve, had they remained faithful to God, were a constant state of happiness in this life and everlasting glory in the next.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 43
43. Did Adam and Eve remain faithful to God? — Adam and Eve did not remain faithful to God; but broke His command by eating the forbidden fruit.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 44
44. What befell Adam and Eve on account of their sin? — Adam and Eve, on account of their sin, lost innocence and holiness, and were doomed to sickness and death.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 45

45. What evil befell us on account of the disobedience of our first parents? — On account of the disobedience of our first parents, we all share in their sin and punishment, as we should have shared in their happiness if they had remained faithful.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 46

46. What other effects followed from the sin of our first parents? — Our nature was corrupted by the sin of our first parents, which darkened our understanding, weakened our will, and left in us a strong inclination to evil.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 47
47. What is the sin called which we inherit from our first parents? — The sin which we inherit from our first parents is called original sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 48
48. Why is this sin called original? — This sin is called original because it comes down to us from our first parents, and we are brought into the world with its guilt on our soul.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 49
49. Does this corruption of our nature remain in us after original sin is forgiven? — This corruption of our nature and other punishments remain in us after original sin is forgiven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 5. On Our First Parents and the Fall · Q. 50

50. Was any one ever preserved from original sin? — The Blessed Virgin Mary, through the merits of her Divine Son, was preserved free from the guilt of original sin, and this privilege is called her Immaculate Conception.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 51
51. Is original sin the only kind of sin? — Original sin is not the only kind of sin; there is another kind of sin, which we commit ourselves, called actual sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 52
52. What is actual sin? — Actual sin is any wilful thought, word, deed, or omission contrary to the law of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 53
53. How many kinds of actual sin are there? — There are two kinds of actual sin--mortal and venial.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 54
54. What is mortal sin? — Mortal sin is a grievous offense against the law of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 55
55. Why is this sin called mortal? — This sin is called mortal because it deprives us of spiritual life, which is sanctifying grace, and brings everlasting death and damnation on the soul.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 56
56. How many things are necessary to make a sin mortal? — To make a sin mortal three things are necessary: a grievous matter, sufficient reflection, and full consent of the will.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 57

57. What is venial sin? — Venial sin is a slight offense against the law of God in matters of less importance, or in matters of great importance it is an offense committed without sufficient reflection or full consent of the will.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 58

58. Which are the effects of venial sin? — The effects of venial sin are the lessening of the love of God in our heart, the making us less worthy of His help, and the weakening of the power to resist mortal sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 6. On Sin and Its Kinds · Q. 59
59. Which are the chief sources of sin? — The chief sources of sin are seven: Pride, Covetousness, Lust, Anger, Gluttony, Envy, and Sloth; and they are commonly called capital sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 60
60. Did God abandon man after he fell into sin? — God did not abandon man after he fell into sin, but promised him a Redeemer, who was to satisfy for man's sin and reopen to him the gates of heaven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 61
61. Who is the Redeemer? — Our Blessed Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ is the Redeemer of mankind.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 62
62. What do you believe of Jesus Christ? — I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the second Person of the Blessed Trinity, true God and true man.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 63
63. Why is Jesus Christ true God? — Jesus Christ is true God because He is the true and only Son of God the Father.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 64
64. Why is Jesus Christ true man? — Jesus Christ is true man because He is the Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary and has a body and soul like ours.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 65
65. How many natures are there in Jesus Christ? — In Jesus Christ there are two natures, the nature of God and the nature of man.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 66
66. Is Jesus Christ more than one person? — No, Jesus Christ is but one Divine Person.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 67
67. Was Jesus Christ always God? — Jesus Christ was always God, as He is the second Person of the Blessed Trinity, equal to His Father from all eternity.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 68
68. Was Jesus Christ always man? — Jesus Christ was not always man, but became man at the time of His Incarnation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 69
69. What do you mean by the Incarnation? — By the Incarnation I mean that the Son of God was made man.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 70
70. How was the Son of God made man? — The Son of God was conceived and made man by the power of the Holy Ghost, in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 71

71. Is the Blessed Virgin Mary truly the Mother of God? — The Blessed Virgin Mary is truly the Mother of God, because the same Divine Person who is the Son of God is also the Son of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 72

72. Did the Son of God become man immediately after the sin of our first parents? — The Son of God did not become man immediately after the sin of our first parents, but was promised to them as a Redeemer.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 73

73. How could they be saved who lived before the Son of God became man? — They who lived before the Son of God became man could be saved by believing in a Redeemer to come, and by keeping the commandments.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 74

74. On what day was the Son of God conceived and made man? — The Son of God was conceived and made man on Annunciation day--the day on which the Angel Gabriel announced to the Blessed Virgin Mary that she was to be the Mother of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 75
75. On what day was Christ born? — Christ was born on Christmas day in a stable at Bethlehem, over nineteen hundred years ago.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 76
76. How long did Christ live on earth? — Christ lived on earth about thirty-three years, and led a most holy life in poverty and suffering.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 7. On the Incarnation and Redemption · Q. 77
77. Why did Christ live so long on earth? — Christ lived so long on earth to show us the way to heaven by His teachings and example.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 78
78. What did Jesus Christ suffer? — Jesus Christ suffered a bloody sweat, a cruel scourging, was crowned with thorns, and was crucified.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 79
79. On what day did Christ die? — Christ died on Good Friday.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 80

80. Why do you call that day "good" on which Christ died so sorrowful a death? — We call that day "good" on which Christ died because by His death He showed His great love for man, and purchased for him every blessing.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 81
81. Where did Christ die? — Christ died on Mount Calvary.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 82
82. How did Christ die? — Christ was nailed to the Cross and died on it between two thieves.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 83
83. Why did Christ suffer and die? — Christ suffered and died for our sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 84

84. What lessons do we learn from the sufferings and death of Christ? — From the sufferings and death of Christ we learn the great evil of sin, the hatred God bears to it, and the necessity of satisfying for it.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 85
85. Where did Christ's soul go after His death? — After Christ's death His soul descended into hell.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 86

86. Did Christ's soul descend into the hell of the damned? — The hell into which Christ's soul descended was not the hell of the damned, but a place or state of rest called Limbo, where the souls of the just were waiting for Him.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 87
87. Why did Christ descend into Limbo? — Christ descended into Limbo to preach to the souls who were in prison--that is, to announce to them the joyful tidings of their redemption.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 88
88. Where was Christ's body while His soul was in Limbo? — While Christ's soul was in Limbo His body was in the holy sepulchre.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 89
89. On what day did Christ rise from the dead? — Christ rose from the dead, glorious and immortal, on Easter Sunday, the third day after His death.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 90
90. How long did Christ stay on earth after His resurrection? — Christ stayed on earth forty days after His resurrection to show that He was truly risen from the dead, and to instruct His Apostles.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 91
91. After Christ had remained forty days on earth whither did He go? — After forty days Christ ascended into heaven, and the day on which He ascended into heaven is called Ascension day.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 92
92. Where is Christ in heaven? — In heaven Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father Almighty.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 8. On Our Lord's Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Ascension · Q. 93

93. What do you mean by saying that Christ sits at the right hand Of God? — When I say that Christ sits at the right hand of God I mean that Christ as God is equal to His Father in all things, and that as man He is in the highest place in heaven next to God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 94
94. Who is the Holy Ghost? — The Holy Ghost is the third Person of the Blessed Trinity.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 95
95. From whom does the Holy Ghost proceed? — The Holy Ghost proceeds from the Father and the Son.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 96
96. Is the Holy Ghost equal to the Father and the Son? — The Holy Ghost is equal to the Father and the Son, being the same Lord and God as They are.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 97

97. On what day did the Holy Ghost come down upon the Apostles? — The Holy Ghost came down upon the Apostles ten days after the Ascension of our Lord; and the day on which He came down upon the Apostles is called Whitsunday, or Pentecost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 98
98. How did the Holy Ghost come down upon the Apostles? — The Holy Ghost came down upon the Apostles in the form of tongues of fire.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 99
99. Who sent the Holy Ghost upon the Apostles? — Our Lord Jesus Christ sent the Holy Ghost upon the Apostles.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 100
100. Why did Christ send the Holy Ghost? — Christ sent the Holy Ghost to sanctify His Church, to enlighten and strengthen the Apostles, and to enable them to preach the Gospel.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 9. On the Holy Ghost and his Descent Upon the Apostles · Q. 101
101. Will the Holy Ghost abide with the Church forever? — The Holy Ghost will abide with the Church forever, and guide it in the way of holiness and truth.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 102

102. Which are the chief effects of the Redemption? — The chief effects of the Redemption are two: The satisfaction of God's justice by Christ's sufferings and death, and the gaining of grace for men.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 103
103. What do you mean by grace? — By grace I mean a supernatural gift of God bestowed on us, through the merits of Jesus Christ, for our salvation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 104
104. How many kinds of grace are there? — There are two kinds of grace, sanctifying grace and actual grace.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 105
105. What is sanctifying grace? — Sanctifying grace is that grace which makes the soul holy and pleasing to God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 106

106. What do you call those graces or gifts of God by which we believe in Him, hope in Him, and love Him? — Those graces or gifts of God by which we believe in Him, and hope in Him, and love Him, are called the Divine virtues of Faith, Hope, and Charity.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 107
107. What is Faith? — Faith is a Divine virtue by which we firmly believe the truths which God has revealed.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 108
108. What is Hope? — Hope is a Divine virtue by which we firmly trust that God will give us eternal life and the means to obtain it.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 109
109. What is Charity? — Charity is a Divine virtue by which we love God above all things for His own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for the love of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 110
110. What is actual grace? — Actual grace is that help of God which enlightens our mind and moves our will to shun evil and do good.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 111
111. Is grace necessary to salvation? — Grace is necessary to salvation, because without grace we can do nothing to merit heaven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 112
112. Can we resist the grace of God? — We can and unfortunately often do resist the grace of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 10. On the Effects of the Redemption · Q. 113
113. What is the grace of perseverance? — The grace of perseverance is a particular gift of God which enables us to continue in the state of grace till death.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 114

114. Which are the means instituted by our Lord to enable men at all times to share in the fruits of the Redemption? — The means instituted by our Lord to enable men at all times to share in the fruits of His Redemption are the Church and the Sacraments.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 115

115. What is the Church? — The Church is the congregation of all those who profess the faith of Christ, partake of the same Sacraments, and are governed by their lawful pastors under one visible head.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 116
116. Who is the invisible Head of the Church? — Jesus Christ is the invisible Head of the Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 117
117. Who is the visible Head of the Church? — Our Holy Father the Pope, the Bishop of Rome, is the Vicar of Christ on earth and the visible Head of the Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 118

118. Why is the Pope, the Bishop of Rome, the visible Head of the Church? — The Pope, the Bishop of Rome, is the visible Head of the Church because he is the successor of St. Peter, whom Christ made the chief of the Apostles and the visible Head of the Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 119
119. Who are the successors of the other Apostles? — The successors of the other Apostles are the bishops of the Holy Catholic Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 120
120. Why did Christ found the Church? — Christ founded the Church to teach, govern, sanctify, and save all men.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 11. On the Church · Q. 121
121. Are all bound to belong to the Church? — All are bound to belong to the Church, and he who knows the Church to be the true Church and remains out of it cannot be saved.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 122
122. Which are the attributes of the Church? — The attributes of the Church are three: authority infallibility, and indefectibility.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 123

123. What do you mean by the authority of the Church? — By the authority of the Church I mean the right and power which the Pope and the bishops, as the successors of the Apostles, have to teach and to govern the faithful.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 124
124. What do you mean by the infallibility of the Church? — By the infallibility of the Church I mean that the Church cannot err when it teaches a doctrine of faith or morals.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 125

125. When does the Church teach infallibly? — The Church teaches infallibly when it speaks through the Pope and the bishops, united in general council, or through the Pope alone when he proclaims to all the faithful a doctrine of faith or morals.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 126
126. What do you mean by the indefectibility of the Church? — By the indefectibility of the Church I mean that the Church, as Christ founded it, will last till the end of time.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 127

127. In whom are these attributes found in their fullness? — These attributes are found in their fullness in the Pope, the visible Head of the Church, whose infallible authority to teach bishops, priests, and people in matters of faith or morals will last till the end of the world.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 128
128. Has the Church any marks by which it may be known? — The Church has four marks by which it may be known: it is One; it is Holy; it is Catholic; it is Apostolic.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 129
129. How is the Church One? — The Church is One because all its members agree in one faith, are all in one communion, and are all under one Head.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 130

130. How is the Church Holy? — The Church is Holy because its founder, Jesus Christ, is holy; because it teaches a holy doctrine; invites all to a holy life; and because of the eminent holiness of so many thousands of its children.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 131
131. How is the Church Catholic or universal? — The Church is Catholic or universal because it subsists in all ages, teaches all nations, and maintains all truth.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 132

132. How is the Church Apostolic? — The Church is Apostolic because it was founded by Christ on His Apostles, and is governed by their lawful successors, and because it has never ceased, and never will cease, to teach their doctrine.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 133
133. In which Church are these attributes and marks found? — These attributes and marks are found in the Holy Roman Catholic Church alone.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 134

134. From whom does the Church derive its undying life and infallible authority? — The Church derives its undying life and infallible authority from the Holy Ghost, the spirit of truth, who abides with it forever.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 12. On the Attributes and Marks of the Church · Q. 135

135. By whom is the Church made and kept One, Holy, and Catholic? — The Church is made and kept One, Holy, and Catholic by the Holy Ghost, the spirit of love and holiness, who unites and sanctifies its members throughout the world.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 136
136. What is a Sacrament? — A Sacrament is an outward sign instituted by Christ to give grace.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 137
137. How many Sacraments are there? — There are seven Sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Penance, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, and Matrimony.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 138
138. Whence have the Sacraments the power of giving grace? — The Sacraments have the power of giving grace from the merits of Jesus Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 139
139. What grace do the Sacraments give? — Some of the Sacraments give sanctifying grace, and others increase it in our souls.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 140
140. Which are the Sacraments that give sanctifying grace? — The Sacraments that give sanctifying grace are Baptism and Penance; and they are called Sacraments of the dead.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 141

141. Why are Baptism and Penance called Sacraments of the dead? — Baptism and Penance are called Sacraments of the dead, because they take away sin, which is the death of the soul, and give grace, which is its life.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 142

142. Which are the Sacraments that increase sanctifying grace in our soul? — The Sacraments that increase sanctifying grace in our soul are: Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, and Matrimony; and they are called Sacraments of the living.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 143

143. Why are Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, and Matrimony called Sacraments of the living? — Confirmation, Holy Eucharist, Extreme Unction, Holy Orders, and Matrimony are called Sacraments of the living, because those who receive them worthily are already living the life of grace.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 144

144. What sin does he commit who receives the Sacraments of the living in mortal sin? — He who receives the Sacraments of the living in mortal sin commits a sacrilege, which is a great sin, because it is an abuse of a sacred thing.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 145
145. Besides sanctifying grace do the Sacraments give any other grace? — Besides sanctifying grace the Sacraments give another grace, called sacramental.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 146
146. What is sacramental grace? — Sacramental grace is a special help which God gives, to attain the end for which He instituted each Sacrament.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 147
147. Do the Sacraments always give grace? — The Sacraments always give grace, if we receive them with the right dispositions.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 148
148. Can we receive the Sacraments more than once? — We can receive the Sacraments more than once, except Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 149

149. Why can we not receive Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders more than once? — We cannot receive Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders more than once, because they imprint a character in the soul.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 150
150. What is the character which these Sacraments imprint in the soul? — The character which these Sacraments imprint in the soul is a spiritual mark which remains forever.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 13. On the Sacraments in General · Q. 151

151. Does this character remain in the soul even after death? — This character remains in the soul even after death: for the honor and glory of those who are saved; for the shame and punishment of those who are lost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 152
152. What is Baptism? — Baptism is a Sacrament which cleanses us from original sin, makes us Christians, children of God, and heirs of heaven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 153
153. Are actual sins ever remitted by Baptism? — Actual sins and all the punishment due to them are remitted by Baptism, if the person baptized be guilty of any.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 154
154. Is Baptism necessary to salvation? — Baptism is necessary to salvation, because without it we cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 155
155. Who can administer Baptism? — The priest is the ordinary minister of Baptism; but in case of necessity any one who has the use of reason may baptize.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 156

156. How is Baptism given? — Whoever baptizes should pour water on the head of the person to be baptized, and say, while pouring the water: I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 157
157. How many kinds of Baptism are there? — There are three kinds of Baptism: Baptism of water, of desire, and of blood.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 158

158. What is Baptism of water? — Baptism of water is that which is given by pouring water on the head of the person to be baptized, and saying at the same time: I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 159
159. What is Baptism of desire? — Baptism of desire is an ardent wish to receive Baptism, and to do all that God has ordained for our salvation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 160
160. What is Baptism of blood? — Baptism of blood is the shedding of one's blood for the faith of Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 161

161. Is Baptism of desire or of blood sufficient to produce the effects of Baptism of water? — Baptism of desire or of blood is sufficient to produce the effects of the Baptism of water, if it is impossible to receive the Baptism of water.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 162
162. What do we promise in Baptism? — In Baptism we promise to renounce the devil with all his works and pomps.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 163
163. Why is the name of a saint given in Baptism? — The name of a saint is given in Baptism in order that the person baptized may imitate his virtues and have him for a protector.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 164

164. Why are godfathers and godmothers given in Baptism? — Godfathers and godmothers are given in Baptism in order that they may promise, in the name of the child, what the child itself would promise if it had the use of reason.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 14. On Baptism · Q. 165
165. What is the obligation of a godfather and a godmother? — The obligation of a godfather and a godmother is to instruct the child in its religious duties, if the parents neglect to do so or die.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 166
166. What is Confirmation? — Confirmation is a Sacrament through which we receive the Holy Ghost to make us strong and perfect Christians and soldiers of Jesus Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 167
167. Who administers Confirmation? — The bishop is the ordinary minister of Confirmation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 168

168. How does the bishop give Confirmation? — The bishop extends his hands over those who are to be confirmed, prays that they may receive the Holy Ghost, and anoints the forehead of each with holy chrism in the form of a cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 169
169. What is holy chrism? — Holy chrism is a mixture of olive-oil and balm, consecrated by the bishop.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 170

170. What does the bishop say in anointing the person he confirms? — In anointing the person he confirms the bishop says: I sign thee with the sign of the cross, and I confirm thee with the chrism of salvation, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 171

171. What is meant by anointing the forehead with chrism in the form of a cross? — By anointing the forehead with chrism in the form of a cross is meant, that the Christian who is confirmed must openly profess and practice his faith, never be ashamed of it, and rather die than deny it.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 172

172. Why does the bishop give the person he confirms a slight blow on the cheek? — The bishop gives the person he confirms a slight blow on the cheek, to put him in mind that he must be ready to suffer everything, even death, for the sake of Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 173
173. To receive Confirmation worthily is it necessary to be in the state of grace? — To receive Confirmation worthily it is necessary to be in the state of grace.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 174

174. What special preparation should be made to receive Confirmation? — Persons of an age to learn should know the chief mysteries of faith and the duties of a Christian, and be instructed in the nature and effects of this Sacrament.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 15. On Confirmation · Q. 175
175. Is it a sin to neglect Confirmation? — It is a sin to neglect Confirmation, especially in these evil days when faith and morals are exposed to so many and such violent temptations.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 176
176. Which are the effects of Confirmation? — The effects of Confirmation are an increase of sanctifying grace, the strengthening of our faith, and the gifts of the Holy Ghost.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 177
177. Which are the gifts of the Holy Ghost? — The gifts of the Holy Ghost are Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Fortitude, Knowledge, Piety and Fear of the Lord.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 178
178. Why do we receive the gift of Fear of the Lord? — We receive the gift of Fear of the Lord to fill us with a dread of sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 179
179. Why do we receive the gift of Piety? — We receive the gift of Piety to make us love God as a Father and obey Him because we love Him.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 180
180. Why do we receive the gift of Knowledge? — We receive the gift of Knowledge to enable us to discover the will of God in all things.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 181
181. Why do we receive the gift of Fortitude? — We receive the gift of Fortitude to strengthen us to do the will of God in all things.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 182
182. Why do we receive the gift of Counsel? — We receive the gift of Counsel to warn us of the deceits of the devil, and of the dangers to salvation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 183
183. Why do we receive the gift of Understanding? — We receive the gift of Understanding to enable us to know more clearly the mysteries of faith.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 184
184. Why do we receive the gift of Wisdom? — We receive the gift of Wisdom to give us a relish for the things of God, and to direct our whole life and all our actions to His honor and glory.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 185
185. Which are the Beatitudes? — The Beatitudes are:
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 16. On the Gifts and Fruits of the Holy Ghost · Q. 186

186. Which are the twelve fruits of the Holy Ghost? — The twelve fruits of the Holy Ghost are Charity, Joy, Peace, Patience, Benignity, Goodness, Long-suffering, Mildness, Faith, Modesty, Continency, and Chastity.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 187
187. What is the Sacrament of Penance? — Penance is a Sacrament in which the sins committed after Baptism are forgiven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 188

188. How does the Sacrament of Penance remit sin, and restore to the soul the friendship of God? — The Sacrament of Penance remits sins and restores the friendship of God to the soul by means of the absolution of the priest.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 189

189. How do you know that the priest has the power of absolving from the sins committed after Baptism? — I know that the priest has the power of absolving from the sins committed after Baptism, because Jesus Christ granted that power to the priests of His Church when He said: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you shall retain, they are retained."
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 190

190. How do the priests of the Church exercise the power of forgiving sins? — The priests of the Church exercise the power of forgiving sins by hearing the confession of sins, and granting pardon for them as ministers of God and in His name.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 191
191. What must we do to receive the Sacrament of Penance worthily? — To receive the Sacrament of Penance worthily we must do five things:
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 192
192. What is the examination of conscience? — The examination of conscience is an earnest effort to recall to mind all the sins we have committed since our last worthy confession.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 193

193. How can we make a good examination of conscience? — We can make a good examination of conscience by calling to memory the commandments of God, the precepts of the Church, the seven capital sins, and the particular duties of our state in life, to find out the sins we have committed.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 17. On the Sacrament of Penance · Q. 194

194. What should we do before beginning the examination of conscience? — Before beginning the examination of conscience we should pray to God to give us light to know our sins and grace to detest them.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 195
195. What is contrition, or sorrow for sin? — Contrition, or sorrow for sin, is a hatred of sin and a true grief of the soul for having offended God, with a firm purpose of sinning no more.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 196
196. What kind of sorrow should we have for our sins? — The sorrow we should have for our sins should be interior, supernatural, universal, and sovereign.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 197
197. What do you mean by saying that our sorrow should be interior? — When I say that our sorrow should be interior, I mean that it should come from the heart, and not merely from the lips.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 198

198. What do you mean by saying that our sorrow should be supernatural? — When I say that our sorrow should be supernatural, I mean that it should be prompted by the grace of God, and excited by motives which spring from faith, and not by merely natural motives.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 199
199. What do you mean by saying that our sorrow should be universal? — When I say that our sorrow should be universal, I mean that we should be sorry for all our mortal sins without exception.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 200

200. What do you mean when you say that our sorrow should be sovereign? — When I say that our sorrow should be sovereign, I mean that we should grieve more for having offended God than for any other evil that can befall us.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 201

201. Why should we be sorry for our sins? — We should be sorry for our sins, because sin is the greatest of evils and an offense against God our Creator, Preserver, and Redeemer, and because it shuts us out of heaven and condemns us to the eternal pains of hell.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 202
202. How many kinds of contrition are there? — There are two kinds of contrition: perfect contrition and imperfect contrition.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 203
203. What is perfect contrition? — Perfect contrition is that which fills us with sorrow and hatred for sin, because it offends God, who is infinitely good in Himself and worthy of all love.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 204
204. What is imperfect contrition? — Imperfect contrition is that by which we hate what offends God, because by it we lose heaven and deserve hell; or because sin is so hateful in itself.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 205
205. Is imperfect contrition sufficient for a worthy confession? — Imperfect contrition is sufficient for a worthy confession, but we should endeavor to have perfect contrition.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 206
206. What do you mean by a firm purpose of sinning no more? — By a firm purpose of sinning no more I mean a fixed resolve not only to avoid all mortal sin, but also its near occasions.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 18. On Contrition · Q. 207
207. What do you mean by the near occasions of sin? — By the near occasions of sin I mean all the persons, places, and things that may easily lead us into sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 208
208. What is Confession? — Confession is the telling of our sins to a duly authorized priest, for the purpose of obtaining forgiveness.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 209
209. What sins are we bound to confess? — We are bound to confess all our mortal sins, but it is well also to confess our venial sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 210
210. Which are the chief qualities of a good Confession? — The chief qualities of a good Confession are three: it must be humble, sincere, and entire.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 211
211. When is our Confession humble? — Our Confession is humble, when we accuse our selves of our sins, with a deep sense of shame and sorrow for having offended God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 212
212. When is our Confession sincere? — Our Confession is sincere, when we tell our sins honestly and truthfully, neither exaggerating nor excusing them.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 213
213. When is our Confession entire? — Our Confession is entire, when we tell the number and kinds of our sins and the circumstances which change their nature.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 214

214. What should we do if we cannot remember the number of our sins? — If we cannot remember the number of our sins, we should tell the number as nearly as possible, and say how often we may have sinned in a day, a week, or a month, and how long the habit or practice has lasted.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 215

215. Is our Confession worthy if, without our fault, we forget to confess a mortal sin? — If without our fault we forget to confess a mortal sin, our Confession is worthy, and the sin is forgiven; but it must be told in Confession if it again comes to our mind.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 216

216. Is it a grievous offense wilfully to conceal a mortal sin in Confession? — It is a grievous offense wilfully to conceal a mortal sin in Confession, because we thereby tell a lie to the Holy Ghost, and make our Confession worthless.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 217

217. What must he do who has wilfully concealed a mortal sin in Confession? — He who has wilfully concealed a mortal sin in Confession must not only confess it, but must also repeat all the sins he has committed since his last worthy Confession.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 218
218. Why does the priest give us a penance after Confession? — The priest gives us a penance after Confession, that we may satisfy God for the temporal punishment due to our sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 219

219. Does not the Sacrament of Penance remit all punishment due to sin? — The Sacrament of Penance remits the eternal punishment due to sin, but it does not always remit the temporal punishment which God requires as satisfaction for our sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 220

220. Why does God require a temporal punishment as a satisfaction for sin? — God requires a temporal punishment as a satisfaction for sin, to teach us the great evil of sin and to prevent us from falling again.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 221

221. Which are the chief means by which we satisfy God for the temporal punishment due to sin? — The chief means by which we satisfy God for the temporal punishment due to sin are: Prayer, Fasting, Almsgiving, all spiritual and corporal works of mercy, and the patient suffering of the ills of life.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 222

222. Which are the chief spiritual works of mercy? — The chief spiritual works of mercy are seven: To admonish the sinner, to instruct the ignorant, to counsel the doubtful, to comfort the sorrowful, to bear wrongs patiently, to forgive all injuries, and to pray for the living and the dead.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 19. On Confession · Q. 223

223. Which are the chief corporal works of mercy? — The chief corporal works of mercy are seven: To feed the hungry, to give drink to the thirsty, to clothe the naked, to ransom the captive, to harbor the harborless, to visit the sick, and to bury the dead.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 224

224. What should we do on entering the confessional? — On entering the confessional we should kneel, make the sign of the Cross, and say to the priest, Bless me, Father; then add, I confess to Almighty God and to you, Father, that I have sinned.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 225

225. Which are the first things we should tell the priest in Confession? — The first things we should tell the priest in Confession are the time of our last Confession, and whether we said the penance and went to Holy Communion.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 226

226. After telling the time of our last Confession and Communion what should we do? — After telling the time of our last Confession and Communion we should confess all the mortal sins we have since committed, and all the venial sins we may wish to mention.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 227
227. What must we do when the confessor asks us questions? — When the confessor asks us questions we must answer them truthfully and clearly.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 228
228. What should we do after telling our sins? — After telling our sins we should listen with attention to the advice which the confessor may think proper to give.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 229
229. How should we end our Confession? — We should end our Confession by saying, I also accuse myself of all the sins of my past life, telling, if we choose, one or several of our past sins.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 20. On the Manner of Making a Good Confession · Q. 230
230. What should we do while the priest is giving us absolution? — While the priest is giving us absolution we should from our heart renew the Act of Contrition.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 231
231. What is an Indulgence? — An Indulgence is the remission in whole or in part of the temporal punishment due to sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 232

232. Is an Indulgence a pardon of sin, or a license to commit sin? — An Indulgence is not a pardon of sin, nor a license to commit sin, and one who is in a state of mortal sin cannot gain an Indulgence.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 233
233. How many kinds of Indulgences are there? — There are two kinds of Indulgences--Plenary and Partial.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 234
234. What is a Plenary Indulgence? — A Plenary Indulgence is the full remission of the temporal punishment due to sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 235
235. What is a Partial Indulgence? — A Partial Indulgence is the remission of a part of the temporal punishment due to sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 236

236. How does the Church by means of Indulgences remit the temporal punishment due to sin? — The Church by means of Indulgences remits the temporal punishment due to sin by applying to us the merits of Jesus Christ, and the superabundant satisfactions of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of the saints; which merits and satisfactions are its spiritual treasury.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 21. On Indulgences · Q. 237
237. What must we do to gain an Indulgence? — To gain an Indulgence we must be in the state of grace and perform the works enjoined.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 238
238. What is the Holy Eucharist? — The Holy Eucharist is the Sacrament which contains the body and blood, soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ under the appearances of bread and wine.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 239
239. When did Christ institute the Holy Eucharist? — Christ instituted the Holy Eucharist at the Last Supper, the night before He died.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 240
240. Who were present when our Lord instituted the Holy Eucharist? — When our Lord instituted the Holy Eucharist the twelve Apostles were present.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 241

241. How did our Lord institute the Holy Eucharist? — Our Lord instituted the Holy Eucharist by taking bread, blessing, breaking, and giving to His Apostles, saying: Take ye and eat. This is My body; and then by taking the cup of wine, blessing and giving it, saying to them: Drink ye all of this. This is My blood which shall be shed for the remission of sins. Do this for a commemoration of Me.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 242

242. What happened when our Lord said, This is My body; this is My blood? — When our Lord said, This is My body, the substance of the bread was changed into the substance of His body; when He said, This is My blood, the substance of the wine was changed into the substance of His blood.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 243
243. Is Jesus Christ whole and entire both under the form of bread and under the form of wine? — Jesus Christ is whole and entire both under the form of bread and under the form of wine.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 244

244. Did anything remain of the bread and wine after their substance had been changed into the substance of the body and blood of our Lord? — After the substance of the bread and wine had been changed into the substance of the body and blood of our Lord there remained only the appearances of bread and wine.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 245
245. What do you mean by the appearances of bread and wine? — By the appearances of bread and wine I mean the figure, the color, the taste, and whatever appears to the senses.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 246
246. What is this change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of our Lord called? — This change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of our Lord is called Transubstantiation.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 247

247. How was the substance of the bread and wine changed into the substance of the body and blood of Christ? — The substance of the bread and wine was changed into the substance of the body and blood of Christ by His almighty power.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 248

248. Does this change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ continue to be made in the Church? — This change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ continues to be made in the Church by Jesus Christ through the ministry of His priests.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 249

249. When did Christ give His priests the power to change bread and wine into His body and blood? — Christ gave His priests the power to change bread and wine into His body and blood when He said to the Apostles, Do this in commemoration of Me.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 22. On the Holy Eucharist · Q. 250

250. How do the priests exercise this power of changing bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ? — The priests exercise this power of changing bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ through the words of consecration in the Mass, which are the words of Christ: This is My body; this is My blood.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 251
251. Why did Christ institute the Holy Eucharist? — Christ instituted the Holy Eucharist--
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 252
252. How are we united to Jesus Christ in the Holy Eucharist? — We are united to Jesus Christ in the Holy Eucharist by means of Holy Communion.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 253
253. What is Holy Communion? — Holy Communion is the receiving of the body and blood of Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 254

254. What is necessary to make a good Communion? — To make a good Communion it is necessary to be in the state of sanctifying grace, to have a right intention, and to obey the laws of fasting. (See Q. 257.)
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 255

255. Does he who receives Communion in mortal sin receive the body and blood of Christ? — He who receives Communion in mortal sin receives the body and blood of Christ, but does not receive His grace, and he commits a great sacrilege.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 256

256. Is it enough to be free from mortal sin to receive plentifully the graces of Holy Communion? — To receive plentifully the graces of Holy Communion it is not enough to be free from mortal sin, but we should be free from all affection to venial sin, and should make acts of faith, hope, and love.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 257

257. What is the fast necessary for Holy Communion? — The fast necessary for Holy Communion is to abstain from all food, beverages, and alcoholic drinks for one hour before Holy Communion. Water may be taken at any time. The sick may take food, non-alcoholic drinks, and any medicine up to Communion time.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 258

258. Is any one ever allowed to receive Holy Communion when not fasting? — Any one in danger of death is allowed to receive Holy Communion when not fasting or when it is necessary to save the Blessed Sacrament from insult or injury.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 259
259. When are we bound to receive Holy Communion? — We are bound to receive Holy Communion, under pain of mortal sin, during the Easter time and when in danger of death.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 260

260. Is it well to receive Holy Communion often? — It is well to receive Holy Communion often, as nothing is a greater aid to a holy life than often to receive the Author of all grace and the Source of all good.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 23. On the Ends for Which the Holy Eucharist Was Instituted · Q. 261

261. What should we do after Holy Communion? — After Holy Communion we should spend some time in adoring our Lord, in thanking Him for the grace we have received, and in asking Him for the blessings we need.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 262
262. When and where are the bread and wine changed into the body and blood of Christ? — The bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of Christ at the Consecration in the Mass.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 263
263. What is the Mass? — The Mass is the unbloody sacrifice of the body and blood of Christ.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 264
264. What is a sacrifice? — A sacrifice is the offering of an object by a priest to God alone, and the consuming of it to acknowledge that He is the Creator and Lord of all things.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 265
265. Is the Mass the same sacrifice as that of the Cross? — The Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 266

266. How is the Mass the same sacrifice as that of the Cross? — The Mass is the same sacrifice as that of the Cross because the offering and the priest are the same--Christ our Blessed Lord; and the ends for which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered are the same as those of the sacrifice of the Cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 267

267. What were the ends for which the sacrifice of the Cross was offered? — The ends for which the sacrifice of the Cross was offered were: 1st, To honor and glorify God; 2d, To thank Him for all the graces bestowed on the whole world; 3d, To satisfy God's justice for the sins of men; 4th, To obtain all graces and blessings.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 268

268. Is there any difference between the sacrifice of the Cross and the sacrifice of the Mass? — Yes; the manner in which the sacrifice is offered is different. On the Cross Christ really shed His blood and was really slain; in the Mass there is no real shedding of blood nor real death, because Christ can die no more; but the sacrifice of the Mass, through the separate consecration of the bread and the wine, represents His death on the Cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 269
269. How should we assist at Mass? — We should assist at Mass with great interior recollection and piety and with every outward mark of respect and devotion.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 24. On the Sacrifice of the Mass · Q. 270

270. Which is the best manner of hearing Mass? — The best manner of hearing Mass is to offer it to God with the priest for the same purpose for which it is said, to meditate on Christ's sufferings and death, and to go to Holy Communion.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 271

271. What is the Sacrament of Extreme Unction? — Extreme Unction is the Sacrament which, through the anointing and prayer of the priest, gives health and strength to the soul, and sometimes to the body, when we are in danger of death from sickness.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 272
272. When should we receive Extreme Unction? — We should receive Extreme Unction when we are in danger of death from sickness, or from a wound or accident.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 273

273. Should we wait until we are in extreme danger before we receive Extreme Unction? — We should not wait until we are in extreme danger before we receive Extreme Unction, but if possible we should receive it whilst we have the use of our senses.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 274

274. Which are the effects of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction? — The effects of Extreme Unction are: 1st, To comfort us in the pains of sickness and to strengthen us against temptation; 2d, To remit venial sins and to cleanse our soul from the remains of sin; 3d, To restore us to health, when God sees fit.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 275

275. What do you mean by the remains of sin? — By the remains of sin I mean the inclination to evil and the weakness of the will which are the result of our sins, and which remain after our sins have been forgiven.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 276
276. How should we receive the Sacrament of Extreme Unction? — We should receive the Sacrament of Extreme Unction in the state of grace, and with lively faith and resignation to the will of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 277
277. Who is the minister of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction? — The priest is the minister of the Sacrament of Extreme Unction.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 278

278. What is the Sacrament of Holy Orders? — Holy Orders is a Sacrament by which bishops, priests, and other ministers of the Church are ordained and receive the power and grace to perform their sacred duties.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 279

279. What is necessary to receive Holy Orders worthily? — To receive Holy Orders worthily it is necessary to be in the state of grace, to have the necessary knowledge and a divine call to this sacred office.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 280
280. How should Christians look upon the priests of the Church? — Christians should look upon the priests of the Church as the messengers of God and the dispensers of His mysteries.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 25. On Extreme Unction and Holy Orders · Q. 281
281. Who can confer the Sacrament of Holy Orders? — Bishops can confer the Sacrament of Holy Orders.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 282
282. What is the Sacrament of Matrimony? — The Sacrament of Matrimony is the Sacrament which unites a Christian man and woman in lawful marriage.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 283

283. Can a Christian man and woman be united in lawful marriage in any other way than by the Sacrament of Matrimony? — A Christian man and woman cannot be united in lawful marriage in any other way than by the Sacrament of Matrimony, because Christ raised marriage to the dignity of a Sacrament.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 284
284. Can the bond of Christian marriage be dissolved by any human power? — The bond of Christian marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 285

285. Which are the effects of the Sacrament of Matrimony? — The effects of the Sacrament of Matrimony are: 1st, To sanctify the love of husband and wife; 2d, To give them grace to bear with each other's weaknesses; 3d, To enable them to bring up their children in the fear and love of God.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 286

286. To receive the Sacrament of matrimony worthily is it necessary to be in the state of grace? — To receive the Sacrament of Matrimony worthily it is necessary to be in the state of grace, and it is necessary also to comply with the laws of the Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 287

287. Who has the right to make laws concerning the Sacrament of marriage? — The Church alone has the right to make laws concerning the Sacrament of marriage, though the state also has the right to make laws concerning the civil effects of the marriage contract.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 288

288. Does the Church forbid the marriage of Catholics with persons who have a different religion or no religion at all? — The Church does forbid the marriage of Catholics with persons who have a different religion or no religion at all.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 289

289. Why does the Church forbid the marriage of Catholics with persons who have a different religion or no religion at all? — The Church forbids the marriage of Catholics with persons who have a different religion or no religion at all, because such marriages generally lead to indifference, loss of faith, and to the neglect of the religious education of the children.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 290
290. Why do many marriages prove unhappy? — Many marriages prove unhappy because they are entered into hastily and without worthy motives.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 26. On Matrimony · Q. 291

291. How should Christians prepare for a holy and happy marriage? — Christians should prepare for a holy and happy marriage by receiving the Sacraments of Penance and Holy Eucharist; by begging God to grant them a pure intention and to direct their choice; and by seeking the advice of their parents and the blessing of their pastors.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 292

292. What is a sacramental? — A sacramental is anything set apart or blessed by the Church to excite good thoughts and to increase devotion, and through these movements of the heart to remit venial sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 293

293. What is the difference between the Sacraments and the sacramentals? — The difference between the Sacraments and the sacramentals is: 1st, The Sacraments were instituted by Jesus Christ and the sacramentals were instituted by the Church; 2d, The Sacraments give grace of themselves when we place no obstacle in the way; the sacramentals excite in us pious dispositions, by means of which we may obtain grace.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 294
294. Which is the chief sacramental used in the Church? — The chief sacramental used in the Church is the sign of the Cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 295

295. How do we make the sign of the Cross? — We make the sign of the Cross by putting the right hand to the forehead, then on the breast, and then to the left and right shoulders, saying, In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 296
296. Why do we make the sign of the Cross? — We make the sign of the Cross to show that we are Christians and to profess our belief in the chief mysteries of our religion.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 297

297. How is the sign of the Cross a profession of faith in the chief mysteries of our religion? — The sign of the Cross is a profession of faith in the chief mysteries of our religion because it expresses the mysteries of the Unity and Trinity of God and of the Incarnation and death of our Lord.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 298

298. How does the sign of the Cross express the mystery of the Unity and Trinity of God? — The words, In the name, express the Unity of God; the words that follow, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, express the mystery of the Trinity.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 299

299. How does the sign of the Cross express the mystery of the Incarnation and death of our Lord? — The sign of the Cross expresses the mystery of the Incarnation by reminding us that the Son of God, having become man, suffered death on the cross.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 300
300. What other sacramental is in very frequent use? — Another sacramental in very frequent use is holy water.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 301
301. What is holy water? — Holy water is water blessed by the priest with solemn prayer to beg God's blessing on those who use it, and protection from the powers of darkness.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 27. On the Sacramentals · Q. 302

302. Are there other sacramentals besides the sign of the Cross and holy water? — Besides the sign of the Cross and holy water there are many other sacramentals, such as blessed candles, ashes, palms, crucifixes, images of the Blessed Virgin and of the saints, rosaries, and scapulars.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 303
303. Is there any other means of obtaining God's grace than the Sacraments? — There is another means of obtaining God's grace, and it is prayer.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 304

304. What is prayer? — Prayer is the lifting up of our minds and hearts to God to adore Him, to thank Him for His benefits, to ask His forgiveness, and to beg of Him all the graces we need whether for soul or body.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 305
305. Is prayer necessary to salvation? — Prayer is necessary to salvation, and without it no one having the use of reason can be saved.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 306
306. At what particular times should we pray? — We should pray particularly on Sundays and holydays, every morning and night, in all dangers, temptations, and afflictions.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 307

307. How should we pray? — We should pray: 1st, With attention; 2d, With a sense of our own helplessness and dependence upon God; 3d, With a great desire for the graces we beg of God; 4th, With trust in God's goodness; 5th, With perseverance.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 308

308. Which are the prayers most recommended to us? — The prayers most recommended to us are the Lord's Prayer, the Hail Mary, the Apostles' Creed, the Confiteor, and the Acts of Faith, Hope, Love, and Contrition.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 28. On Prayer · Q. 309
309. Are prayers said with distractions of any avail? — Prayers said with wilful distractions are of no avail.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 29. On the Commandments of God · Q. 310
310. Is it enough to belong to God's Church in order to be saved? — It is not enough to belong to the Church in order to be saved, but we must also keep the Commandments of God and of the Church.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 29. On the Commandments of God · Q. 311

311. Which are the Commandments that contain the whole law of God? — The Commandments which contain the whole law of God are these two: 1st, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, with thy whole soul, with thy whole strength, and with thy whole mind; 2d, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 29. On the Commandments of God · Q. 312

312. Why do these two Commandments of the love of God and of our neighbor contain the whole law of God? — These two Commandments of the love of God and of our neighbor contain the whole law of God because all the other Commandments are given either to help us to keep these two, or to direct us how to shun what is opposed to them.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 29. On the Commandments of God · Q. 313
313. Which are the Commandments of God? — The Commandments of God are these ten.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 29. On the Commandments of God · Q. 314
314. Who gave the Ten Commandments? — God Himself gave the Ten Commandments to Moses on Mount Sinai, and Christ our Lord confirmed them.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 315
315. What is the first Commandment? — The first Commandment is: I am the Lord thy God: thou shalt not have strange gods before Me.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 316

316. How does the first Commandment help us to keep the great Commandment of the love of God? — The first Commandment helps us to keep the great Commandment of the love of God because it commands us to adore God alone.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 317
317. How do we adore God? — We adore God by faith, hope, and charity, by prayer and sacrifice.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 318

318. How may the first Commandment be broken? — The first Commandment may be broken by giving to a creature the honor which belongs to God alone; by false worship; and by attributing to a creature a perfection which belongs to God alone.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 319

319. Do those who make use of spells and charms, or who believe in dreams, in mediums, spiritists, fortune-tellers, and the like, sin against the first Commandment? — Those who make use of spells and charms, or who believe in dreams, in mediums, spiritists, fortunetellers and the like, sin against the first Commandment, because they attribute to creatures perfections which belong to God alone.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 320
320. Are sins against faith, hope and charity also sins against the first Commandment? — Sins against faith, hope, and charity are also sins against the first Commandment.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 321

321. How does a person sin against faith? — A person sins against faith: 1st, by not trying to know what God has taught; 2d, by refusing to believe all that God has taught; 3d, by neglecting to profess his belief in what God has taught.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 322
322. How do we fail to try to know what God has taught? — We fail to try to know what God has taught by neglecting to learn the Christian doctrine.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 323
323. Who are they who do not believe all that God has taught? — They who do not believe all that God has taught are the heretics and infidels.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 324

324. Who are they who neglect to profess their belief in what God has taught? — They who neglect to profess their belief in what God has taught are all those who fail to acknowledge the true Church in which they really believe.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 325

325. Can they who fail to profess their faith in the true Church in which they believe expect to be saved while in that state? — They who fail to profess their faith in the true Church in which they believe cannot expect to be saved while in that state, for Christ has said: "Whoever shall deny Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father who is in heaven."
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 326

326. Are we obliged to make open profession of our faith? — We are obliged to make open profession of our faith as often as God's honor, our neighbor's spiritual good, or our own requires it. "Whosoever," says Christ, "shall confess Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father who is in heaven."
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 327
327. Which are the sins against hope? — The sins against hope are presumption and despair.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 328
328. What is presumption? — Presumption is a rash expectation of salvation without making proper use of the necessary means to obtain it.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 329
329. What is despair? — Despair is the loss of hope in God's mercy.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 30. On the First Commandment · Q. 330
330. How do we sin against the love of God? — We sin against the love of God by all sin, but particularly by mortal sin.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 331

331. Does the first Commandment forbid the honoring of the saints? — The first Commandment does not forbid the honoring of the saints, but rather approves of it; because by honoring the saints, who are the chosen friends of God, we honor God Himself.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 332
332. Does the first Commandment forbid us to pray to the saints? — The first Commandment does not forbid us to pray to the saints.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 333
333. What do we mean by praying to the saints? — By praying to the saints we mean the asking of their help and prayers.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 334
334. How do we know that the saints hear us? — We know that the saints hear us, because they are with God, who makes our prayers known to them.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 335
335. Why do we believe that the saints will help us? — We believe that the saints will help us because both they and we are members of the same Church, and they love us as their brethren.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 336

336. How are the saints and we members of the same Church? — The saints and we are members of the same Church, because the Church in heaven and the Church on earth are one and the same Church, and all its members are in communion with one another.
The Baltimore Catechism · Lesson 31. The First Commandment--on the Honor and Invocation of Saints · Q. 337
337. What is the communion of the members of the Church called? — The communion of the members of the Church is called the communion of saints.
