‘Who are you, Lord?’ was Paul’s first prayer as a Christian. Ask it today, and let Christ answer.

Two of Saint Paul’s closest companions, to whom he wrote the letters that bear their names. Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, travelled with Paul for years and was left in charge of the church at Ephesus. Titus, a Gentile convert, was sent to Corinth to make peace and then to Crete to organise the young Church there. Tradition counts them the first bishops of those places.

Paul met Timothy at Lystra, where the young man’s mother Eunice and grandmother Lois had taught him the Scriptures from childhood. Paul called him his beloved son and fellow worker, and sent him on difficult errands to Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi. In his letters Paul urges him not to let anyone despise his youth, to take a little wine for his frequent ailments, and to guard what has been entrusted to him. Tradition holds that Timothy was killed at Ephesus for protesting against a pagan festival. Titus was a Greek whom Paul took to the council at Jerusalem as a sign that Gentiles need not be circumcised. Sent to Corinth after Paul had written them a severe letter, he came back with good news, to Paul’s great comfort. Left in Crete to appoint elders in every town, he is said to have died there in old age. The letters to them still guide bishops and pastors.
Saints Timothy and Titus · Prayer to

Saints Timothy and Titus, you learned the faith from Paul and handed it on whole. Pray for our bishops and priests, that they may preach the word in season and out of season. Pray for parents and grandparents who teach the faith at home, and for me, that I may guard what has been entrusted to me. Amen.
Paul told Timothy to stir into flame the gift of God that was within him. What gift has God given you that is burning low?

An Italian laywoman who founded the Company of Saint Ursula, a community of consecrated women who lived in their own homes and served in the world, teaching girls the faith at a time when few girls were taught at all. Her company later grew into the Ursuline nuns, whose schools spread across Europe and the Americas.

Angela was born at Desenzano on Lake Garda and lost both parents while still a girl. She became a Franciscan tertiary and gave herself to prayer and to teaching the children of her neighbourhood. Tradition tells of a vision in which she saw a ladder reaching to heaven with young women climbing it, and understood that she was to found a community. She moved to Brescia, where she became known as a peacemaker and counsellor, and made pilgrimages to the Holy Land and to Rome. In 1535, with twenty-eight companions, she founded the Company of Saint Ursula, under the patronage of the virgin martyr. Its members took no vows of enclosure and wore no habit; they lived with their families, prayed and taught girls. After her death the company was reshaped, and in many places it became an enclosed religious order, the Ursulines. She was canonised in 1807.

Saint Angela, you saw that the Church needed women who would teach and serve in the middle of the world. Pray for teachers and all who form the young, for consecrated women, and for me, that I may live my faith at home and at work, and hand it on with patience and love. Amen.
Angela believed a woman could belong wholly to God without leaving her own home. Where in your daily surroundings is God asking you to belong to Him more completely?

A Dominican friar from southern Italy whose Summa Theologiae is the greatest synthesis of Catholic theology. He showed that faith and reason come from the same God and cannot finally contradict each other. He wrote the hymns of Corpus Christi, among them the Pange Lingua and Tantum Ergo. He is called the Angelic Doctor and is patron of Catholic schools and universities.

Thomas was born at Roccasecca, near Aquino, into a noble family who sent him at five to the abbey of Monte Cassino, hoping he would one day be its abbot. At Naples he met the new Order of Preachers and joined it. His family seized him on the road and kept him at home for a year, but he would not be moved. He studied under Saint Albert the Great at Cologne, where his silence earned him the name of the dumb ox; Albert replied that this ox would one day bellow so loud that the whole world would hear. He taught at Paris, Rome and Naples and wrote with astonishing speed. In December 1273, after an experience at Mass, he stopped writing, leaving the Summa unfinished. Summoned to the Council of Lyon, he fell ill on the way and died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova on 7 March 1274. Today’s date marks the translation of his relics to Toulouse.

Saint Thomas, you used every gift of mind in the service of truth and knelt in wonder before the Eucharist. Pray for students, teachers and all who seek the truth, that they may find it in Christ. Pray for me, that I may love God with all my mind, think clearly and stay humble before the mystery. Amen.
Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore, masked by these bare shadows, shape and nothing more, see, Lord, at thy service low lies here a heart lost, all lost in wonder at the God thou art.
At the end he said that all he had written seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. Of all you are busy with, what will matter in the end?

A Roman virgin and martyr honoured in the city since early times. Her story, written long after her death, tells that she was the daughter of a consul and was tortured and beheaded for refusing to worship the gods. Her relics were rediscovered in 1634 in an ancient church beside the Forum, and she has long been counted among the patron saints of Rome.

Almost nothing about Martina can be known with certainty except that the Roman Church honoured her as a martyr. Her legendary acts place her death in the reign of Alexander Severus in the third century, and describe a young noblewoman who gave her wealth to the poor and endured many torments before she was beheaded. A church dedicated to her stood beside the Forum from at least the seventh century. In 1634, during work on the building, her remains were found, and Pope Urban VIII, who was devoted to her, had the church rebuilt by the painter and architect Pietro da Cortona, who spent his own money on her crypt and was later buried there. Urban also wrote the hymns for her feast in the Breviary. The church of Santi Luca e Martina still stands near the Arch of Septimius Severus. Whatever its details, her story speaks for the many young Christians of Rome who chose Christ over life.

Saint Martina, faithful daughter of the Church of Rome, you loved Christ more than wealth, comfort or life itself. Pray for all who suffer for their faith today, for the city of Rome and its bishop, and for me, that I may hold lightly to the things of this world and hold fast to Christ. Amen.

O God, Who among the other miracles of thy power have bestowed the victory of martyrdom even upon the weaker sex, graciously grant that we who commemorate the anniversary of the death of blessed N., thy Virgin and Martyr, may come to thee by the path of her example. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Her name survived when the details of her life were lost, because she belonged to Christ. What in your life will last when everything else is forgotten?

A priest of Turin who gave his life to poor and abandoned boys in the growing industrial city. He gathered them in his oratory, taught them trades, fed and housed them, and led them to Christ with cheerfulness rather than fear. He founded the Salesians, named after Saint Francis de Sales, and with Saint Mary Mazzarello the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians.

John was born near Castelnuovo in Piedmont and lost his father at the age of two. His mother, Margaret, raised him in poverty and deep faith. At nine he dreamed that a gentle lady showed him a pack of wild animals turning into lambs, and told him that this would be his work. As a boy he juggled and did tricks to draw other children, then repeated the Sunday sermon to them. Ordained in 1841, he found Turin full of boys living on the streets or in prison. He gathered them on Sundays, and in time built a home, workshops and schools at Valdocco, where his mother came to cook and mend. His method, he said, rested on reason, religion and loving kindness. Among his pupils was Saint Dominic Savio. He founded the Salesian Society in 1859, built the basilica of Mary Help of Christians and sent missionaries to South America. He was canonised on Easter Sunday 1934.

Saint John Bosco, father and teacher of the young, you won hearts with kindness and led them to Christ through joy. Pray for children and young people, especially those who are poor, lost or alone. Pray for parents and teachers, and for me, that I may be patient, cheerful and generous with all whom God puts in my care. Amen.
Don Bosco said that it is not enough to love the young: they must know that they are loved. Who in your life needs to know that they are loved?
The Presentation of the Lord · Life

Forty days after His birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the Temple in Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord, as the Law of Moses required. There the old man Simeon took Him in his arms and greeted Him as the light of the nations, and the prophetess Anna spoke of Him to all who were waiting. Candles are blessed today, and the feast is called Candlemas.
The Presentation of the Lord · Life

The Law required that a firstborn son be offered to God and redeemed, and that a mother be purified after childbirth. Mary and Joseph, too poor to offer a lamb, brought a pair of turtle doves or two young pigeons. Saint Luke tells that Simeon, a just and devout man, had been promised that he would not die before seeing the Christ. Taking the child, he blessed God in the words of the Nunc Dimittis, sung each night at Compline, and warned Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul. The feast was kept in Jerusalem by the fourth century and in Rome by the seventh. The blessing of candles and the procession recall Christ the light entering His temple. In England, Candlemas was long one of the great days of the year. Since 1997 it has also been the World Day for Consecrated Life, for all who, like the child Jesus, are offered to God.
The Presentation of the Lord · Prayer to

Lord Jesus, light of the nations, you were carried into your Temple in your mother’s arms and received by the faithful who had waited for you. Let me wait for you as Simeon did, welcome you as Anna did, and offer myself to the Father with you. Let me depart in peace when my eyes have seen your salvation. Amen.
The Presentation of the Lord · Prayer

Almighty, eternal God, we humbly beseech Your majesty that, as Your only-begotten Son was this day presented in the temple in the nature of our flesh, so may You grant us to be presented to You with purified minds. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Presentation of the Lord · Meditation
Simeon waited his whole life and was not disappointed. What are you waiting for from God, and will you go on waiting in hope?

A bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, now Sivas in Turkey, martyred in the early fourth century. Tradition says that on the way to his death he saved a boy who was choking on a fish bone, and so on his feast the Church blesses throats with two crossed candles. He is one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, the saints popularly invoked in particular needs.

Almost all we know of Blaise comes from his legend, written centuries later, though his cult is ancient in both East and West. The story tells of a physician who became bishop of Sebaste and, when persecution came under the emperor Licinius, withdrew to a cave in the hills, where wild animals came to him to be healed. Hunters found him and he was taken to the governor. On the way a mother brought her son, choking on a fish bone, and Blaise prayed over him and he recovered. A poor woman whose pig had been carried off by a wolf had it returned at his word, and she later brought candles to his prison. He was torn with iron combs, like those used to card wool, and beheaded. Wool combers took him as their patron, and in the wool towns of Yorkshire his day was once kept with processions. The blessing of throats keeps his memory alive in parishes everywhere.

Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, you cared for the sick and brought healing even on the road to your death. Pray for all who are ill, especially those with diseases of the throat. Guard my speech, that it may give praise to God and do no harm to others, and pray that I may be delivered from every evil of body and soul. Amen.
Yesterday’s candles are often used for today’s blessing. Ask God to bless not only your throat but every word that passes through it.

A young Florentine of noble family whose wild youth ended when his mother told him that, before his birth, she had offered him to God and Our Lady. He became a Carmelite friar and later, much against his will, bishop of Fiesole, where he was known for his care of the poor, his gift as a peacemaker and his hidden penances.

Andrew was born into the powerful Corsini family. Tradition says that his mother dreamed she had given birth to a wolf that ran into a Carmelite church and became a lamb. As a young man he fell in with bad company, until his mother told him of her dream and her vow; he went to the Carmelite church to pray, and stayed. He was professed as a friar, studied abroad, and became a preacher and prior in Florence and Tuscany. When he was chosen as bishop of Fiesole he hid, the story goes, until he was found and persuaded to accept. As bishop he kept his religious rule, visited the poor, slept little and gave away his income. Pope Urban V sent him to make peace between warring factions at Bologna, and he succeeded. He died on the feast of the Epiphany and was canonised in 1629. A chapel in the Lateran basilica is dedicated to him.

Saint Andrew, your mother’s prayers brought you home, and God made a lamb of you. Pray for all mothers who weep for their children, and for young people who have lost their way. Pray for me, that I may turn back to God whenever I wander, and become a peacemaker where there is division. Amen.

O God, Who establish ever new examples of virtue in Your Church, grant that Your people may follow the footsteps of blessed Andrew, Your Confessor and Bishop, so that they may also obtain his reward. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
A mother’s faith turned a wolf into a lamb. For whom are you praying, and will you keep praying however long it takes?

A young Christian of Catania in Sicily who had consecrated her virginity to God and was martyred in the persecution of Decius around 251. Her cult spread quickly through the Church, and her name is said in the Roman Canon. She is patron of Catania and of Malta, and is invoked against fire, the eruptions of Mount Etna and diseases of the breast.

Agatha’s story, written down some time after her death, tells of a girl of good family who refused the advances of the governor Quintianus. He handed her over to a woman who kept a brothel, hoping to break her will, but she remained steadfast. She was then imprisoned and cruelly tortured, and her breasts were cut off. Tradition holds that Saint Peter appeared to her in prison and healed her wounds. She died after further torments, praying to Christ who had given her strength. A year after her death, the story goes, Mount Etna erupted, and the people of Catania carried her veil before the lava, which stopped. Saint Gregory the Great dedicated a church to her in Rome that had been taken from the Arians. In paintings she carries her breasts on a dish, and in Sicily small cakes in that shape are still made for her feast.

Saint Agatha, bride of Christ, you kept faith through cruelty and shame, and the Lord healed and crowned you. Pray for all women who are abused or exploited, for those who suffer from cancer, and for me, that I may stand firm in trial and trust Christ to heal what has been wounded. Amen.

O God, Who among the other miracles of thy power have bestowed the victory of martyrdom even upon the weaker sex, graciously grant that we who commemorate the anniversary of the death of blessed Agatha, thy Virgin and Martyr, may come to thee by the path of her example. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Agatha found strength in Christ when everything was taken from her. What do you have left when your own strength runs out?
Saint Paul Miki and Companions · Life

Twenty-six Catholics crucified on a hill outside Nagasaki on 5 February 1597, under the regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi. They included three Japanese Jesuits, six Franciscan friars from Spain, Mexico and India, and seventeen Japanese laymen, among them catechists, craftsmen and three boys. Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit and a gifted preacher, preached his last sermon from the cross and forgave his executioners.
Saint Paul Miki and Companions · Life

Christianity had come to Japan with Saint Francis Xavier in 1549 and spread widely, but by the 1590s Hideyoshi had come to fear it. In December 1596 he ordered the arrest of friars and Christians in Kyoto and Osaka. Each had part of an ear cut off, and they were marched hundreds of miles through the winter to Nagasaki as a warning to others. Paul Miki, born around 1564 into a well-to-do family and educated by the Jesuits, was close to ordination. On the cross he told the crowd that he was Japanese and a Christian, and that he forgave the regent and all who had caused his death. The martyrs sang psalms and encouraged one another until they were killed with lances. Persecution followed for more than two centuries, yet when missionaries returned in the 1860s they found hidden Christians who had kept the faith in secret. The martyrs were canonised in 1862.
Saint Paul Miki and Companions · Prayer to

Saint Paul Miki and holy martyrs of Japan, you sang and forgave as you died on your crosses. Pray for the Church in Japan and for Christians who suffer for their faith today. Pray for me, that I may never be ashamed of Christ, and that I may forgive those who wrong me as freely as you forgave. Amen.
Saint Paul Miki and Companions · Meditation
From the cross Paul Miki prayed for the men who had condemned him. Is there anyone you would find it impossible to pray for?

Kidnapped as a child in Darfur and sold into slavery, she suffered years of cruelty before being brought to Italy, where she came to know Christ through the Canossian Sisters. Declared free by an Italian court, she was baptised, entered their order and spent some fifty years in quiet service. She is patron of Sudan and of the victims of human trafficking.

Born in Darfur around 1869, she was seized by slave traders at about the age of eight. The shock was such that she forgot her own name, and her captors called her Bakhita, which means fortunate. She was bought and sold several times and treated with great cruelty; one owner had her body cut with scores of patterns and rubbed with salt. Eventually an Italian consul bought her in Khartoum and took her to Italy, where she became nanny to a family near Venice. Left in the care of the Canossian Sisters, she came to know the God she had sensed as a child. When her mistress wished to take her back to Africa she refused, and in 1889 an Italian court ruled that she was free. She was baptised Josephine in 1890 and professed as a Canossian in 1896. At Schio she served as cook, sacristan and doorkeeper, much loved by all. She died in 1947 and was canonised in 2000.

Saint Josephine Bakhita, you were enslaved and wounded, and in Christ you found the Master who loved you and set you free. Pray for all who are trafficked, enslaved or exploited, and for those who work to free them. Pray for me, that I may know I am loved by God and forgive as you forgave. Amen.
Benedict XVI wrote that Bakhita came to know she was definitively loved, and that whatever happened, this Love was waiting for her. Do you believe that about yourself?

Patriarch of Alexandria for over thirty years and one of the great theologians of the Incarnation. When Nestorius of Constantinople taught that Mary should not be called Mother of God, Cyril defended the truth that Christ is one divine Person, and presided at the Council of Ephesus in 431, which upheld the title Theotokos. Leo XIII named him a Doctor of the Church.

Cyril succeeded his uncle Theophilus as patriarch of Alexandria in 412. His early years were marked by fierce conflict in a turbulent city, and his methods were sometimes harsh; the Church honours him for his teaching and his holiness, not for every act of his life. From 428 he gave himself to the question raised by Nestorius. If Mary is only the mother of the man Jesus, Cyril argued, then the one who was born, suffered and died for us is not truly God, and we are not saved. He wrote to Nestorius, to Rome and to the emperor, and Pope Celestine entrusted him with the case. At Ephesus in 431 the council deposed Nestorius and proclaimed Mary Mother of God, to the joy of the people. In 433 Cyril reached agreement with the bishops of Antioch, who had opposed him. His commentaries on Scripture are still read.
Saint Cyril of Alexandria · Prayer to

Saint Cyril, you fought for the truth that the Child of Mary is God made man. Pray for theologians and teachers, that they may serve the faith humbly and well. Pray for me, that I may honour Mary as Mother of God, worship her Son in spirit and truth, and defend the faith with charity as well as zeal. Amen.

O God, Who made Cyril, Your Confessor and Bishop, an unconquerable champion of the most Blessed Virgin Mary’s divine motherhood, grant that we who believe that she is truly the Mother of God may be saved by her motherly protection. Through the same Christ our Lord…
Cyril saw that everything depends on who Christ is. If someone asked you today who Jesus is, what would you say?

The sister, and by tradition the twin, of Saint Benedict, she consecrated herself to God from childhood and led a community of women near Monte Cassino. All we know of her comes from Saint Gregory the Great, who tells of her last meeting with her brother, when her prayer won a storm that kept him with her through the night. She is patron of Benedictine nuns.

Gregory tells that Scholastica and Benedict met once a year at a house near the monastery, since she could not enter it. At their last meeting they spent the day in praise of God and holy conversation. As night fell she begged him to stay and talk until morning about the joys of heaven. Benedict refused, since his rule forbade a monk to spend a night away. Scholastica laid her head on her hands in prayer, and at once a storm broke so violently that he could not leave. ‘What have you done?’ he asked. She answered that she had asked him and he would not listen, so she had asked God, and God had listened. They talked until dawn. Three days later Benedict saw her soul rise to heaven in the form of a dove, and he buried her in the tomb he had prepared for himself. Gregory says she could do more because she loved more.

Saint Scholastica, you loved God and your brother so much that heaven answered your prayer. Pray for brothers and sisters, for families divided by distance or quarrels, and for all Benedictine monks and nuns. Pray for me, that I may love more, pray with confidence and long for the joys of heaven. Amen.
She could do more, Gregory said, because she loved more. Where would a little more love change what you are able to do?

On 11 February 1858 a lady in white appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, a poor girl of fourteen, at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes in the Pyrenees. In eighteen appearances she asked for prayer and penance, and on 25 March named herself: ‘I am the Immaculate Conception.’ The Church approved the apparitions in 1862, and Lourdes became one of the great places of pilgrimage, especially for the sick.

Bernadette’s family were so poor that they lived in a former jail. She was gathering firewood with her sister and a friend when she saw the lady in a hollow of the rock. In the following weeks crowds came with her, though only she saw the lady. On 25 February, told to drink at the spring, she scraped at the muddy ground until water came; the spring has flowed ever since, and of the many cures reported there the Church has recognised a small number as miraculous after strict medical examination. Questioned again and again by clergy and officials, Bernadette never changed her account. She did not know what the words Immaculate Conception meant, but they convinced her parish priest. In 1862 the bishop of Tarbes declared that the faithful were justified in believing. Lourdes is approved private revelation:
Catholics are not bound to believe it, but the Church finds in it nothing contrary to faith.
Our Lady of Lourdes · Prayer to

Our Lady of Lourdes, you came to a poor and sickly girl and called the world to prayer and penance. Pray for all the sick, for those who care for them, and for all who come to you on pilgrimage. Pray for me, that I may come to the spring of grace your Son has opened, and be healed in body and soul as He wills. Amen.
The lady told Bernadette that she did not promise to make her happy in this world, but in the next. What are you asking of God that He may wish to give in another way?

Two brothers from Thessalonica in Greece who carried the Gospel to the Slav peoples of central Europe. They devised an alphabet for the Slavonic language, translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into it, and won the Pope’s approval for worship in the people’s own tongue. In 1980 Saint John Paul II named them patrons of Europe alongside Saint Benedict.

Constantine, later called Cyril, was a brilliant scholar and teacher at Constantinople; his elder brother Methodius had been a governor before becoming a monk. In 863 Prince Rastislav of Moravia asked the emperor for teachers who could instruct his people in their own language, and the brothers were sent. Cyril created the Glagolitic alphabet, from which the later Cyrillic script, named in his honour, developed. Their use of Slavonic in the liturgy was attacked by Frankish clergy, so they went to Rome, where Pope Adrian II received them warmly and approved their books. Cyril became a monk there and died in 869; he is buried in the basilica of San Clemente. Methodius, consecrated archbishop, returned to the Slavs. He was imprisoned for over two years by bishops who opposed him, freed at the Pope’s command, and worked on until his death in 885.
The Slav churches of East and West venerate them as their apostles.
Saints Cyril and Methodius · Prayer to

Saints Cyril and Methodius, apostles of the Slavs, you gave the Gospel to a people in their own words and suffered for it with patience. Pray for Europe, that it may remember its Christian roots. Pray for the unity of East and West, for missionaries and translators, and for me, that I may speak of Christ in words others can understand. Amen.
The brothers believed every people should be able to praise God in its own tongue. How could you speak of your faith in words your neighbours would understand?
The Seven Holy Founders of the Servite Order · Life

Seven men of Florence, members of a confraternity devoted to Our Lady, who left their homes and businesses in 1233 to live together in poverty and prayer. They withdrew to Monte Senario outside the city and founded the Order of the Servants of Mary, the Servites, known for their devotion to the Seven Sorrows of Our Lady. They were canonised together in 1888.
The Seven Holy Founders of the Servite Order · Life

Thirteenth-century Florence was rich, busy and torn by faction. The seven, most of them merchants and some married or widowed, met in a lay confraternity devoted to the Virgin. Servite tradition holds that on the feast of the Assumption in 1233 Our Lady inspired them to leave the world. Having provided for their families, they lived together in a poor house outside the walls, then moved to the solitude of Monte Senario, where they lived in great austerity. People came to them for guidance, and they began to accept disciples. Adopting the Rule of Saint Augustine, they became an order of friars, preaching and serving in the towns, and received the final approval of the Holy See in 1304. In religion they were named Bonfilius, Alexis, Manettus, Amideus, Hugh, Sostenes and Buonagiunta. Alexis Falconieri, the last of them, lived to a great age and died on this day in 1310.
The Seven Holy Founders of the Servite Order · Prayer to

Holy Founders, you left the riches of Florence to stand with Mary beneath the cross of her Son. Pray for all who serve her, for the Servite friars and sisters, and for me, that I may share her sorrows with love, leave behind whatever keeps me from God, and find true brotherhood in Christ. Amen.
The Seven Holy Founders of the Servite Order · Meditation
Seven busy men left their counting houses to stand with Mary at the foot of the cross. What would you need to leave to stand there with her?
The Chair of Saint Peter · Life

A feast not of a piece of furniture but of the mission Christ gave to Peter: ‘You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church.’ The chair, or cathedra, is the sign of a bishop’s authority to teach. The Church honours the ministry of Peter and his successors, the bishops of Rome, as the visible foundation of its unity in faith and charity.
The Chair of Saint Peter · Life

The feast is among the oldest in the Roman calendar. A list of Roman feasts from the year 354 already marks 22 February as the day of Peter’s chair. It may have begun as a Christian answer to the pagan custom of feasting for dead relatives at this time of year. For centuries Rome kept two feasts, one on 18 January for Peter’s chair at Rome and one today for his chair at Antioch, where he was held to have first presided; in 1960 they were joined. In Saint Peter’s Basilica, Bernini’s great bronze throne, borne up by four Doctors of the Church, encloses an ancient wooden chair long venerated as Peter’s. Above it a window of golden alabaster shows the Holy Spirit as a dove. It is a day to pray for the Pope and for the Church of Rome, which, in the words of Saint Ignatius of Antioch, presides in love.
The Chair of Saint Peter · Prayer to

Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, the Lord made you the rock of His Church and prayed that your faith would not fail. Pray for our Holy Father the Pope, that he may strengthen his brothers in the faith. Pray for the unity of the Church, and for me, that after every failure I may turn back, as you did, and strengthen others. Amen.
The Chair of Saint Peter · Prayer

O God, who together with the keys of the kingdom of heaven didst bestow on thy blessed Apostle Peter the pontifical power of binding and loosing, grant that by the aid of this intercession, we may be released from the bonds of our sins. Who livest…
The Chair of Saint Peter · Meditation
Christ built His Church on a man who had denied Him three times. What does that tell you about what He can build on you?

Bishop of Smyrna, in what is now Turkey, and a disciple of the apostle John. He received a letter from Saint Ignatius of Antioch, who was on his way to martyrdom, and long afterwards was martyred himself, burned at the stake in old age. The account of his death, written by his own church, is the oldest record of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament.

Saint Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp as a boy, remembered him speaking of his conversations with John and others who had seen the Lord. As bishop he guarded the faith against those who twisted it, and his letter to the Philippians, full of the words of the apostles, survives. In old age he travelled to Rome to discuss the date of Easter with Pope Anicetus; they did not agree, but they parted in peace, and Anicetus invited him to celebrate the Eucharist. When persecution broke out in Smyrna, Polycarp was found at a farm outside the city. He ordered food for those who came to arrest him and asked for time to pray. In the stadium the proconsul urged him to curse Christ. He replied that he had served Christ for eighty-six years and Christ had done him no wrong: how could he blaspheme his King who had saved him?
The account says the flames formed an arch around him, and he was killed with a dagger.

Saint Polycarp, you heard the apostles and kept their teaching whole to the end. Pray for bishops, for the elderly who keep the faith alive, and for the unity of Christians. Pray for me, that I may stay faithful to Christ all my days and, when my hour comes, offer my life to Him in thanksgiving. Amen.
Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He has done me no wrong. Look back over your own life today and count the ways Christ has been faithful to you.

A prince of Poland and Lithuania, son of King Casimir IV, who lived at the heart of a powerful court as quietly as a monk. He prayed through the night, gave freely to the poor, loved Our Lady and refused a royal marriage to remain chaste. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-five and is the patron of Lithuania.

Casimir was the second son of Casimir IV Jagiellon and Elizabeth of Austria, and was taught by the historian Jan Długosz. In 1471, at thirteen, his father sent him with an army to take the crown of Hungary, offered by nobles opposed to King Matthias Corvinus. The venture failed and Casimir came home, and he seems never to have wanted a throne again. For a time he governed Poland while his father was in Lithuania, and he was known for fairness and for his care of the poor. He slept little, often praying at church doors before they opened, and was said to wear a hair shirt beneath his fine clothes. He declined a proposed marriage to a daughter of the Emperor. He died at Grodno on 4 March 1484 and was buried in Vilnius Cathedral, by tradition with a copy of the Marian hymn Omni die dic Mariae, which he loved.

Saint Casimir, you lived among wealth and power and kept your heart for God alone. Teach me to use what I have for the poor, to guard my purity, and to love the Mother of God with a simple and faithful love. Pray for Lithuania and Poland, and for all who carry responsibility for others. Amen.
He had every comfort a court could give and chose to kneel at the church door before dawn. What comfort keeps you from prayer?

Two young mothers martyred together in the amphitheatre at Carthage: Perpetua, a well-born woman of twenty-two nursing her baby son, and Felicity, a slave who gave birth in prison days before she died. Perpetua kept a prison diary, one of the earliest writings we have by a Christian woman. Both are named in the Roman Canon.

In 203, under the Emperor Septimius Severus, a group of catechumens was arrested at Carthage: Perpetua, the slaves Felicity and Revocatus, Saturninus and Secundulus, and later their teacher Saturus, who gave himself up to share their fate. They were baptised while under guard. Perpetua’s father, a pagan, came again and again to beg her to sacrifice for the sake of her child. She pointed to a water jug and asked whether it could be called anything but what it was; nor, she said, could she be called anything but a Christian. In prison she recorded visions, among them a narrow ladder to heaven guarded by a serpent. Felicity, eight months pregnant, feared she would be left behind, since the law forbade the execution of pregnant women; she gave birth to a daughter, who was taken in by a Christian woman.
On 7 March they were sent into the arena with wild beasts and then put to the sword, giving each other the kiss of peace.
Saints Perpetua and Felicity · Prayer to

Saints Perpetua and Felicity, noblewoman and slave, you went into the arena side by side, sisters in Christ. Pray for mothers and their children, for all who suffer for the faith, and for me, that I may never be ashamed to be called what I am, a Christian. Amen.
Could this jug be called by any other name? So I cannot be called anything but what I am, a Christian. Where are you tempted to answer to another name?

A Portuguese shepherd, soldier and bookseller who, moved to tears by a sermon of Saint John of Ávila, gave everything away and was locked up as a madman. He came out to found a hospital for the sick poor of Granada, and his followers became the Brothers Hospitallers. He is a patron of hospitals, nurses and the sick.

João Cidade left his home at Montemor-o-Novo as a boy of eight and grew up in Spain, working as a shepherd near Oropesa. He served as a soldier, fought against the Turks at Vienna, and wandered for years, working in North Africa and then selling books in Gibraltar and Granada. In Granada, around 1537, he heard John of Ávila preach and was so overcome with sorrow for his sins that he tore up his books and ran through the streets crying for mercy. He was put in the Royal Hospital among the insane, and saw how the sick were treated there. John of Ávila steered his zeal toward service. He rented a house, carried the sick to it on his back, and begged for them at night, calling out, ‘Do good, brothers, to yourselves.’ He died on 8 March 1550, weakened after trying to save a drowning man.
Saint John of God · Prayer to

Saint John of God, you were thought a fool for Christ and became a father to the sick and the forgotten. Pray for the sick, for those with troubled minds, and for all who nurse them. Give me eyes to see the suffering I would rather pass by, and hands ready to help. Amen.
Do good, brothers, to yourselves. Whatever you give to the poor, he taught, you give to your own soul. Whom will you do good to today?

A Roman noblewoman who wanted to be a nun but was married at twelve, and became a saint as wife, mother and widow. Through plague, war and the deaths of two of her children she nursed the sick and fed the poor of Rome. She founded the Oblates of Tor de’ Specchi and is said to have seen her guardian angel.

Francesca Bussa de’ Leoni was married to Lorenzo Ponziani, of a rich Roman family, and lived with her husband for forty years in deep affection. With her sister-in-law Vannozza she visited hospitals, nursed the sick and gave away food from the family stores, to the anger of her father-in-law until, tradition says, the granary was found full again. Rome was torn by the Great Schism and occupied by the troops of Ladislas of Naples; the Ponziani lost their property, Lorenzo was wounded and their son Battista was taken hostage. Two of her children died in plague years. In 1425 she founded a community of women living under the Benedictine Olivetans, without enclosure, serving the poor of the city. When Lorenzo died in 1436 she joined them as superior. She is the patron of motorists, from the tradition that her angel lit her way at night.
Saint Frances of Rome · Prayer to

Saint Frances, you sought God in the chapel and found Him also in the kitchen, the sickroom and the streets of Rome. Pray for wives, mothers and widows, for families in hardship, and for me, that I may serve God faithfully in the duties of my state of life. Amen.
She was often called away from prayer by her family, and tradition says that once she came back to find the page she had left written in gold. Which interruption today is God’s?

A Briton taken as a slave to Ireland at sixteen, who escaped, became a priest and went back to the people who had enslaved him. As bishop he preached through much of Ireland, baptised thousands and ordained clergy. His own Confession, written in plain, humble Latin, tells his story. He is the patron of Ireland.

Patrick was born in Roman Britain, the son of a deacon, Calpurnius, and grandson of a priest. He tells us that he did not know the true God when Irish raiders carried him off. For six years he herded animals, and in hunger and cold he began to pray, up to a hundred times a day and as often at night. A voice in a dream told him a ship was ready, and he walked some two hundred miles to find it. Home again, he dreamed of a man bringing letters, ‘the voice of the Irish’, begging him to come and walk among them once more. He was trained and ordained, and returned as a bishop. In his Letter to Coroticus he condemned a British chieftain whose men had killed and enslaved newly baptised converts. The shamrock and the banished snakes are later legend; the Confession shows a man astonished at God’s mercy.

Saint Patrick, you forgave those who enslaved you and brought them the faith. Pray for Ireland and her people throughout the world, for all held in slavery today, and for me, that Christ may be before me, behind me and within me, and that I may never be ashamed of Him. Amen.

Christ be with me, Christ within me, Christ behind me, Christ before me, Christ beside me, Christ to win me, Christ to comfort and restore me. Christ beneath me, Christ above me, Christ in quiet, Christ in danger, Christ in hearts of all that love me, Christ in mouth of friend and stranger.
I, Patrick, a sinner, the most unlearned of men, so his Confession begins. He knew he had been found by mercy. Can you begin your own story the same way?

Bishop of Jerusalem in the stormy years after the Council of Nicaea, three times driven into exile. His Catechetical Lectures, given to those preparing for baptism at Easter, are a priceless picture of how the early Church taught the Creed and the sacraments. Leo XIII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1883.

Cyril was probably born in or near Jerusalem and was ordained priest there. Around 350 he gave his famous lectures in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built by Constantine over the place of the crucifixion and resurrection: a series on the Creed for those to be baptised at Easter, and a further set, which bear his name, on the mysteries of baptism, chrism and the Eucharist for the newly baptised. He became bishop soon after. Caught up in the Arian controversy and in a rivalry with Acacius of Caesarea, he was exiled three times, once on the charge of selling church treasures to feed the poor in a famine. In all he spent some sixteen years away from his see. He took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381, which confirmed the faith of Nicaea and his own orthodoxy, and died in Jerusalem in 386.
Saint Cyril of Jerusalem · Prayer to

Saint Cyril, you taught the newly baptised to receive the Body of Christ as a king, with reverence and wonder. Pray for catechists and for all preparing to enter the Church this Easter. Help me to know the Creed I profess and to treasure the sacraments I receive. Amen.
The lectures that bear his name teach the communicant to make the left hand a throne for the right, since it is to receive a King. How do you approach Holy Communion?

The husband of the Virgin Mary and foster father of Jesus, a just man of the house of David. The Gospels record no word of his, only his obedience: four times God spoke to him in dreams and four times he rose and did as he was told. Pius IX declared him Patron of the Universal Church in 1870.

Joseph was a craftsman of Nazareth, a tekton, which may mean a carpenter or a builder. Betrothed to Mary, he found she was with child and, being a just man, resolved to divorce her quietly, until an angel told him in a dream to take her as his wife. He took the family to Bethlehem for the census, fled with them by night into Egypt, and brought them home to Nazareth. With Mary he searched three days for the boy Jesus and found Him in the Temple. He is not mentioned again in the public ministry, and tradition holds that he died before it, in the arms of Jesus and Mary, which is why he is the patron of a happy death. Saint Teresa of Ávila spread devotion to him, Leo XIII wrote an encyclical on him, and John XXIII added his name to the Roman Canon.

Saint Joseph, guardian of the Redeemer and husband of Mary, you protected the Holy Family in silence and obedience. Protect my family and the whole Church. Teach me to work honestly, to listen for God’s voice and to act on it, and be with me at the hour of my death. Amen.
Joseph says nothing in the Gospels. He rises and does what he is told. What has God already asked of you that you have not yet risen to do?
Saint John Baptist de La Salle · Life

A wealthy canon of Reims who gave up his position and his fortune to train teachers for the children of the poor. He founded the Brothers of the Christian Schools, taught in French rather than Latin, grouped pupils in classes and opened some of the first colleges for teachers. Pius XII named him patron of teachers.
Saint John Baptist de La Salle · Life

Jean-Baptiste de La Salle was the eldest son of a noble family of Reims, a canon of the cathedral at sixteen and a priest at twenty-seven. In 1679 he met Adrien Nyel, who wanted to open free schools for poor boys, and helped him find teachers. Seeing how unprepared they were, he took them into his own house to live and pray with him, to the dismay of his family. He resigned his canonry and, in the famine of 1684, gave away his inheritance to the hungry, so that he would stand with his teachers in poverty. From them grew the Brothers of the Christian Schools, religious who were not priests and gave their lives to teaching. He met fierce opposition, lawsuits from the writing masters and conflict within his own institute, and went through periods of deep discouragement. He died at Rouen on Good Friday, 7 April 1719.
Saint John Baptist de La Salle · Prayer to

Saint John Baptist de La Salle, you gave up wealth and honour so that poor children might learn and know God. Pray for teachers, for all who form the young, and for children who have no one to teach them. Help me to remember that I stand always in the holy presence of God. Amen.
Saint John Baptist de La Salle · Meditation
Every lesson in his schools began with the words: let us remember that we are in the holy presence of God. Where do you most forget it?

Bishop of Kraków who rebuked King Bolesław II for his cruelty and his sins, and was killed in 1079, by tradition at the king’s own hand while celebrating Mass. The facts of the quarrel are disputed by historians, but Poland has honoured him for centuries as a martyr for the moral law and as one of her patrons.

Stanislaus was born at Szczepanów in southern Poland, studied, perhaps at Gniezno, and was ordained priest. In 1072 he became bishop of Kraków. King Bolesław II, called the Bold, was a capable soldier and ruler, but the bishop came into conflict with him; the later chronicles speak of the king’s cruelty and immorality and of the bishop’s rebukes, ending in excommunication. Tradition holds that Bolesław, unable to find men willing to kill the bishop, struck him down himself in the church on the Skałka in Kraków. A popular legend tells that Stanislaus once raised a dead man, Piotrowin, to testify in a dispute over land. The king was driven into exile soon after. Stanislaus was canonised at Assisi in 1253, and his relics rest in Wawel Cathedral. John Paul II, his successor in Kraków, called him a patron of the moral order.

Saint Stanislaus, shepherd of Kraków, you spoke the truth to a king and paid for it with your life. Pray for bishops and for all who must correct the powerful. Give me courage to speak for what is right, gently and without fear, and to stand by the truth when it costs me. Amen.
He was killed, the tradition says, at the altar, in the middle of the Mass. Is there any truth you have kept quiet because speaking it would cost you?

A pope who defended the truth that Christ has a human will as well as a divine one, against the policy of the Emperor. Arrested in Rome, tried in Constantinople and exiled to the Crimea, he died there of hunger and ill-treatment in 655. He is the last pope honoured as a martyr.

Martin, born at Todi in Umbria, was a deacon of Rome and the pope’s representative at Constantinople before his election in 649. The Emperor had forbidden all debate on whether Christ had one will or two, hoping to silence a dispute that divided the East. Within months of his election Martin held a synod at the Lateran, with Saint Maximus the Confessor’s support, which taught that Christ, true God and true man, has both a divine and a human will, and condemned the imperial decree. In 653 the Emperor Constans II had him seized in the Lateran, sick in bed, and shipped to Constantinople. There he was imprisoned, tried for treason, publicly stripped and condemned to death, a sentence changed to exile at Cherson in the Crimea. His letters from exile speak of hunger and of feeling forgotten. He died there in 655.

Saint Martin, you would not trade the truth about Christ for the favour of an emperor. Pray for the Pope and for all who suffer for the faith in prison or exile. When I feel forgotten, help me to trust that God forgets no one, and to stay faithful to the end. Amen.
Hungry and forgotten in exile, he still commended his Church to God. Whom do you find it hardest to pray for?

An Italian who became abbot of Bec in Normandy and then Archbishop of Canterbury, Anselm was the greatest theologian of his age. He described his work as faith seeking understanding, and wrote the Proslogion and Why God Became Man. Twice exiled for defending the freedom of the Church, he was named a Doctor of the Church in 1720.

Born at Aosta, Anselm left home after a quarrel with his father and crossed the Alps to the abbey of Bec, drawn by the fame of its prior, Lanfranc. He became a monk there in 1060, then prior and abbot, and was loved as a gentle and patient teacher. At Bec he wrote the Monologion and the Proslogion, in which he speaks of God as that than which nothing greater can be thought. In 1093, during a visit to England, he was made Archbishop of Canterbury against his will, the crozier pressed into his closed hand. He clashed with William Rufus and then Henry I over the rights of the Church, and spent years in exile. At the Council of Bari in 1098 he defended the Western teaching on the Holy Spirit. In exile he finished Cur Deus Homo, on why God became man. He died at Canterbury on 21 April 1109.

Saint Anselm, you sought to understand what you believed, and to love what you understood. Pray for theologians, for students and for the Church in England. Teach me to seek God with my mind and my heart, and to find, in seeking Him, that He has already found me. Amen.

O God, who didst give blessed Anselm to be thy people’s minister in eternal salvation; grant, we pray, that we who have him for teacher of life here on earth, may also deserve now that he is in heaven, to have him for an advocate. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
I do not seek to understand in order to believe, he wrote, but I believe in order to understand. What do you believe that you would like to understand better?

Two early popes kept together on one day. Soter led the Roman Church around 166 to 175 and was known for its generosity to poorer churches. Caius governed it from 283 to 296, in the years of peace before the great persecution of Diocletian, and was buried in the catacomb of Callixtus. Both are honoured in tradition as martyrs.

Little is known of either pope, and the Church honours them for what is certain. Eusebius preserves part of a letter from Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, thanking Soter and the Roman Christians for the alms they sent to churches in need and to Christians condemned to the mines, a custom Dionysius says Rome had kept from the beginning; he adds that Soter wrote to Corinth like a father to his children. Caius, according to the Liber Pontificalis, came from Dalmatia, and later legend made him a relative of the Emperor Diocletian. His tomb was found in the catacomb of Callixtus in the nineteenth century, with part of his epitaph. Whether either man died a martyr is not known for certain; the old calendar honours them as such, and both lived and led their flock when to be a Christian, still more its bishop, was to live under threat.
Saints Soter and Caius · Prayer to

Saints Soter and Caius, shepherds of the Church of Rome, you cared for poor and distant churches and kept the faith in dangerous times. Pray for the Pope and the bishops, for Christians in need throughout the world, and for me, that I may be generous to those I will never meet. Amen.

Look forgivingly on thy flock, Eternal Shepherd, and keep it in thy constant protection, by the intercession of blessed Sotérem et Caium and Sotérem et Caium thy Martyrs and Sovereign Pontiffs, whom thou didst constitute Shepherds of the whole Church. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Dionysius thanked Soter for writing to them as a loving father writes to his children. Who needs a letter from you?

A soldier martyred at Lydda in Palestine, probably under Diocletian, and venerated across East and West from the earliest centuries. The story of the dragon came much later and is legend. Crusaders brought his cult home, Edward III placed the Order of the Garter under his protection, and he became the patron saint of England.

Almost nothing is known for certain of George’s life. His tomb at Lydda, the modern Lod, was a place of pilgrimage by the sixth century, and churches were dedicated to him throughout the Christian East. Pope Gelasius in 494 counted him among those whose names are rightly honoured but whose deeds are known only to God. The legend of the dragon, slain to save a princess and a town that then accepted baptism, was spread through the West by the Golden Legend in the thirteenth century. English devotion grew with the Crusades; his feast was kept in England from 1222, Edward III founded the Order of the Garter in his honour around 1348, and his red cross became the national flag. He is also a patron of soldiers, scouts, Georgia, Catalonia and Portugal, and Eastern Christians call him the Great Martyr.

Saint George, soldier of Christ, you gave up rank and life rather than deny your Lord. Pray for England, for soldiers and all who serve and protect others, and for me, that I may fight the dragons of my own sins with courage and trust in the grace of God. Amen.
The dragon is legend; the courage is not. What is the dragon in your own life that you have been afraid to face?

A lawyer known as the poor man’s advocate who left the courts to become a Capuchin friar. Sent to preach in the Swiss canton of the Grisons during years of bitter religious and political conflict, he was killed there in 1622. He was the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.

Mark Roy was born at Sigmaringen in Swabia and took a doctorate in law at Freiburg. He spent some years travelling through Europe as tutor to young noblemen, and then practised law at Ensisheim in Alsace, where he took the cases of the poor without fee. Disgusted by the dishonesty of his profession, he entered the Capuchins in 1612, and was given the name Fidelis, from the promise in the Apocalypse: be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. He served as guardian of several friaries and nursed soldiers through an epidemic. In 1622 the new Congregation de Propaganda Fide sent him to preach in the Prättigau valley, then caught in war between Austrian forces and local Protestant communities. On 24 April, after preaching at Seewis, he was attacked by armed men on the road and killed. He was canonised in 1746.
Saint Fidelis of Sigmaringen · Prayer to

Saint Fidelis, you defended the poor in the courts and preached Christ in a land divided by war. Pray for lawyers and judges, for missionaries, and for peace between Christians. Help me to be faithful unto death, to speak the truth in love, and to forgive those who oppose me. Amen.

God, Who didst vouchsafe to enkindle in blessed Fidelis the fire of thy Seraphim, and to glorify his toil to give men a true knowledge of thee by the palm-branch of martyrdom and by great signs and wonders, be entreated, we beseech thee, for his sake and by his prayers, and so establish us in the knowledge and love of thee, that we also, like him, may be found faithful even unto death in serving of thee. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. In what small thing is God asking you to be faithful today?

John Mark, the companion of Paul, Barnabas and Peter, wrote the shortest of the four Gospels, probably the first. Early tradition says he set down the preaching of Peter in Rome. He is held to have founded the Church of Alexandria, and his relics were carried to Venice in 828. His symbol is the lion.

The Acts of the Apostles tells us that the first Christians of Jerusalem met in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, and that Peter went there when an angel freed him from prison. Mark set out with his cousin Barnabas and with Paul on their first journey, but left them at Perga, and Paul refused to take him again, so that Barnabas and Paul parted. Years later Paul asked for him, ‘for he is useful to me for ministry’, and Peter calls him ‘my son’. Papias, writing early in the second century, says that Mark was Peter’s interpreter and wrote down accurately what Peter remembered of the Lord. His Gospel is vivid and urgent, full of the word ‘immediately’, and shows the disciples’ failures plainly. Some think he was the young man who fled naked from Gethsemane. Tradition says he was martyred at Alexandria.
Saint Mark the Evangelist · Prayer to

Saint Mark, you once turned back from the work, and by God’s grace became useful for His service and wrote the Good News of Jesus Christ. Pray for all who have failed and been given a second chance, and for me, that I may follow Christ without turning back. Amen.
Paul once refused to take him; later he called him useful. Is there someone you have written off whom God has not?

Two popes kept on one day. Cletus, also called Anacletus, was the third bishop of Rome after Peter and Linus, and is named in the Roman Canon. Marcellinus led the Roman Church from 296 to 304, as the great persecution under Diocletian broke out, and died in or soon after it. Both are honoured by tradition as martyrs.

Saint Irenaeus, writing around 180, lists the bishops of Rome from the apostles: Linus, then Anacletus, then Clement. That is almost all we know of Cletus, but it is a great deal: he stood in the line of those who kept the faith handed on by Peter and Paul, and the Church names him every day in the Roman Canon. Marcellinus became pope in 296. In 303 Diocletian ordered churches destroyed, the Scriptures burned and Christians compelled to sacrifice. Later sources say that Marcellinus gave way under pressure and offered incense, then repented and died a martyr; others say nothing of a lapse, and historians are uncertain. He was buried in the catacomb of Priscilla. Whatever the truth, his story as the Church has told it is one of weakness and mercy, and of a shepherd who came back.
Saints Cletus and Marcellinus · Prayer to

Saints Cletus and Marcellinus, shepherds of Rome in its first centuries, you handed on the faith of the apostles in times of danger. Pray for the Pope and for all who are tempted to give way under pressure. If I fall, help me to rise again quickly and return to Christ. Amen.

Look forgivingly on thy flock, Eternal Shepherd, and keep it in thy constant protection, by the intercession of blessed N. thy Sovereign Pontiff, whom thou didst constitute Shepherd of the whole Church. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Church names Cletus every day in the Roman Canon, and we know almost nothing else about him. Can you be content to be faithful and unknown?

The first Dutch Jesuit, who spent fifty years renewing the Catholic faith in Germany, Austria and Switzerland after the upheaval of the Reformation. He founded colleges, preached tirelessly and wrote catechisms that went through hundreds of editions. He is called the second apostle of Germany and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1925.

Peter Kanis was born at Nijmegen and studied at Cologne. In 1543 he made the Spiritual Exercises under Saint Peter Faber at Mainz and entered the young Society of Jesus. He attended the Council of Trent as a theologian, taught at Ingolstadt and Vienna, and became the first provincial of the Jesuits in Upper Germany. He founded or helped found colleges at Prague, Munich, Innsbruck and elsewhere, preached constantly and refused the archbishopric of Vienna. His catechisms, beginning in 1555, were so widely used that in some German lands a catechism was simply called a ‘Canisius’. He urged that those who had left the Church be treated with patience and charity, and he relied more on teaching and example than on argument. His last years were spent at Fribourg in Switzerland, where he founded the college of Saint Michael and died in 1597.

Saint Peter Canisius, you rebuilt the Church in your time by patient teaching and tireless love. Pray for catechists, priests and teachers, and for all who have drifted from the faith. Give me a clear knowledge of what the Church believes, and the charity to share it gently. Amen.

O God, who didst give strength and learning to blessed Peter thy Confessor for the defense of the Catholic faith, mercifully grant, that by his example and teaching the erring may be saved and the faithful remain constant in the confession of truth. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He spent fifty years teaching the faith to children and simple people, one question and answer at a time. Could you explain your faith simply if a child asked you?
Saint Louis Grignion de Montfort · Life

A Breton priest who walked the roads of western France preaching missions to the poor, singing hymns he wrote himself and setting up great calvaries. Often opposed and expelled, he founded the Company of Mary and, with Blessed Marie-Louise Trichet, the Daughters of Wisdom. His True Devotion to Mary taught total consecration to Jesus through Mary.
Saint Louis Grignion de Montfort · Life

Louis-Marie Grignion was born at Montfort-sur-Meu in Brittany, studied at Saint-Sulpice in Paris and was ordained in 1700. As chaplain of the hospital at Poitiers he met Marie-Louise Trichet, with whom he founded the Daughters of Wisdom to care for the sick and poor. His blunt preaching and his austerity made enemies, and he was more than once forbidden to preach in a diocese. In 1706 he walked to Rome, and Pope Clement XI named him missionary apostolic. Back in France he preached some two hundred missions, mostly in country parishes, restored churches, wrote a great many hymns and built a huge calvary at Pontchâteau, which the authorities ordered pulled down. His treatise on True Devotion lay hidden until 1842 and has since shaped millions, among them John Paul II, whose motto Totus Tuus came from it. He died at Saint-Laurent-sur-Sèvre in 1716, aged forty-three.
Saint Louis Grignion de Montfort · Prayer to

Saint Louis de Montfort, you gave yourself wholly to Jesus through Mary and spent your life for the poor. Pray for missionaries and for all who preach the Gospel to the forgotten. Teach me to belong entirely to Christ through His Mother, and to bear opposition with patience and joy. Amen.
Saint Louis Grignion de Montfort · Meditation
Totus tuus: I am all yours. Is there any part of your life you have kept back from Christ?

A dyer’s daughter of Siena, a Dominican tertiary who never learned to write well, yet counselled popes and princes, made peace between cities and urged the Pope to return from Avignon to Rome. Her Dialogue and her letters make her one of the great teachers of the Church. She is a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Europe and Italy.

Caterina Benincasa was one of the youngest of more than twenty children of a dyer and his wife Lapa. As a girl she gave herself to Christ and resisted every plan for her marriage. At about sixteen she joined the Mantellate, Dominican laywomen who lived at home, and spent three years in near silence in a small room of her father’s house. Then she went out to nurse the sick and serve the poor, above all in the plague of 1374, and a circle of disciples gathered round her, among them Blessed Raymond of Capua, her confessor. She received the stigmata at Pisa in 1375, visible to no one. In 1376 she went to Avignon and urged Gregory XI to return to Rome, which he did. When the Great Schism broke out she supported Urban VI and spent herself praying for the unity of the Church. She died in Rome, aged thirty-three.
Saint Catherine of Siena · Prayer to

Saint Catherine, you loved Christ crucified and His Church with a fire that the whole world felt. Pray for the Pope, for the unity and renewal of the Church, and for Europe. Help me to dwell in the cell of self-knowledge, and to speak the truth with courage and love. Amen.
She taught that we must build a cell of self-knowledge within the soul, and there find both our own nothingness and the goodness of God. Where is your inner cell?

A Dominican friar from a poor family who became pope in 1566 and put the reforms of the Council of Trent into effect. He issued the Roman Catechism, the reformed Breviary and the Missal of 1570, and lived as austerely as a friar. He called Christendom to pray the Rosary before the victory of Lepanto in 1571.

Antonio Ghislieri was born at Bosco, near Alessandria, and kept sheep as a boy. He entered the Dominicans at fourteen, taking the name Michele, and taught theology for years. He served as an inquisitor, then as bishop and cardinal, and was elected pope in 1566. He set about carrying out the decrees of Trent: he published the Roman Catechism, reformed the Breviary and the Missal, insisted that bishops live in their dioceses, cleared the papal court of luxury and named Saint Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church. He went on wearing his white Dominican habit, from which, tradition says, comes the white cassock of the popes. He visited hospitals and washed the feet of the poor. Facing the advance of the Ottoman fleet, he formed the Holy League and asked all Christendom to pray the Rosary. He died on 1 May 1572 and was canonised in 1712.

Saint Pius, shepherd and reformer, you lived simply in the midst of great power and gave the Church the treasures of her worship. Pray for the Pope and the bishops, for the reform of the Church in every age, and for me, that I may begin with the reform of my own life. Amen.
He kept the habit of a friar on the throne of Peter. What habit of simplicity could you keep in the midst of your own comforts?

Pius XII instituted this feast in 1955 to give May Day, the festival of labour, a Christian meaning. Jesus was known in Nazareth as the carpenter’s son, and Joseph shows the dignity of ordinary work done honestly for family and neighbour. The day is a reminder of the Church’s teaching on the rights of workers.

The Gospels call Joseph a tekton, a craftsman, and Jesus Himself was known as ‘the carpenter’. For some thirty years the Son of God lived a hidden life of work in a small town, learning a trade from His foster father. The Church has always seen in this a sign that work is not a curse but a share in God’s own creating. In 1891 Leo XIII, in Rerum Novarum, defended the right of workers to a just wage and to form associations, and later popes developed his teaching. When Pius XII addressed Italian workers on 1 May 1955 he gave them this feast, so that the day already kept by working people around the world would also honour the patron of workers. John Paul II, who had himself worked in a quarry and a factory, wrote in Laborem Exercens that through work man becomes more a man.
Saint Joseph the Worker · Prayer to

Saint Joseph the Worker, you earned your bread by the work of your hands and taught the Son of God your trade. Pray for all who work and all who cannot find work, for employers and those they employ. Help me to do my work well, honestly and for the glory of God. Amen.

O God, Creator of all things, Who dost impose on man the law of work; grant in Thy goodness that, by the example and patronage of blessed Joseph, we may both accomplish the work Thou dost command and attain the reward Thou hast promised. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Is not this the carpenter? The townspeople meant it as a dismissal. How might your own ordinary work become a place of holiness?

Bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years, Athanasius was the great defender of the faith of Nicaea, that the Son is true God, of one substance with the Father. Exiled five times by four emperors, he never gave way. He wrote On the Incarnation and the Life of Antony, and is a Doctor of the Church.

As a young deacon Athanasius went with his bishop Alexander to the Council of Nicaea in 325, which condemned Arius’s teaching that the Son was a creature. Three years later he succeeded Alexander as bishop. The Arian party, often supported by the imperial court, worked to remove him, and he was banished five times, to Trier in Gaul, to Rome and, more than once, to hiding among the monks of the Egyptian desert. In all he spent about seventeen years in exile. His short book On the Incarnation explains why the Word became flesh: to restore the image of God in us and to overcome death. His Life of Antony spread the ideal of monastic life through the West. In his Easter letter of 367 he listed the twenty-seven books of the New Testament as we have them. He died in Alexandria in 373, at peace with his flock.

Saint Athanasius, you stood for the truth that Jesus Christ is God, though emperors and bishops turned against you. Pray for the Church in every age of confusion, and for me, that I may hold fast to the faith, worship the Son as true God, and not fear standing alone. Amen.
He became man so that we might be made god. What does it mean for you that God wishes to share His own life with you?

Two of the Twelve, honoured together since their relics were placed in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome. Philip of Bethsaida brought Nathanael to Jesus and asked Him at the Last Supper to show them the Father. James, son of Alphaeus, is identified in the Western tradition with James, the brother of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem.

Saint John’s Gospel gives us Philip in a few sharp moments. Called by Jesus, he went at once to Nathanael: come and see. Before the feeding of the five thousand Jesus tested him by asking where to buy bread, and Philip could only count the cost. When some Greeks wished to see Jesus, they came to Philip. At the Last Supper he said, ‘Lord, show us the Father,’ and heard the answer: whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Tradition says he preached in Phrygia and died at Hierapolis. James, son of Alphaeus, is called James the Less. The Latin Church has long identified him with James the brother of the Lord, who led the Church in Jerusalem, spoke at the Council of Jerusalem and, according to Josephus, was stoned around 62. Their relics were enshrined in Rome in the sixth century.
Saints Philip and James · Prayer to

Saints Philip and James, apostles of the Lord, you saw the face of the Father in Jesus and gave your lives for Him. Pray for the Church, for those who seek God, and for me, that I may see Christ more clearly, and that my faith may show itself in works. Amen.
Lord, show us the Father, and we shall be satisfied. Have I been so long with you, and yet you do not know me? Where have you missed Him?

A Dominican friar of Florence who became its archbishop and lived as poor as his flock. He helped found the friary of San Marco, gave away almost everything he had, set up a confraternity to help families ashamed to beg, and wrote a great work of moral theology that dealt with trade, money and the just price.

Antonino Pierozzi, son of a Florentine notary, entered the Dominicans at Fiesole as a teenager, under the influence of Blessed John Dominici and his strict reform. He was prior of several friaries, and with the help of Cosimo de’ Medici founded San Marco in Florence, where Fra Angelico painted the cells. He served as a theologian at the Council of Florence. In 1446 Pope Eugene IV named him archbishop of Florence, and he accepted only under obedience. His household was tiny and his clothes poor; he sold his own goods in famine and plague, visited his parishes on foot, and was known for settling disputes. He founded the Buonomini di San Martino to help the ‘shamefaced poor’, families fallen into need who were too proud to beg; it still exists. His Summa of moral theology was one of the first to treat economic life seriously. He died in 1459.

Saint Antoninus, you governed your city as a shepherd and lived as a poor friar. Pray for Florence, for bishops and civic leaders, and for those who work in trade and finance. Help me to be honest in all my dealings and generous to those who are ashamed to ask for help. Amen.

O Lord, may the merits of St. Antoninus, Your Confessor and Bishop, help us; and just as we praise You for the wonders You have wrought in him, so may we glory in Your mercy toward us. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He cared especially for the poor who hid their poverty. Who around you is struggling in silence?
Saints Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras · Life

Three early Roman martyrs. Nereus and Achilleus were soldiers who, Pope Damasus recorded in verse, threw down their arms when they came to believe, and died for Christ. Pancras was a boy of about fourteen beheaded on the Via Aurelia, probably under Diocletian. His cult reached England early, and churches in Canterbury and London bear his name.
Saints Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras · Life

Nereus and Achilleus were buried in the catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina, where a basilica was later built over their tomb. Pope Damasus, in the fourth century, wrote an inscription for them: they had served a tyrant’s cruel orders as soldiers, then, suddenly converted, they fled the camp, threw away their shields and weapons, and rejoiced to bear witness to Christ. A later legend linked them with Flavia Domitilla, a Christian of the imperial family. Of Pancras we know the place of his burial on the Via Aurelia and the great devotion paid him; tradition says he was an orphan from Phrygia brought to Rome by his uncle, and that he was beheaded at about fourteen. Gregory of Tours wrote that false oaths sworn at his tomb were punished. Pope Gregory the Great sent relics of Pancras to England, and a church in his honour stood in Canterbury.
Saints Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras · Prayer to

Saints Nereus and Achilleus, you laid down your weapons for Christ; Saint Pancras, you gave your young life for Him. Pray for soldiers, for children and young people, and for all who must choose between the faith and the demands of the world. Give me courage to be faithful in small things and in great. Amen.
Saints Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras · Prayer
May the holy feast of Your Martyrs, Nereus, Achilleus, Domitilla and Pancras, ever comfort us, we beseech You, O Lord, and make us worthy to serve You. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Saints Nereus, Achilleus and Pancras · Meditation
They threw away their shields and rejoiced to carry the triumph of Christ. What defences would you have to lay down to follow Him more freely?

From 13 May to 13 October 1917, Our Lady appeared six times to three shepherd children at the Cova da Iria near Fátima in Portugal, asking for prayer, penance and the daily Rosary. The apparitions were approved by the local bishop in 1930. Two of the children, Francisco and Jacinta Marto, were canonised in 2017.

Lúcia dos Santos, aged ten, and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, eight and seven, were minding sheep when, they said, a lady brighter than the sun appeared above a holm oak. She asked them to return on the thirteenth of each month, to pray the Rosary every day for peace and the end of the war, and to offer sacrifices for sinners. The children suffered disbelief, threats and even a short imprisonment. In July they were shown a vision of hell and given a message asking for devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. On 13 October a large crowd, tens of thousands strong, reported seeing the sun dance in the sky. Francisco and Jacinta died young in the influenza epidemic; Lúcia became a Carmelite and died in 2005. John Paul II, shot on 13 May 1981, believed Our Lady had saved his life.
As with all approved apparitions, belief in them is not required, but they are a trustworthy call to the Gospel.
Our Lady of Fatima · Prayer to

Our Lady of Fatima, you asked three children to pray and to make sacrifices for sinners, and they answered with generous hearts. Teach me to pray the Rosary faithfully, to offer my small sufferings for others, and to take refuge in your Immaculate Heart. Pray for peace in the world. Amen.
The children were asked to offer small sacrifices for others. What small, hidden sacrifice could you make today for someone far from God?

The disciple chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve, after the Ascension and before Pentecost. He had followed Jesus from the baptism of John to the day He was taken up, and so could be a witness to the resurrection. Scripture says nothing more of him. He is the patron of reformed lives.

In the first chapter of Acts, Peter stands up among some hundred and twenty disciples and says that one must be chosen to replace Judas, a man who had been with them all the time the Lord Jesus went in and out among them. Two were put forward, Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias. The apostles prayed, ‘Lord, you know the hearts of all men,’ and cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias. That is all the New Testament tells us. Later traditions say he preached in Judea and further afield, in Cappadocia or Ethiopia, and died a martyr. Relics said to be his were brought to Trier, where the abbey of Saint Matthias claims the only tomb of an apostle north of the Alps. He was chosen for one task: to be a witness to the resurrection. He took the place left by a betrayal.

Saint Matthias, you were chosen to fill the place of one who betrayed the Lord, and you bore faithful witness to His resurrection. Pray for all who are called to new responsibilities, for those discerning their vocation, and for me, that I may accept whatever task God gives me. Amen.
Lord, you know the hearts of all. Matthias was not the obvious choice; God chose him. Are you willing to be chosen for what you did not seek?

A pope sent against his will by Theodoric, the Arian Gothic king of Italy, to plead with the Emperor in Constantinople on behalf of the Arians. He was the first pope to visit Constantinople and was received with great honour. When he returned, Theodoric had him imprisoned at Ravenna, where he died. He is honoured as a martyr.

John was a Tuscan, an elderly deacon of the Roman Church when he was elected pope in 523. Italy was ruled by Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, an Arian Christian who had governed tolerantly for many years but grew suspicious as he aged; he had the philosopher Boethius put to death around this time. When the Emperor Justin I began to take churches from the Arians in the East, Theodoric forced the pope to lead an embassy to Constantinople to have the measures reversed. John was greeted there by the Emperor and the people, and celebrated Easter in Hagia Sophia in the Latin rite. The mission was only partly successful, and on his return Theodoric held him at Ravenna, where he died in May 526, worn out by his treatment. His body was carried to Rome and buried in Saint Peter’s.

Saint John, you were sent on an impossible errand and suffered for refusing to betray your flock. Pray for the Pope, for Christians who live under hostile powers, and for unity between East and West. When I am placed in a hard position, help me to act with honesty and trust in God. Amen.
