He was asked to do what he could not in conscience fully do, and he went anyway, as far as he could go. Where must you obey without compromising the truth?

A Franciscan friar and the most famous preacher of fifteenth-century Italy, who crossed the country on foot drawing vast crowds. He spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, showing a tablet with the letters IHS surrounded by rays of the sun. He refused three bishoprics and helped renew the Observant Franciscans.

Bernardino degli Albizzeschi was born at Massa Marittima, orphaned young and raised by devout aunts in Siena. When plague struck the city in 1400 he and a group of young men ran the great hospital of Santa Maria della Scala for months, and he nearly died. In 1402 he joined the Franciscans of the strict Observance. After years of quiet he began to preach, and for the rest of his life travelled Italy, preaching for hours in the open air because no church could hold the crowds. He spoke plainly about gambling, usury, vanity and the feuds that divided Italian towns, and people burned dice, cards and ornaments in the squares. Some accused his devotion to the Holy Name of novelty, but Pope Martin V cleared him. As vicar general he helped the Observants grow from a few hundred friars to thousands. He died at L’Aquila and was canonised in 1450.
Saint Bernardine of Siena · Prayer to

Saint Bernardine, you preached the Holy Name of Jesus to the crowds and turned many from vanity and hatred. Pray for preachers and for all who speak in public. Teach me to honour the name of Jesus, to use my words to heal and not to wound, and to make peace. Amen.
He held up the name of Jesus, carved and gilded, so that people would love it. How do you speak His name?
Saint Christopher Magallanes and Companions · Life

Twenty-five Mexican martyrs, twenty-two priests and three laymen, killed in the years when the public practice of the faith was restricted and priests were hunted, above all during the Cristero War of 1926 to 1929. Christopher Magallanes, a parish priest of Jalisco, was shot in 1927 after forgiving his executioners. John Paul II canonised them in 2000.
Saint Christopher Magallanes and Companions · Life

Cristóbal Magallanes Jara was born in 1869 at Totatiche in Jalisco and worked the land before entering the seminary. As parish priest of his home town he built schools, founded a seminary, and cared for the poor and for the native Huichol people. When the laws of the 1920s closed churches and forbade priests to minister, he kept serving his people in secret and reopened his seminary in hiding. He wrote against taking up arms, though many Catholics had joined the Cristero rising. On 21 May 1927 he was arrested on his way to celebrate Mass, and four days later he was shot at Colotlán without trial, together with his young assistant, Saint Agustín Caloca. He gave away his last possessions to the soldiers, absolved them, and prayed that his blood might bring peace to Mexico. His companions were priests and laymen from several dioceses who died in similar ways.
Saint Christopher Magallanes and Companions · Prayer to

Saint Christopher Magallanes and holy martyrs of Mexico, you served Christ’s people when it was forbidden and forgave those who killed you. Pray for the Church in Mexico and wherever priests are persecuted. Give me courage to keep the faith in hidden ways when I cannot keep it openly, and a heart that forgives. Amen.
Saint Christopher Magallanes and Companions · Meditation
He gave his executioners his blessing and what little he had. What would it take for you to bless someone who has harmed you?

A wife, mother, widow and Augustinian nun of Cascia in Umbria. Tradition says she bore an unhappy marriage with patience, forgave her husband’s murderers and brought peace between feuding families before entering the convent, where she received a wound from a thorn of the crown of Christ. She is the patron of impossible causes and difficult marriages.

Most of what we know of Rita comes from tradition written down after her death, but it has been loved for centuries. She was born at Roccaporena, near Cascia, and married young to Paolo Mancini, a man given to violence. By her patience and prayer, it is said, he was changed. He was murdered in a feud, and Rita forgave his killers, but her two sons vowed revenge; she prayed that they would rather die than commit murder, and both died of illness soon after. She asked to enter the Augustinian convent of Saint Mary Magdalene at Cascia and was refused three times, until she had reconciled the families involved in the feud. In the convent she lived in prayer and obedience, and around 1442 a wound like that of a thorn opened in her forehead and stayed with her for fifteen years. Roses are blessed on her feast.
Saint Rita of Cascia · Prayer to

Saint Rita, you bore suffering in marriage and loss with patience, and chose forgiveness over revenge. Pray for those in hard marriages, for families divided by anger, and for all who face what seems impossible. Help me to forgive, to make peace, and to trust God with what I cannot change. Amen.
She would not enter the convent until she had made peace between the families who had killed her husband. What reconciliation is God waiting for before you go further?

A monk of Jarrow in Northumbria who scarcely left his monastery, yet became one of the most learned men in Europe. His Ecclesiastical History of the English People is the chief source for the conversion of England, and he made dating from the birth of Christ widely known. He is the only English Doctor of the Church.

Bede was born on lands belonging to the monastery of Wearmouth and was given to its abbot, Benedict Biscop, at the age of seven. He moved to the new house at Jarrow under Ceolfrith, and spent the rest of his life there, ordained deacon at nineteen and priest at thirty. He wrote of himself that his delight had always been to learn, to teach and to write. He commented on most of the Bible, wrote on time, grammar and the reckoning of Easter, composed lives of saints and poetry, and in 731 finished his history of the English Church. His disciple Cuthbert described his death: he was translating Saint John’s Gospel into English, finished the last sentence, and died on the floor of his cell singing the Glory Be, on the eve of the Ascension, 735. His relics lie in Durham Cathedral. Leo XIII named him a Doctor in 1899.
Saint Bede the Venerable · Prayer to

Saint Bede, you gave your whole life to learning, teaching and praising God in the cloister. Pray for England, for scholars and teachers, and for monks and nuns. Help me to love the Scriptures, to do my work faithfully to the end, and to die, as you did, giving glory to God. Amen.
In Bede’s History a counsellor of King Edwin compares our life to a sparrow flying through a lit hall in winter, in at one door and out at the other. What do you know of where you are going?

A Florentine who came to Rome as a young man and became its apostle, drawing people of every kind to God by friendship, prayer and laughter. He founded the Congregation of the Oratory, whose informal gatherings of prayer, Scripture and music gave the oratorio its name. Cheerful and humble, he is one of the best loved saints of Rome.

Philip was born in Florence and taught by the Dominicans at San Marco. At eighteen he was sent to learn business from a relative, but soon left for Rome, where he lived very simply, tutored two boys, and spent nights praying in the catacombs. At Pentecost 1544, in the catacomb of San Sebastiano, he felt a ball of fire enter his heart, and his heart was said to beat visibly ever after. For years he worked as a layman, talking to people in the streets and shops and founding a confraternity to care for pilgrims. Ordained in 1551, he heard confessions for hours each day. In a room above his church he gathered men to pray, read, discuss and sing, and from this came the Oratory, approved in 1575. He used jokes to keep himself and others humble. John Henry Newman brought the Oratory to England.

Saint Philip, you won souls by kindness and joy, and kept them humble with a smile. Pray for the city of Rome, for priests and confessors, and for the Oratories. Give me a cheerful heart, a love for prayer and the sacraments, and the grace not to take myself too seriously. Amen.

O God, Who raised blessed Philip, Your Confessor, to the glory of Your Saints, graciously grant that we who rejoice in his feast may profit by the example of his virtues. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He would wear his clothes inside out or shave half his beard so that no one would think him a saint. What would it cost you to look foolish for God?

A Roman monk sent by Pope Gregory the Great to bring the Gospel to the English. He landed in Kent in 597, was welcomed by King Æthelberht, whose Frankish queen Bertha was already a Christian, and baptised the king and many of his people. As first Archbishop of Canterbury he founded the Church from which English Christianity grew.

Augustine was prior of Gregory’s own monastery of Saint Andrew on the Caelian Hill when the pope chose him to lead some forty monks to England in 596. In Gaul they lost heart at the tales of a fierce people, and Augustine went back to ask that they be excused; Gregory sent him on with letters of encouragement. They landed on Thanet in 597. Bede tells us the king met them in the open air for fear of magic, listened, and allowed them to preach in Canterbury, where they prayed in the old church of Saint Martin. Æthelberht was baptised, and great numbers followed at Christmas. Augustine was consecrated bishop in Gaul, founded Christ Church and the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul at Canterbury, and set up sees at London and Rochester. Gregory advised him to purify pagan temples rather than destroy them. His talks with the bishops of the older British Church did not reach agreement.
Saint Augustine of Canterbury · Prayer to

Saint Augustine of Canterbury, you came to a strange land with fear and obeyed, and God made you the father of the faith in England. Pray for England and for her conversion, for bishops and missionaries, and for me, that I may obey when I am afraid and trust God to finish His work. Amen.
He turned back once, and was sent on again. Where have you turned back from what God asked, and are you ready to go on?
Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi · Life

A Carmelite nun of Florence, of one of the city’s great families, whose life of prayer was marked by long ecstasies, recorded word for word by her sisters, and by years of spiritual darkness. She burned with love for God and grief that He was so little loved, and wrote to popes and bishops pleading for the renewal of the Church.
Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi · Life

Caterina de’ Pazzi was drawn to prayer as a child, made her first Communion at ten and soon after promised herself to God. Against her family’s wishes she entered the Carmelite monastery of Santa Maria degli Angeli in Florence in 1582, taking the name Mary Magdalene. Gravely ill as a novice, she was allowed to make her vows early on a stretcher, and then began a series of ecstasies in which she spoke aloud of the love of God, the Passion and the Holy Spirit; her sisters wrote down what she said, and these records fill several volumes. For five years she endured temptation and dryness, which she called the lions’ den. She served as mistress of novices and subprioress, and was loved for her gentleness. Tradition remembers her crying out that Love is not loved. After a long and painful illness she died in 1607, aged forty-one.
Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi · Prayer to

Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi, you burned with love for God and grieved that Love is not loved. Pray for contemplatives, for all in spiritual darkness, and for the renewal of the Church. Teach me to love God with my whole heart, and to persevere in prayer when it is dry. Amen.
Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi · Prayer

O God, lover of chastity, Who endowed with heavenly gifts blessed Mary Magdalen, a virgin on fire with love for You, grant that we who keep this feast-day in her honor may imitate her by purity and love. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Saint Mary Magdalene de’ Pazzi · Meditation
Love is not loved, she is said to have cried through the cloister. What would it mean for you to love Love today?
The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

Soon after the Annunciation, Mary went in haste to the hill country of Judah to visit her kinswoman Elizabeth, who was carrying John the Baptist. At Mary’s greeting the child leapt in Elizabeth’s womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, called her blessed among women. Mary answered with the Magnificat, the song the Church sings every evening.
The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

Saint Luke tells the story in the first chapter of his Gospel. Mary, having heard from the angel that Elizabeth had conceived in her old age, set out at once, travelling some distance to a town that tradition places at Ein Karem, near Jerusalem. Elizabeth’s words, blessed are you among women and blessed is the fruit of your womb, became part of the Hail Mary. Mary’s reply, my soul magnifies the Lord, echoes the song of Hannah and praises the God who scatters the proud and fills the hungry with good things. She stayed about three months. The Franciscans kept the feast from 1263, and Urban VI extended it to the whole Church in 1389, praying for an end to the Great Schism. It was kept on 2 July until 1969, when it moved to the last day of May, between the Annunciation and the birth of John the Baptist.
The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Prayer to

Holy Mary, you carried Christ in haste to your kinswoman, and the child in her womb leapt for joy. Bring Him to me and to all I meet today. Pray for expectant mothers and for the elderly, and teach me to magnify the Lord with you in every circumstance of my life. Amen.
The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Meditation
Mary did not wait to be visited; she went in haste. Who is waiting for you to come?

A philosopher from Samaria who searched the schools of the Greeks for the truth and found it in Christ. He kept his philosopher’s cloak and opened a school in Rome, where he defended the faith in writing before the emperor. His account of a Sunday Mass is the earliest we have. He was beheaded for refusing to sacrifice to the gods.

Justin was born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis, the modern Nablus. He tried the Stoics, a follower of Aristotle, a Pythagorean and the Platonists in turn. By his own account an old man he met walking by the sea told him of the prophets, who had spoken of Christ long before, and a fire was kindled in his soul. Baptised, he taught in Rome as a Christian philosopher. His First Apology, addressed to the Emperor Antoninus Pius, describes how Christians gathered on the day of the sun, read the memoirs of the apostles, prayed, and received bread and wine which they believed to be the flesh and blood of Jesus. His Dialogue with Trypho records a long, courteous debate with a Jew. Around 165 he and six companions were tried before the prefect Rusticus, and the record of their trial survives.

Saint Justin, you sought the truth with all your mind and gave your life when you had found it. Pray for all who study and search, for teachers and for those who doubt. Help me to give a reason for the hope that is in me, with gentleness and courage, and to love the Mass you described so faithfully. Amen.
Justin held that every seed of truth in the philosophers belonged to Christ, the Word. Where have you seen a seed of His truth in someone who does not yet know Him?

A priest and an exorcist of Rome, martyred in the persecution of Diocletian and named every day in the Roman Canon. Pope Damasus wrote that as a boy he had heard the story of their deaths from the very man who beheaded them. Constantine built a basilica over their tomb, and his mother Helena was buried beside them.

Little is certain about Marcellinus and Peter beyond their deaths, but that little is unusually well attested. In the great persecution that began under Diocletian in 303, Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, were arrested in Rome. Tradition holds that in prison they converted their jailer and his family. They were led to a wood outside the city, made to clear the ground where they would be buried, and beheaded there in secret, so that Christians would not find the place. The faithful found it all the same. Pope Damasus, later in the century, set up a verse inscription at their tomb, saying he had learned of their deaths from their executioner, who had himself become a Christian. Their catacomb on the Via Labicana, with its paintings, can still be visited, and the ruins of Helena’s mausoleum stand beside it.
Saints Marcellinus and Peter · Prayer to

Saints Marcellinus and Peter, you were killed in secret and your tomb was hidden, yet the Church remembers your names at every Mass. Pray for all who suffer unseen for Christ, for prisoners and those who guard them, and for me, that I may be faithful when no one is watching. Amen.
Their killers chose a hidden place so they would be forgotten, and the hidden place became a shrine. What hidden faithfulness is God asking of you?
Saints Charles Lwanga and Companions · Life

Twenty-two young Catholic men of the Ugandan royal court, most of them pages, killed for their faith under King Mwanga II. Charles Lwanga, their leader, baptised the catechumens among them on the night before their arrest and was burned at Namugongo on 3 June 1886. Anglican Christians died with them. Paul VI canonised them in 1964.
Saints Charles Lwanga and Companions · Life

The Missionaries of Africa, the White Fathers, reached Buganda in 1879, and many at the court of the kabaka came to faith. King Mwanga, who came to the throne in 1884, grew to fear the new religions and to resent Christian pages who refused his sexual demands. In November 1885 he had Joseph Mukasa, the head of the pages, beheaded for rebuking him. Charles Lwanga took his place as protector of the young men. In May 1886 the king summoned the pages and demanded that the Christians separate themselves. They stepped forward, the youngest, Kizito, about fourteen. Marched to Namugongo, many were burned there together on 3 June, praying as they died. Anglican pages were among them, and the Church of Uganda honours them too. Paul VI, the first pope to visit sub-Saharan Africa, prayed at their shrine in 1969.
Saints Charles Lwanga and Companions · Prayer to

Saint Charles Lwanga and holy martyrs of Uganda, you were young and you chose Christ over the favour of a king. Pray for the young, especially those under pressure to do wrong, for the Church in Africa, and for unity among all who love Christ. Make me brave enough to step forward when I am asked who I am. Amen.
Saints Charles Lwanga and Companions · Meditation
When the king asked the Christians to stand apart, they stepped forward. In what company do you keep quiet about Christ?

An English monk from Wessex, born Wynfrith, who became the Apostle of Germany. He felled the sacred oak of Donar at Geismar, organised the Church across the German lands as archbishop of Mainz, and founded the abbey of Fulda. In old age he returned to Frisia as a missionary and was martyred at Dokkum with his companions.

Wynfrith was given to the monastery at Exeter as a boy and later taught at Nursling near Southampton, where he wrote a Latin grammar. In 716 he sailed for Frisia, but war closed the mission. In Rome Pope Gregory II gave him the name Boniface and a commission to preach in Germany. At Geismar in Hesse he took an axe to the oak sacred to the thunder god, and when nothing befell him many were baptised; tradition says he built a chapel from its wood. He drew monks and nuns from England to help him, among them Saint Lioba, founded dioceses and held reforming synods for the Frankish Church. Past seventy he went back to Frisia. On 5 June 754, at Dokkum, a band of raiders fell on his camp. Tradition holds that he raised a book of the Gospels over his head as the blow fell.

Saint Boniface, you left England to carry the Gospel to the peoples beyond the sea, and you never stopped being a missionary. Pray for England and Germany, for all who bring the faith to new places, and for me, that I may not be afraid to cut down the idols in my own life. Amen.

O God, Who, through the zeal of blessed Boniface, Your Martyr and Bishop, graciously called a multitude of people to the knowledge of Your name, mercifully grant that we who keep his feast may also enjoy his patronage. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He was nearly eighty when he set out for Frisia again. Is there a work for God you have decided you are too old or too tired for?

A deacon of the Syrian Church whose hymns earned him the name Harp of the Holy Spirit. He wrote in Syriac, the language closest to the Aramaic of Christ, and taught the faith to his people through poetry and song, above all on Christ and on the Virgin Mary. Benedict XV named him a Doctor of the Church in 1920.

Ephrem was born at Nisibis, on the border between the Roman and Persian empires, and served its bishops as a deacon and teacher. He wrote hundreds of hymns, many for choirs of women to sing, so that sound teaching would be carried in melody against the heresies of his day. His images are rich and concrete: the pearl, the womb, the robe, the medicine of life. When Nisibis was handed to Persia in 363, Ephrem went with the Christian refugees to Edessa, where he taught in the school and lived simply. He never sought the priesthood. In the famine of 372 he organised relief for the hungry, and he died the following year. His writing shaped the worship of the Syriac Churches and later of the Greek and Latin Churches as well.

Saint Ephrem, you sang the mysteries of Christ and of His Mother, and taught the faith with beauty. Pray for the Christians of Syria and Iraq, for all who write and sing for God, and for me, that my praise may be warm and my faith true. Amen.
Ephrem compared the Word of God to a spring that no one can drink dry. Return to one passage today and drink again.

A Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, son of encouragement. He sold a field and laid the money at their feet, vouched for Saul when the Church in Jerusalem feared him, and later brought him to Antioch. Together they made the first great missionary journey. Tradition says Barnabas was martyred in Cyprus.

The Acts of the Apostles calls Barnabas a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. When the new convert Saul came to Jerusalem and the disciples were afraid of him, Barnabas took him to the apostles and told how he had preached boldly in Damascus. Sent to Antioch, where Gentiles were turning to the Lord, Barnabas rejoiced, then went to Tarsus to find Saul and bring him to help. It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians. The Holy Spirit set the two apart, and they sailed to Cyprus and on into Asia Minor. Later they disagreed sharply over taking Barnabas’s cousin John Mark with them, and parted, Barnabas taking Mark to Cyprus. Paul later speaks warmly of both. Tradition holds that Barnabas was stoned at Salamis.
Saint Barnabas the Apostle · Prayer to

Saint Barnabas, son of encouragement, you saw good in Saul when others saw only danger, and you gave a second chance to Mark. Pray for me, that I may be generous with my goods and with my trust, and that my words may build others up in Christ. Amen.

O God, Who gladden us by the merits and intercession of blessed Barnabas, Your Apostle, mercifully grant that we, who ask Your favors through him, may obtain them by the gift of Your grace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Without Barnabas, Saul might have been left alone. Whom could you stand beside who has been kept at a distance?

A Spanish priest, called John of San Facundo after his birthplace, who became an Augustinian friar and the great preacher of Salamanca. In a city torn by feuds between noble families he worked tirelessly to make peace. He was known for his long, devout celebration of Mass and for the frankness of his preaching. He is the patron of Salamanca.

John González de Castrillo was born at Sahagún in the kingdom of León and studied at the University of Salamanca. Ordained priest, he held several benefices but gave them up to live simply and preach. In 1463 he entered the Augustinian friars at Salamanca. The city was then divided by violent rivalry between two factions of nobles, and John, preaching and visiting both sides, brought many to reconciliation. He spoke plainly against injustice and the vices of the powerful, which won him enemies. He celebrated Mass slowly and with great recollection, and his brothers believed he was granted a vision of Christ at the altar. Tradition holds that he died after being poisoned by a woman whose lover he had converted. He was canonised in 1690.
Saint John of Sahagún · Prayer to

Saint John of Sahagún, peacemaker of Salamanca, you went between enemies with nothing but the Gospel. Pray for families and communities divided by old quarrels, for preachers who must speak hard truths, and for me, that I may love the Mass and work for peace where I live. Amen.

O God, author of peace and lover of charity, Who endowed blessed John, Your Confessor, with a wondrous grace for reconciling enemies; grant by his merits and intercession, that, being ourselves firmly rooted in Your charity, we may not be separated from You by any temptations. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Blessed are the peacemakers. Is there a feud near you that you have simply accepted?

A Portuguese canon who became a Franciscan, hoping for martyrdom in Morocco, and instead became the most famous preacher of his age. He taught theology to the friars at Saint Francis’s request and preached across Italy and France. He died at thirty-six and was canonised within a year. He is a Doctor of the Church and the patron of lost things.

Fernando Martins was born in Lisbon and joined the Augustinian canons, studying Scripture deeply at Coimbra. In 1220 the bodies of five Franciscans martyred in Morocco were brought there, and he resolved to follow them, taking the name Anthony. He reached Morocco but fell ill, and the ship bringing him home was driven to Sicily. Unknown and unregarded, he served in a hermitage until, at an ordination at Forlì, he was asked to preach without preparation and astonished everyone. Francis wrote to him as ‘my bishop’ and asked him to teach the brothers theology, so long as study did not quench the spirit of prayer. He preached against heresy and usury, and crowds too large for churches gathered in fields to hear him. Worn out, he died near Padua on 13 June 1231. Pius XII declared him a Doctor in 1946.
Saint Anthony of Padua · Prayer to

Saint Anthony, preacher of the Gospel and friend of the poor, you knew the Scriptures by heart and loved Christ in them. Help me to find what I have lost, and above all to find again any grace I have let slip. Pray for the poor, and teach me to give to them freely. Amen.
Anthony said that actions speak louder than words, and urged preachers to let their words teach and their deeds speak. Which of your words is still waiting for its deed?

A Venetian nobleman and diplomat who became a priest, cardinal and model bishop of the reform of Trent, first at Bergamo and then for over thirty years at Padua. He nursed the sick in the Roman plague, visited every parish, founded a great seminary with its own press, and longed for reunion with the Christians of the East.

Gregorio Barbarigo, of an old Venetian family, accompanied the Venetian ambassador to the peace talks at Münster that ended the Thirty Years’ War, and there met the papal envoy, the future Alexander VII, who encouraged his vocation. Ordained in 1655, he worked in Rome during the plague of 1656, caring for the sick and dying. He was made bishop of Bergamo in 1657 and cardinal in 1660, and in 1664 was moved to Padua, where he stayed until his death. Taking Saint Charles Borromeo as his model, he visited every parish, taught catechism himself, and gave away so much that he was often short of money. His seminary at Padua became famous for learning, and its press printed books in Greek, Arabic and other languages of the East, in hope of unity with separated Christians. John XXIII, who had served at Bergamo, canonised him in 1960.

Saint Gregory, faithful shepherd, you served the plague-stricken, taught the children and spent yourself for your people. Pray for our bishops and priests, for seminarians, and for the unity of Christians of East and West. Help me to serve gladly, without counting the cost. Amen.

O God, Who have willed that Blessed Gregory, Your Confessor and Bishop, be renowned for the care of his flock and compassion for the poor; favorably grant that we who honor his merits may imitate the example of his charity. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He carried the plans of a reformer and the purse of a poor man. What would change in your parish if you gave it a little more of your time?

A nobleman of Ravenna who became a monk in penance for a killing by his father, and spent his long life founding hermitages and monasteries across Italy. At Camaldoli in Tuscany he united the solitary life of hermits with life in community, and the Camaldolese still follow his way. He taught his monks to sit in their cell as in paradise.

Romuald’s father killed a relative in a duel over property, and Romuald, about twenty, went to the monastery of Sant’Apollinare in Classe to do forty days of penance on his behalf. He stayed and became a monk, but found the community lax and left to live under a strict hermit in the marshes near Venice. For the rest of his life he moved from place to place, reforming monasteries, gathering hermits and founding new houses, often to the annoyance of comfortable monks. Around 1012 he founded the hermitage of Camaldoli high in the Apennines, with a monastery below to receive guests and the sick. His disciple Saint Bruno of Querfurt recorded his short rule for hermits: sit in your cell as in paradise, watch your thoughts as a fisherman watches for fish, and keep to the psalms. He died at Val di Castro in 1027.

Saint Romuald, you left a life of privilege to make amends and stayed to seek God in solitude. Pray for monks and hermits, for those who do penance for others, and for me, that I may find in my own room a place of prayer, and in prayer a taste of paradise. Amen.
Sit in your cell as in paradise. Where is your cell, the place where you could be still before God each day?

The eldest son of a marquis, trained for soldiering and the court, who gave up his inheritance to become a Jesuit. He studied in Rome under the direction of Saint Robert Bellarmine and died at twenty-three after nursing the sick in an epidemic. He is the patron of young people and of those who care for the sick.

Luigi Gonzaga was born at Castiglione delle Stiviere, heir to his father’s title, and was dressed as a little soldier almost as soon as he could walk. Serving at the courts of Florence, Mantua and Madrid, he saw their violence and vanity and turned to prayer. He received his first Communion from Saint Charles Borromeo. His father resisted his vocation for years, but in 1585 Aloysius signed his rights over to his brother and entered the Jesuit novitiate in Rome. He was not naturally gentle, and worked hard against his own stubbornness. In 1591 an epidemic struck Rome and the Jesuits opened a hospital. Aloysius begged in the streets for the sick and nursed them himself, and after carrying a dying man from the street he caught the disease. He died on 21 June 1591. Bellarmine, who had been his confessor, asked to be buried beside him.

Saint Aloysius, you gave up a title and a fortune to belong wholly to Christ, and you gave your life caring for the sick. Pray for young people, that they may be pure, brave and free. Pray for nurses and carers, and for me, that I may serve the sick as I would serve Christ. Amen.

O God, bestower of heavenly gifts, Who in the angelic youth Aloysius joined wondrous innocence of life to an equally wondrous love of penance; grant, by his merits and prayers, that we who have not followed him in his innocence may imitate him in his penance. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He asked what each thing he did would matter for eternity. Ask that question once today before you choose.
Saints John Fisher and Thomas More · Life

A bishop and a layman who were put to death under Henry VIII for refusing to accept the king as head of the Church in England. John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, was beheaded on 22 June 1535; Thomas More, the former Lord Chancellor, on 6 July. Both were canonised in 1935. More is the patron of statesmen and politicians.
Saints John Fisher and Thomas More · Life

John Fisher was a Yorkshireman, a Cambridge scholar and chancellor of the university, confessor to Lady Margaret Beaufort and for thirty years bishop of the poor diocese of Rochester, which he refused to leave for richer sees. Thomas More was a London lawyer, a devoted father who educated his daughters as well as his son, the author of Utopia and a friend of Erasmus. He rose to be Lord Chancellor in 1529 and resigned in 1532. Both men held that the king’s first marriage was valid and that the Pope was head of the Church, and both refused the oath demanded by the Act of Succession in 1534. They were imprisoned in the Tower. While Fisher was there, Pope Paul III made him a cardinal. Fisher went to the block on Tower Hill on 22 June 1535, More on 6 July, declaring that he died the king’s good servant, but God’s first.
Saints John Fisher and Thomas More · Prayer to

Saint John Fisher and Saint Thomas More, you served your king and your country faithfully, but you would not betray your conscience or the Church. Pray for all in public life, for lawyers and judges, for bishops, and for England. Give me a conscience formed by truth, and the courage and good humour to follow it. Amen.
Saints John Fisher and Thomas More · Meditation
The king’s good servant, but God’s first. Where in your work do these two loyalties meet, and which comes first?
The Birth of Saint John the Baptist · Life

Only three births are kept as feasts in the Church’s calendar: Christ’s, Our Lady’s and John the Baptist’s. John was born to Zechariah and Elizabeth in their old age, sanctified, the Church holds, when he leapt in his mother’s womb at the Visitation. His feast falls six months before Christmas, as the days begin to shorten.
The Birth of Saint John the Baptist · Life

Saint Luke tells how the angel Gabriel appeared to the priest Zechariah in the Temple and promised that his wife Elizabeth, long childless, would bear a son. Zechariah doubted and was struck dumb. When Mary, carrying Christ, visited her cousin, the child leapt in Elizabeth’s womb. At his circumcision the neighbours wanted to call him after his father, but Zechariah wrote, ‘His name is John,’ and at once his tongue was loosed and he sang the Benedictus, which the Church prays every morning. John grew up in the desert and came to prepare the way of the Lord, the last of the prophets and the greatest born of women. Saint Augustine saw meaning in the dates: after John’s birth the days grow shorter, after Christ’s they lengthen, for he must increase and I must decrease. The hymn for this feast, Ut queant laxis, gave us the names of the notes of the scale.
The Birth of Saint John the Baptist · Prayer to

Saint John the Baptist, you leapt for joy at the coming of Christ before you were born, and you spent your life pointing to Him. Pray for me, that I may make way for Him in my heart, speak truthfully, and be glad to decrease so that He may increase. Pray for mothers and for children not yet born. Amen.
The Birth of Saint John the Baptist · Prayer

O God, Who made this a day most worthy of our celebration because of blessed John; grant Your people the grace of spiritual joys and direct the minds of all the faithful into the path of eternal salvation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Birth of Saint John the Baptist · Meditation
He must increase, but I must decrease. Where do you need to step aside today, so that Christ may be seen?

A northern Italian who, after a pilgrimage to Compostela as a youth, became a hermit in the mountains of southern Italy. Disciples gathered round him on Monte Vergine, near Avellino, and he founded the monastery there, which became the head of a Benedictine congregation and one of the great Marian shrines of Italy.

William was born at Vercelli in Piedmont and orphaned young. Still in his teens, he set out as a pilgrim to the shrine of Saint James at Compostela, and on his return resolved to go on to Jerusalem. On the way south he was stopped, tradition holds, by robbers or by a sense that God wanted him in Italy, and he settled as a hermit on Monte Vergine. Others came to share his life, and around 1119 a church and monastery rose there. He gave his followers a strict rule of poverty and prayer, but some later wanted an easier life, and William left them in peace to found other houses in the south, among them the abbey of Goleto, where he died in 1142. King Roger II of Sicily valued his counsel. The shrine of Our Lady of Montevergine still draws great crowds of pilgrims.
Saint William of Vercelli · Prayer to

Saint William, pilgrim and hermit, you set out on the road and found God waiting on a mountain. Pray for all pilgrims and for those who do not know where God is leading them. Help me to travel lightly, to pray often, and to rest at last in the Lord. Amen.

O God, Who made Your Saints an example and a help for our weakness; grant us, as we walk the path of salvation, so to venerate the virtues of the blessed Abbot William that we may obtain his intercession and follow in his footsteps. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He set out for Jerusalem and God stopped him halfway. Can you accept a plan of yours being changed for a better one?

Two Roman martyrs named every day in the Roman Canon. Tradition holds they were brothers and Christian officials of the imperial household, put to death in their own house on the Caelian Hill under Julian the Apostate. A basilica was built over the house, and the rooms beneath it, with early Christian paintings, can still be seen.

The story of John and Paul comes down in a later account of their passion whose details cannot all be trusted, but their cult in Rome is very old and their names have stood in the Canon of the Mass since early times. According to that account, they had served Constantia, daughter of the Emperor Constantine, and when Julian, who abandoned the faith, came to the throne in 361, they refused to serve him or to offer incense to the gods. Given ten days to reconsider, they spent them giving away their goods to the poor. They were executed secretly in their house and buried there. In the late fourth century the senator Pammachius, a friend of Saint Jerome, built a church over the site. Excavations in the nineteenth century uncovered beneath it a Roman house with rooms painted with Christian scenes, including a figure at prayer.
Saints John and Paul · Prayer to

Saints John and Paul, you were given ten days to deny Christ and you spent them giving to the poor. Pray for those who serve in public life, for brothers and sisters, and for households of faith. Make my home a place where Christ is loved, and my goods a gift to those in need. Amen.

We beseech You, almighty God, that on this feast-day we may have the double joy of celebrating blessed John and Paul, true brothers who obtained eternal glory through one faith and one martyrdom. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Their house became a church. What would it take for Christ to be truly at home in yours?

A Greek from Smyrna who as a boy listened to Saint Polycarp, the disciple of Saint John, and became bishop of Lyons in Gaul. His great work Against Heresies refuted the Gnostics by appealing to Scripture and to the faith handed down in the churches from the apostles. Pope Francis named him a Doctor of the Church, the Doctor of Unity, in 2022.

Irenaeus remembered in old age how Polycarp used to describe his conversations with John and others who had seen the Lord. He went west to Lyons as a priest, and in 177 was sent to Rome with a letter to Pope Eleutherius. While he was away a fierce persecution broke out, and the aged bishop Pothinus died in prison with many of his flock. Irenaeus returned to become bishop in his place. Against the Gnostics, who claimed secret knowledge and despised the material world, he insisted on the one God who made heaven and earth, on the true flesh of Christ, and on the tradition preserved in the churches by the succession of bishops, giving the list of the bishops of Rome. When Pope Victor threatened to cut off the churches of Asia over the date of Easter, Irenaeus urged him to keep the peace. He is honoured as a martyr, though how he died is not known.

Saint Irenaeus, you received the faith from those who had known the apostles and handed it on whole. Pray for the unity of the Church, for teachers of the faith, and for me, that I may love creation as God’s gift and believe all that He has revealed. Amen.
The glory of God is a living man, Irenaeus wrote, and the life of man is the vision of God. Where are you most fully alive?

The fisherman Christ made the rock of His Church, and the persecutor He made the apostle to the nations. Both were martyred in Rome under Nero, Peter crucified, by tradition upside down, near the Vatican Hill, and Paul beheaded on the road to Ostia. The Church has kept their feast together on this day since at least the third century.

Simon of Bethsaida left his nets at Christ’s word, confessed Him as the Son of the living God, and received the name Peter and the keys of the kingdom. He denied his Lord three times and three times was asked, ‘Do you love me?’ After Pentecost he led the Church in Jerusalem and, by ancient tradition, came at last to Rome. Saul of Tarsus, a zealous Pharisee, was thrown to the ground on the road to Damascus and rose an apostle. He crossed the Mediterranean founding churches and wrote the letters that form much of the New Testament. Writing near the end, he said, ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.’ Excavations beneath Saint Peter’s in the twentieth century uncovered the ancient shrine over Peter’s grave, and Paul lies beneath the basilica that bears his name outside the walls.
Saints Peter and Paul · Prayer to

Saint Peter and Saint Paul, pillars of the Church, one who fell and was forgiven, one who persecuted and was called, pray for the Pope and for the whole Church. Give me Peter’s love and Paul’s zeal, and help me to keep the faith to the end. Amen.

O God, Who made this day holy by the martyrdom of Your Apostles Peter and Paul, grant Your Church to follow in all things the teaching of those from whom she first received the faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Christ asked Peter only one question after the Resurrection: do you love me? Hear Him ask you the same.
The First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church · Life

The unnamed Christians of Rome put to death by Nero after the great fire of July 64, which he blamed on them. The Roman historian Tacitus, no friend of the faith, records their deaths with something like pity. The day after Peter and Paul, the Church honours this great multitude who died with the apostles.
The First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church · Life

In July 64 a fire swept through Rome for nearly a week and destroyed much of the city. Rumour held that the Emperor Nero had started it, and to deflect the blame he turned on the Christians, a small and despised community. Tacitus, writing some fifty years later, says that a vast number were convicted, not so much of arson as of hatred of the human race. Some were dressed in the skins of animals and torn by dogs, some crucified, and some set alight to serve as torches in Nero’s gardens, near the Vatican Hill, while he drove among the crowds in a charioteer’s dress. Saint Clement of Rome, writing to the Corinthians at the end of the century, remembers this great multitude of the elect alongside Peter and Paul. Their names are lost, but their blood was, in Tertullian’s phrase, the seed of Christians.
The First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church · Prayer to

Holy martyrs of Rome, you died nameless and despised, and God has written your names in heaven. Pray for Christians persecuted today, for those blamed for what they did not do, and for me, that I may not be ashamed of Christ when the world turns against Him. Amen.
The First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church · Meditation
We do not know a single one of their names. Can you be content to serve God unknown?
The Most Precious Blood of Our Lord · Life

A feast honouring the Blood of Christ, shed for our redemption at the circumcision, in Gethsemane, at the scourging and on the cross, and given to us in the chalice. Pius IX extended it to the whole Church in 1849. Though now joined in the newer calendar to Corpus Christi, July is still kept as the month of the Precious Blood.
The Most Precious Blood of Our Lord · Life

Devotion to the Precious Blood runs through the Church’s history, from Saint Peter’s words that we were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, to the mystics of the Middle Ages. In the nineteenth century it was spread by Saint Gaspar del Bufalo, who founded the Missionaries of the Precious Blood in 1815. In 1849 Pius IX, in exile at Gaeta during the revolution in Rome, was urged by one of Gaspar’s missionaries to promise the feast to the whole Church, and after his return he did so. Pius XI raised its rank in 1934, the nineteenth centenary of the Redemption, and John XXIII approved a litany of the Precious Blood in 1960. The 1969 calendar joined the feast to that of the Body and Blood of Christ, but the devotion remains, and the traditional calendar keeps it on 1 July.
The Most Precious Blood of Our Lord · Prayer to

Lord Jesus Christ, You shed Your Precious Blood for me in the garden, at the pillar and on the cross, and You give it to me in the chalice. Wash me clean of my sins, make me grateful for so great a price, and let Your Blood plead for the whole world before the Father. Amen.
The Most Precious Blood of Our Lord · Prayer

Almighty, eternal God, Who made Your only-begotten Son the Redeemer of the world, and willed to be reconciled by His Blood, grant us, we beseech You, so to worship in this sacred rite the price of our salvation, and to be so protected by its power against the evils of the present life on earth, that we may enjoy its everlasting fruit in heaven. Through the same Christ our Lord…
The Most Precious Blood of Our Lord · Meditation
You were bought with a price. Look at a crucifix today and ask what you are worth to Him.

One of the Twelve, called Didymus, the Twin. He would not believe the others had seen the risen Lord until he could touch His wounds, and when Christ came again he made the clearest confession of faith in the Gospels: ‘My Lord and my God.’ Ancient tradition holds that he carried the Gospel to India and was martyred there.

Saint John’s Gospel gives Thomas a voice of his own. When Jesus resolved to go back to Judaea, where His enemies waited, it was Thomas who said, ‘Let us also go, that we may die with Him.’ At the Last Supper he asked, ‘Lord, we do not know where You are going; how can we know the way?’, and drew the answer, ‘I am the way, the truth and the life.’ Absent when the risen Christ first appeared, he refused to believe without touching the wounds. Eight days later Christ invited him to do so, and he cried out, ‘My Lord and my God.’ Christ blessed those who have not seen and yet believe. The Christians of Kerala in southern India, who call themselves Saint Thomas Christians, trace their faith to him, and tradition places his martyrdom by a spear near Chennai. His relics were later honoured at Edessa and at Ortona in Italy.
Saint Thomas the Apostle · Prayer to

Saint Thomas, you were brave enough to go with Christ to death and honest enough to say you could not believe. Pray for all who doubt, and for the Christians of India. When my faith is weak, lead me to the wounds of Christ, so that I too may say, ‘My Lord and my God.’ Amen.
Christ did not scold Thomas for his doubt; He showed him His wounds. What doubt could you bring honestly to Him today?

A doctor from Cremona who became a priest and founded the Clerics Regular of Saint Paul, known as the Barnabites after their church in Milan, and an order of sisters. Devoted to Saint Paul and to the Eucharist, he worked to renew the faith of clergy and laity in a troubled age. He died at thirty-six.

Anthony Zaccaria was left fatherless as a baby and raised by a devout young mother. He studied medicine at Padua and practised as a doctor in Cremona, caring for the poor, but came to see that souls needed healing too. He taught the catechism, studied theology and was ordained in 1528. Moving to Milan, he joined a confraternity working for reform, and around 1530 founded a congregation of priests dedicated to preaching Saint Paul’s letters and calling people to conversion. It took its popular name from the church of Saint Barnabas, which they served. With Countess Ludovica Torelli he founded the Angelic Sisters of Saint Paul, and he also formed a group of married lay people. He promoted frequent Communion and the Forty Hours’ adoration of the Blessed Sacrament, and the ringing of church bells on Friday afternoons in memory of the Passion.
Exhausted, he died in his mother’s arms at Cremona in 1539.
Saint Anthony Mary Zaccaria · Prayer to

Saint Anthony Mary, physician of bodies and of souls, you loved Christ crucified and burned with the zeal of Saint Paul. Pray for doctors, for priests, and for the renewal of the Church. Help me to read the Scriptures with love and to come often to Christ in the Eucharist. Amen.

Grant us, O Lord God, to learn in the spirit of Paul the Apostle that excelling knowledge of Jesus Christ, by which St. Anthony Mary, himself wondrously learned, gathered together in Your Church new families of clerics and virgins. Through the same Christ our Lord…
He taught that lukewarmness is the great enemy of the soul. In which part of your life have you grown lukewarm?

An Italian farm girl of eleven who was stabbed by a young neighbour when she resisted his attempt to assault her. Before she died the next day she forgave him and said she wanted him with her in heaven. Years later he repented and asked her mother’s forgiveness. Pius XII canonised her in 1950, before the largest crowd ever gathered for a canonisation.

Maria was born at Corinaldo, near Ancona, to a poor farming family. Seeking work, they moved to the marshes near Nettuno, south of Rome, sharing a farmhouse with the Serenelli family. Her father died of malaria in 1900, and while her mother worked the fields, Maria kept house and cared for the younger children. She had little schooling but loved her faith, and made her first Communion not long before she died. On 5 July that year Alessandro Serenelli, aged twenty, tried to force himself on her, and when she refused, saying it was a sin, he stabbed her many times. She died in hospital the next day, having forgiven him. Alessandro was sentenced to thirty years. In prison he dreamed of Maria offering him lilies, and his heart changed. On his release he asked her mother’s forgiveness and received it, and he spent the rest of his life working for Capuchin friars.

Saint Maria Goretti, you were young and poor and you chose to suffer rather than sin, and you forgave the one who killed you. Pray for children and for all who suffer violence, for the healing of those who have been harmed, and for the conversion of those who do harm. Teach me to forgive. Amen.
She wanted the man who killed her to be with her in heaven. Is there anyone you would rather not meet there?

A princess of Aragon, named after her great-aunt Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, who was married young to King Denis of Portugal. She bore his infidelities with patience, cared for the poor and sick, and more than once made peace between her husband and their rebellious son. Widowed, she lived as a Franciscan tertiary beside the Poor Clares at Coimbra.

Elizabeth was married at about twelve to King Denis, a capable ruler but an unfaithful husband. She kept a regular life of prayer at court, founded hospitals, a shelter for abandoned women and foundling homes, and brought up the king’s children by other women with kindness. When her son Afonso rose in arms against his father, she worked tirelessly for reconciliation, and in 1323, tradition says, rode out between the two armies to stop the battle. After Denis died in 1325 she made a pilgrimage to Compostela, then lived simply in a house beside the convent of Poor Clares she had founded at Coimbra. In 1336, though old and ill, she travelled in summer heat to make peace between her son, now king, and the king of Castile. She died at Estremoz soon after and was canonised in 1625. Portugal remembers her as the Holy Queen.
Saint Elizabeth of Portugal · Prayer to

Saint Elizabeth, queen and peacemaker, you answered unfaithfulness with patience and war with reconciliation. Pray for marriages under strain, for families at odds, and for all who rule. Give me the courage to step between those who quarrel, and the humility to begin with myself. Amen.

Most merciful God, Who among other admirable gifts, endowed blessed Queen Elizabeth with the special grace of calming the tumult of war; grant by her intercession that, after the peace for which we humbly pray, we may attain everlasting happiness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
She rode out between her husband and her son. Where could you be a bridge rather than take a side?
Saint Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions · Life

One hundred and twenty martyrs who died in China over nearly three centuries: eighty-seven Chinese Catholics, priests, catechists, laymen, women and children, and thirty-three missionaries from Europe. Augustine Zhao Rong, a soldier who became a priest, died in prison in 1815. Saint John Paul II canonised them together in 2000.
Saint Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions · Life

Christianity reached China more than once, and from the seventeenth century missionaries built communities that endured repeated persecution. The first of these martyrs, the Dominican Francis Fernández de Capillas, was killed in 1648. Augustine Zhao Rong was a soldier who escorted the French missionary bishop Gabriel Taurin Dufresse to his martyrdom in 1815. Moved by the bishop’s patience, he asked for baptism, was ordained priest, and was himself arrested, tortured and died in prison. Many of the others died in the violence of 1900, among them whole families, catechists, seminarians, and girls in their teens, some of whom were offered their lives if they would renounce Christ and refused. The last died in 1930. The Church honours them not for any cause of nation or politics but because they would not deny Christ, and many died praying for those who killed them.
Saint Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions · Prayer to

Holy martyrs of China, you were soldiers and farmers, priests and children, and you would not deny Christ. Pray for the Catholics of China and for all their people, that the Gospel may be heard there in freedom. Pray for me, that I may love Christ more than my life. Amen.
Saint Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions · Meditation
A soldier watched a bishop die and asked to be baptised. Who is watching how you carry your cross?
The Seven Holy Brothers, and Saints Rufina and Secunda · Life

Two groups of early Roman martyrs kept together on this day. The seven brothers, by tradition sons of Saint Felicity, died under Antoninus Pius in the second century; Rufina and Secunda, two sisters who had vowed themselves to God, died under Valerian in the third. The brothers were already honoured on 10 July in the Roman calendar of 354.
The Seven Holy Brothers, and Saints Rufina and Secunda · Life

The old Roman list of the burials of martyrs, compiled in 354, records on this day seven martyrs buried in four different cemeteries around the city: Felix and Philip, Martial, Vitalis and Alexander, Silvanus, and Januarius. A later account made them the seven sons of Saint Felicity, a widow who encouraged each of them to die bravely before she died herself, like the mother in the Book of Maccabees. Whatever their family ties, their cult is ancient and well founded. Rufina and Secunda, according to their tradition, were sisters of a Christian family in Rome who refused marriage in order to belong to Christ, and who were arrested when they would not deny Him. They were put to death on the Via Cornelia, outside the city, around 257. A bishopric near Rome later bore Rufina’s name.
The Seven Holy Brothers, and Saints Rufina and Secunda · Prayer to

Holy brothers and holy sisters, martyrs of Rome, you encouraged one another to be faithful to the end. Pray for brothers and sisters in every family, for mothers who hand on the faith, and for all consecrated virgins. Help my family to strengthen one another in Christ. Amen.
The Seven Holy Brothers, and Saints Rufina and Secunda · Prayer

Grant, we beseech You, almighty God, that we who know how courageously Your holy Martyrs have confessed the faith, may experience their goodness as they intercede for us with You. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Seven Holy Brothers, and Saints Rufina and Secunda · Meditation
Seven brothers, two sisters, one Lord. How do you help those closest to you to be faithful?

The father of monks in the West. Leaving his studies in Rome, he lived as a hermit at Subiaco, then founded the monastery of Monte Cassino and wrote the Rule that has guided monks and nuns ever since. His sons and daughters carried learning and prayer across Europe, and Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964.

All we know of Benedict comes from the Dialogues of Pope Saint Gregory the Great, written about fifty years after his death. Born at Nursia in Umbria, he was sent to study in Rome, but the city’s vice drove him away, and he lived for three years in a cave at Subiaco. Monks nearby asked him to be their abbot, and when his strictness displeased them, they tried to poison him. He went on to found twelve small monasteries around Subiaco, and around 529 moved to Monte Cassino, where he built his great abbey on the site of a pagan temple. There he wrote his Rule, which opens, ‘Listen, my son,’ and orders the day around prayer, work and holy reading with moderation and good sense. Its heart is to prefer nothing to the love of Christ. His twin sister Saint Scholastica led nuns nearby. He died standing in the chapel, supported by his monks.

Saint Benedict, father of monks, you taught that nothing is to be preferred to the love of Christ. Pray for Europe, for all monks and nuns, and for me, that I may listen with the ear of my heart, keep a rhythm of prayer and work, and receive every guest as Christ. Amen.
Listen with the ear of your heart, the Rule begins. When did you last truly listen, to God or to anyone?

A young Florentine nobleman who, on Good Friday, met the man who had killed his brother and, when the man begged for mercy with his arms outstretched like a cross, spared him. Tradition holds that the crucifix in the church where he then prayed bowed its head to him. He became a monk and founded the abbey of Vallombrosa.

John Gualbert was bound by the code of his class to avenge his brother’s murder. Riding into Florence with armed men on Good Friday, he came upon the killer in a narrow way where neither could pass. The man fell to his knees and stretched out his arms, and John, remembering Christ who forgave on that day, put up his sword and embraced him. He went into the church of San Miniato to pray, and the crucifix, as tradition tells it, bowed to him. He became a Benedictine monk there, but left when a new abbot bought his office. After a time at Camaldoli he founded his own community in the forested valley of Vallombrosa, east of Florence, under a strict Benedictine rule. He fought simony fearlessly and cared for the poor in famine. He died in 1073 and was canonised in 1193. Pius XII named him patron of foresters.

Saint John Gualbert, you had every right by the world’s standards to take revenge, and on Good Friday you chose mercy. Pray for all who have been gravely wronged, for those who long for revenge, and for me, that I may forgive as Christ forgave me, from the cross. Amen.

May the intercession of the blessed Abbot Joánnis Gualbérti, commend us to You, O Lord, so that through his merits we may obtain that which we cannot accomplish by our own. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The man who killed his brother held out his arms like a cross, and John saw Christ in him. Whose outstretched arms have you ignored?

Duke of Bavaria, king of Germany and from 1014 Holy Roman Emperor, Henry II governed as a Christian ruler, supported the reform of monasteries and founded the diocese of Bamberg, where he and his wife Saint Cunigunde are buried. He is the only German king to be canonised and is a patron of Benedictine oblates.

Henry was educated by Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, and inherited the duchy of Bavaria. Chosen king in 1002, he spent much of his reign holding together a fractious realm, and his wars were not all glorious, but he saw his office as a service of God and of the Church. He founded the diocese of Bamberg in 1007 and built its cathedral, endowed monasteries and supported the reforming monks of Cluny and Lorraine. Pope Benedict VIII crowned him emperor in Rome in 1014, and at Henry’s request the Creed began to be sung at Mass in Rome, as it already was north of the Alps. He and Cunigunde had no children, and a later tradition held that they lived as brother and sister. He died in 1024 and was canonised in 1146.

Saint Henry, you held great power and tried to use it for God and for your people. Pray for all who govern, for husbands and wives, and for those who serve the Church as lay people. Help me to do my daily work as a service to Christ the King. Amen.
An emperor can be a saint, and so can you, in whatever station God has placed you. What would holiness look like in your job today?

A soldier and gambler who lost everything, was converted while labouring for Capuchin friars, and gave the rest of his life to the sick. He founded the Ministers of the Sick, whose red cross later became a familiar sign of care for the wounded. He is the patron of the sick, of nurses and of hospitals.

Camillus was born at Bucchianico in the Abruzzo, a large, quick-tempered young man who followed his father into soldiering. He gambled away his money and even his shirt. In 1575, working as a labourer at a Capuchin friary in Manfredonia, he was moved by a friar’s words and resolved to change his life. He tried to become a Capuchin but an ulcer on his leg, which troubled him all his life, kept him out. He went instead to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome as a patient and then as a nurse, and rose to run it. Appalled by the neglect of the sick, he gathered men who would care for them as a mother cares for her only child. With Saint Philip Neri as his confessor he was ordained in 1584. His congregation nursed the plague-stricken and served on the battlefield. He died in Rome in 1614.
Saint Camillus de Lellis · Prayer to

Saint Camillus, you knew weakness and sin and you found Christ in the sick. Pray for the sick and dying, for nurses, doctors and carers, and for hospitals. Give me a heart that serves the suffering as a mother serves her only child, and that does not give up on itself. Amen.
He told his brothers to put more heart into their hands. Where could you put more heart into what your hands do?

A Franciscan theologian who taught at Paris alongside Saint Thomas Aquinas, then led the Franciscan order for seventeen years as its minister general, so wisely that he is called its second founder. He wrote the official life of Saint Francis and The Journey of the Mind into God. He is the Seraphic Doctor of the Church.

Giovanni di Fidanza was born at Bagnoregio near Viterbo. Tradition holds that as a child he was cured of a grave illness through the prayers of Saint Francis. He studied at Paris, joined the Franciscans, and became a master of theology at the same time as Aquinas. In 1257 he was elected minister general of an order divided between those who wanted strict poverty and those who wanted to adapt. He held it together with firmness and charity, gave it constitutions, and wrote the Major Life of Francis. His mystical works trace how all creation, rightly seen, leads the soul upward to God. Gregory X made him cardinal bishop of Albano in 1273, and the story is told that when the envoys came with his red hat he was washing dishes and asked them to hang it on a tree. He died during the Council of Lyons in 1274, which he had helped to prepare.

Saint Bonaventure, you studied deeply and loved more deeply still, and you saw the footprints of God in all creation. Pray for teachers and students of theology, for the Franciscan family, and for me, that my learning may lead me to prayer and my prayer to love. Amen.
He asked his readers to look at creation as a ladder to God. What in nature has drawn you towards Him?
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Life

Mount Carmel in the Holy Land is where the prophet Elijah called down fire from heaven. In the twelfth century hermits settled there in honour of Our Lady and became the Carmelite order. This feast, their patronal feast, spread to the whole Church, and with it the Brown Scapular, a sign of consecration to Mary.
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Life

The first Carmelites were Latin hermits who gathered by the spring of Elijah on Mount Carmel and received a rule from Saint Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, in the early thirteenth century. As the Crusader kingdoms fell they moved to Europe, including England, where they became friars. A cherished tradition holds that the English Carmelite Saint Simon Stock, praying for his struggling order, received a vision of Our Lady holding out the scapular, the part of the habit worn over the shoulders, as a sign of her protection. The vision is a matter of pious tradition, but the Church has long approved the small Brown Scapular as a sacramental, worn as a pledge of devotion to Mary and of a Christian life. The feast was kept in England in the fourteenth century and extended to the whole Church in 1726. The Carmelite friars returned to their old priory at Aylesford in Kent in 1949.
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Prayer to

Holy Mary, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, flower of Carmel and splendour of heaven, clothe me in your protection as a mother clothes her child. Help me to live the faith I profess, to pray as the prophets prayed, and to die in the friendship of your Son. Amen.
Our Lady of Mount Carmel · Meditation
Elijah heard God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. Make space today to hear it.

The first bishop of Ravenna, honoured there as a martyr since very early times. Tradition, recorded centuries later, made him a disciple sent from Antioch by Saint Peter. The great basilica of Sant’Apollinare in Classe, consecrated in 549, keeps his memory, and its apse mosaic shows him in prayer among his flock, pictured as sheep.

Almost nothing certain is known of Apollinaris except that he founded the Church in Ravenna and that his people honoured him as their first bishop and a witness for Christ. Saint Peter Chrysologus, preaching in Ravenna in the fifth century, spoke of him as a bishop who had suffered much for the faith, and the city built him two great churches. A later account of his life, written to support Ravenna’s dignity, tells that Peter sent him from Antioch, that he worked wonders, was repeatedly beaten and exiled, and returned each time to his flock until he died of his wounds. Whatever the details, his memory has been kept with great love. In the apse at Classe, above a field of trees, flowers and birds, he stands with his arms raised in prayer beneath a jewelled cross, the shepherd of a flock of twelve white sheep.

Saint Apollinaris, first shepherd of Ravenna, you suffered for your flock and would not abandon them. Pray for bishops and for all who lead the Church, for those who are exiled or driven out, and for me, that I may stand among God’s people with my hands raised in prayer. Amen.
He is remembered not by his words but by his prayer among his people. How do others see you pray?

A Capuchin friar of extraordinary gifts: a master of many languages, a tireless preacher, minister general of his order, and a peacemaker trusted by princes. He was chaplain to the imperial army that fought the Turks in Hungary in 1601. John XXIII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1959, the Apostolic Doctor.

Giulio Cesare Russo was born at Brindisi in Apulia and was orphaned young. He entered the Capuchins at Verona in 1575 and took the name Lawrence. He studied at Padua and mastered Hebrew, Greek, German, Bohemian and other languages, and knew much of the Bible by heart in its original tongues. Sent to preach in Rome and then across Italy, Austria, Bohemia and Germany, he founded friaries and strengthened Catholics in lands divided by the Reformation. In 1601, as chaplain to the imperial forces at Székesfehérvár in Hungary, he rode before the troops holding a crucifix. Elected minister general in 1602, he visited his friars on foot across Europe. He served as an envoy for peace between Catholic princes, and in 1619 travelled to Lisbon to plead with the king of Spain on behalf of the people of Naples against their viceroy. He died there on his birthday, 22 July.
Saint Lawrence of Brindisi · Prayer to

Saint Lawrence, you used every gift God gave you for the Gospel and for peace. Pray for preachers and scholars, for those who work for peace between nations, and for me, that I may love the Word of God, learn it by heart, and speak up for those who are oppressed. Amen.

O God, Who, to enable him to accomplish tasks, no matter how difficult, for the glory of Your name and the salvation of souls, endowed blessed Lawrence, Your Confessor and Doctor, with the spirit of wisdom and fortitude; grant us, in the same spirit, ever to know our duty, and through his prayers to do it. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
He crossed Europe on foot to plead for the poor of Naples. Whose cause could you take up, even in a small way?

A woman of Magdala in Galilee from whom Christ cast out seven devils. She followed Him with the other women, stood by the cross, and was the first to see Him risen, sent by Him to tell the apostles. The Church calls her the apostle to the apostles, and in 2016 her memorial was raised to a feast.

Saint Luke names Mary Magdalene first among the women who travelled with Jesus and provided for Him out of their means. When the apostles fled, she stood at the cross with the Mother of Jesus, and she watched where He was laid. Early on the first day of the week she came to the tomb and found it empty. Weeping, she did not know the risen Christ until He spoke her name, and she answered, ‘Rabboni.’ He told her not to cling to Him but to go to His brethren, and she went and announced, ‘I have seen the Lord.’ Western tradition, following Saint Gregory the Great, long identified her with the woman who wept over Christ’s feet and with Mary of Bethany, and so she became the great model of the repentant sinner. The calendar now distinguishes them, but her love and her tears for the Lord are certain.

Saint Mary Magdalene, you were set free by Christ and loved Him to the end, at the cross and at the empty tomb. Pray for all who are bound by sin or by evil, for those who weep, and for me, that I may know the Lord when He calls my name and run to tell others. Amen.

May the prayers of blessed Mary Magdalen help us, O Lord, Who were moved by her prayers and brought back alive from the grave her brother Lazarus, dead for four days. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
She did not recognise Him until He said her name. Be still today and let Him say yours.

A Maronite monk and priest of Lebanon who spent his last twenty-three years as a hermit, in prayer, fasting and manual work, celebrating Mass with great devotion. After his death light was reported around his grave and his body was found incorrupt. Thousands of healings have been attributed to him. Paul VI canonised him in 1977.

Youssef Antoun Makhlouf was born in the mountain village of Bekaa Kafra, in northern Lebanon, and lost his father when he was three. Raised by his mother and devout uncles, two of whom were hermits, he left home at twenty-three to enter the Lebanese Maronite Order, taking the name Charbel after an early martyr. He was ordained priest in 1859 and lived at the monastery of Saint Maron at Annaya for sixteen years. In 1875 he was allowed to withdraw to the hermitage of Saints Peter and Paul above the monastery, where he prayed, worked the land, ate once a day and spoke little. Each day he offered Mass with deep recollection. In December 1898 he suffered a stroke while celebrating Mass and died on Christmas Eve. His tomb at Annaya draws pilgrims of every faith, Christian and Muslim alike.

Saint Charbel, hermit of Lebanon, you left everything to live hidden with God, and He has made your hiddenness a light to many. Pray for Lebanon and the Christians of the Middle East, for the sick who come to you, and for me, that I may find God in silence and in the Mass. Amen.
He hardly spoke, and yet he still draws the world to God. What would God say through your silence?

James, son of Zebedee and brother of Saint John, was a fisherman whom Christ called from his nets. With Peter and John he saw the Transfiguration and the agony in the garden. He was the first of the Twelve to die for Christ, beheaded by Herod Agrippa in Jerusalem. Tradition links him with Spain and his shrine at Compostela.

Christ found James and John mending nets in their father’s boat, and they left him with the hired men and followed. He called the brothers Boanerges, sons of thunder, perhaps for their temper: they once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that would not receive Him. Their mother asked that they might sit at His right and left in His kingdom, and Christ asked whether they could drink His cup. James said they could, and he did. Around the year 44 Herod Agrippa I had him put to the sword, the only death of an apostle recorded in the New Testament. A tradition holds that James had preached in Spain and that his body was brought there. In the ninth century a tomb believed to be his was found in Galicia, and Santiago de Compostela became, with Rome and Jerusalem, one of the great pilgrimages of Christendom. Pilgrims still walk the Camino, with the scallop shell as their sign.
Saint James the Apostle · Prayer to

Saint James, son of thunder, you promised to drink the cup of Christ and you kept your word with your life. Pray for pilgrims on every road, for Spain, and for me, that my zeal may become charity, that I may walk faithfully with Christ, and that I may reach the end of the way. Amen.
Can you drink the cup that I drink? James answered yes before he knew what it would cost. What is your answer today?

The parents of the Virgin Mary and grandparents of Jesus. Their names are not in Scripture but come from an ancient tradition recorded in the second century. They are honoured as a holy couple who waited long for a child and offered her to God. They are patrons of grandparents, and the Church keeps a World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly near their feast.

The second-century writing known as the Protoevangelium of James tells that Joachim, a wealthy and devout man, and his wife Anne were childless into old age, and that Joachim was turned away from offering his gift in the Temple because of it. He went into the wilderness to fast and pray, and Anne prayed at home, and an angel told each of them that they would have a child. They met at the Golden Gate of Jerusalem in joy, and Mary was born to them. The story is not Scripture, and the Church does not vouch for its details, but it carries a true instinct: that Mary was prepared for by a faithful family. Devotion to Anne grew in the East from the sixth century and spread through the West in the Middle Ages, being especially strong in medieval England. Great shrines to her stand at Auray in Brittany and Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré in Canada.
Saints Joachim and Anne · Prayer to

Saint Joachim and Saint Anne, you waited in faith and raised the Mother of God in a home of prayer. Pray for grandparents and the elderly, for couples who long for children, and for every family. Help me to hand on the faith to those who come after me. Amen.

O God, Who in Your kindness gave blessed Anne the grace to be the mother of her who mothered Your only-begotten Son, graciously grant that we who keep her feast may be helped by her intercession with You. Through the same Christ our Lord…
The grace given to Mary passed through an ordinary home. What are you handing on to the next generation?
Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent · Life

The traditional calendar joins two martyrs of Milan and two popes on this day. Saint Ambrose found the body of Nazarius in a garden outside Milan in 395, and with it that of the boy Celsus. Victor I, an African, was pope at the end of the second century. Innocent I led the Church in Rome when the city was sacked by the Goths in 410.
Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent · Life

Paulinus, the biographer of Saint Ambrose, tells how in 395 the bishop uncovered the body of the martyr Nazarius in a garden outside the walls of Milan and carried it to the new church of the Apostles, where he is still honoured. Nearby lay Celsus, whom tradition makes a boy disciple martyred with him; when or how they died is unknown. Victor I, pope around 189 to 199, is said to have been the first Latin-speaking bishop of Rome and tried to make all the churches keep Easter on a Sunday, threatening to cut off the churches of Asia until Saint Irenaeus urged him to patience. He is honoured as a martyr by tradition. Innocent I, pope from 401 to 417, defended Saint John Chrysostom when he was exiled, confirmed the African bishops’ condemnation of Pelagius, and laboured for Rome through the barbarian invasions, being at Ravenna seeking peace when Alaric sacked the city.
Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent · Prayer to

Holy martyrs Nazarius and Celsus, holy popes Victor and Innocent, you served Christ in times of persecution, division and collapse. Pray for the Church in every hard season, for the Pope and the bishops, and for me, that I may stand firm when the world around me falls apart. Amen.
Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent · Prayer
May the martyrdom of Your Saints Nazarius, Celsus, Victor and Innocent, give us courage, O Lord, and may it give us a help to counter-balance our weakness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Saints Nazarius and Celsus, Victor and Innocent · Meditation
Innocent watched Rome fall and kept the Church steady. When everything feels uncertain, what in your faith stays fixed?

The sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany, whose house was a home to Christ.
