Saint Luke tells of her busy with serving while Mary sat at His feet; Saint John records her great confession of faith at the tomb of Lazarus. Since 2021 the Church keeps the three siblings together on this day. She is the patron of cooks and of all who serve.

Martha appears in the Gospels as practical, warm and direct. When Christ came to the house at Bethany, she was distracted with much serving and asked Him to tell her sister to help, and He answered gently, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; one thing is needful.’ When Lazarus died, it was Martha who went out to meet Jesus and said, ‘Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.’ He told her, ‘I am the resurrection and the life,’ and she answered, ‘Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God.’ At a supper six days before the Passover, after Lazarus had been raised, Martha served again. A medieval tradition says she later went to Provence and tamed a dragon at Tarascon, where she is honoured to this day.

Saint Martha, you welcomed Christ into your home and served Him with your hands, and you believed in Him when your brother lay in the tomb. Pray for all who cook, clean and care for others, and for me, that I may not be anxious about many things, but choose the one thing needful. Amen.
Hear us, O God, our Saviour, that as we are gladdened by the festival of blessed Martha thy virgin, so we may learn from it piety and devotion. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
One thing is needful. What are the many things that are crowding it out today?

Bishop of Ravenna when it was the capital of the Western Empire, Peter was later called Chrysologus, golden word, for his preaching. Many of his sermons survive: short, vivid and full of love for the Incarnation and the Eucharist. He urged loyalty to the Bishop of Rome in matters of faith. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1729.

Peter was born at Imola and served its bishop as a deacon before being made bishop of Ravenna around 433. The imperial court was then at Ravenna, and the Empress Galla Placidia supported his building of churches and care for the city. His people loved his preaching, which was brief because, he said, he did not want to tire them. Around 180 of his sermons survive, on the Gospels, the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer and the mysteries of Christ’s birth, and he often turns to the Eucharist as the bread come down from heaven. When the monk Eutyches, condemned for teaching that Christ had only one nature, appealed to him, Peter replied that he should listen to the Bishop of Rome, through whom Saint Peter still teaches the faith to those who seek it. He died at Imola around 450. Benedict XIII named him a Doctor of the Church in 1729.

Saint Peter Chrysologus, golden-tongued preacher, you spoke briefly and lovingly of the mysteries of Christ. Pray for all who preach, that they may speak with clarity and warmth, and for me, that I may hunger for the Word and for the Bread of life. Amen.
He kept his sermons short for love of his hearers. How could you say what matters more simply today?

A Basque soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona, and who, reading the life of Christ during his long recovery, gave himself to God. From his own experience he wrote the Spiritual Exercises, and with companions from the University of Paris he founded the Society of Jesus. He governed it from Rome until his death.

Íñigo López de Loyola was a courtier and soldier who dreamed of glory and of noble ladies. Wounded at Pamplona in 1521, he lay for months at Loyola with nothing to read but a life of Christ and lives of the saints. He noticed that daydreams of worldly fame left him empty, while thoughts of following Christ left him at peace, and from this he learned to discern spirits. At Montserrat he hung his sword before the image of Our Lady, and at Manresa he spent a year in prayer and penance, drafting the Exercises. He went back to school with boys, and at Paris won over companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber. In 1534 they made vows together at Montmartre, and in 1540 Paul III approved the Society of Jesus. Ignatius spent his last years in Rome writing its constitutions and sending his sons across the world. He died on 31 July 1556.
Saint Ignatius of Loyola · Prayer to

Saint Ignatius, you learned to find God in all things and to seek His greater glory in everything. Pray for the Society of Jesus, for all who make or give the Exercises, and for me, that I may notice how God moves in my heart, choose what leads me to Him, and give Him my whole self. Amen.

O God, Who, to spread abroad the greater glory of Your name through St. Ignatius, strengthened the Church militant with new power; grant that we who are struggling on earth may, by his help and after his example, be found worthy to be crowned with him in heaven. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
For the greater glory of God: Ignatius asked which of two good things would give God more glory. Ask that of one choice you make today.

A brilliant Neapolitan lawyer who left the courts after losing a case through his own oversight, Alphonsus became a priest, founded the Redemptorists to preach to the neglected poor of the countryside, and wrote on moral theology with a gentleness that changed how confessors treated penitents. He is a Doctor of the Church and patron of confessors.

Alphonsus took his doctorate in law at sixteen and practised with great success until 1723, when he lost an important case through a point he had overlooked. He took it as a sign, laid his sword before a statue of Our Lady and was ordained in 1726. Preaching in the hills above Amalfi, he found shepherds and peasants who had no one to teach them, and in 1732 at Scala he founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer. His Moral Theology steered between rigour and laxity and taught confessors to be fathers rather than judges. He also wrote The Glories of Mary and Visits to the Blessed Sacrament, and the Christmas carol Tu scendi dalle stelle. He was bishop of Sant’Agata dei Goti from 1762 to 1775. In old age, crippled and nearly blind, he was shut out of his own congregation through a misunderstanding, and bore it patiently. He died at Pagani in 1787.

Saint Alphonsus, you spent yourself for the poor and the forgotten, and taught confessors to be merciful. Pray for me when I am weighed down by scruples or discouraged by my sins, that I may trust in the mercy of the Redeemer. Help me to visit Him often in the Blessed Sacrament and to love His Mother as you did. Amen.
Alphonsus wrote that whoever prays is certainly saved, and whoever does not pray is certainly lost. Is there a set time in your day that belongs to God alone?

A French priest of the Alps whose life was drawn ever more strongly to the Eucharist. After years as a Marist he founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament in Paris in 1856, a community of priests and brothers devoted to perpetual adoration, and a sister congregation of women. He is remembered as the apostle of the Eucharist.

Peter Julian was born at La Mure, near Grenoble, the son of a cutler. His father opposed his vocation and his health was poor, but he was ordained for the diocese of Grenoble in 1834 and five years later joined the newly founded Society of Mary. As a Marist superior at Lyon he came to believe that Christ in the Eucharist deserved a community wholly given to Him. With the approval of the Archbishop of Paris he founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament in Paris in 1856, and in 1858, with Marguerite Guillot, the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament. He began perpetual exposition in Paris, prepared poor adult workers for their First Communion, and wrote much on prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Worn out, he died in his home town on 1 August 1868. John XXIII canonised him in 1962, during the Second Vatican Council.
Saint Peter Julian Eymard · Prayer to

Saint Peter Julian, you found in the Eucharist the centre of your life and longed for Christ to be adored in every place. Pray that I may come to Him often, kneel before Him with faith, and receive Him with love. Teach me to make my whole day an act of thanksgiving. Amen.
He taught that adoration is not idleness but the most fruitful work of all. What would it mean to bring one real concern of today to Christ in the tabernacle and simply leave it there?

A farmer’s son who struggled with his studies and was nearly refused ordination, John Vianney was sent in 1818 to Ars, a small village near Lyon where faith had grown cold. By prayer, penance and long hours in the confessional he transformed it, and pilgrims came from all over France to confess to him. He is the patron of parish priests.

Jean-Marie Vianney grew up in the years of the Revolution, when Mass was said in secret, and made his First Communion behind shuttered windows. He began his studies late and found Latin almost impossible; the patient Abbé Balley tutored him, and he was ordained in 1815. In 1818 he became curé of Ars, a village of a little over two hundred people. He visited every family, catechised the children, preached against drunkenness and Sunday work, and spent hours before the tabernacle. In time he heard confessions for eleven hours a day and more, and by his later years some twenty thousand pilgrims a year came to Ars. Several times he tried to slip away to a life of solitude, and each time he returned. He lived on very little and gave away everything he had. He died in 1859, was canonised in 1925 and named patron of parish priests in 1929.

Saint John Vianney, you gave your life to the souls of one small parish and to all who came to you for mercy. Pray for my parish priest and for all priests, that they may be holy, and for me, that I may make a good confession and return to God with my whole heart. Amen.
An old peasant told the curé what he did during his long visits in church: I look at Him and He looks at me. Sit before Christ for five minutes today and let yourself be looked at.
Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major · Life

Soon after the Council of Ephesus proclaimed Mary the Mother of God in 431, Pope Sixtus III built a great basilica in her honour on the Esquiline Hill. It is among the oldest churches in the West dedicated to Our Lady and one of the four major basilicas of Rome. A later legend tells of snow falling there in August, so it is also called Our Lady of the Snows.
Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major · Life

The basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore keeps much of its fifth-century form. The mosaics of Sixtus III still shine along the nave and over the triumphal arch, telling the story of the Old Testament and the childhood of Christ, and proclaiming the faith of Ephesus that Mary’s Son is truly God. A medieval legend says that in the time of Pope Liberius a Roman couple and the pope dreamed that Our Lady wished a church built where snow would fall, and on the morning of 5 August snow lay on the Esquiline. Each year white petals are let fall from the ceiling in memory of it. The basilica keeps the relic venerated as the wood of the crib of Bethlehem and the ancient icon of Our Lady called Salus Populi Romani. Several popes are buried there, among them Saint Pius V and, in 2025, Pope Francis.
Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major · Prayer to

Holy Mary, Mother of God, the people of Rome built a house for you when the Church first proclaimed your dignity. Make my heart a dwelling where your Son is welcome. Protect the Church, guard our families, and lead us to the house of the Father, where you wait for us. Amen.
Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major · Prayer

Grant us, Your servants, O Lord God, we beseech You, to enjoy lasting health of mind and body; and by the intercession of glorious and blessed Mary, ever Virgin, may we be delivered from present sorrow and partake to the full of eternal happiness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Dedication of the Basilica of Saint Mary Major · Meditation
The Church honours a building because of the One born of Mary. Where in your life have you made room for Christ, and where is there still no room at the inn?
The Transfiguration of the Lord · Life

Christ took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, by tradition Mount Tabor, and was transfigured before them: His face shone like the sun and His clothes became white as light. Moses and Elijah spoke with Him of His coming death, and the Father’s voice said, This is my beloved Son; listen to Him.
The Transfiguration of the Lord · Life

All three synoptic Gospels tell of the Transfiguration, and Saint Peter recalls it in his second letter: we were eyewitnesses of His majesty, when we were with Him on the holy mountain. It came soon after Christ first foretold His Passion, and the Fathers saw in it a gift to strengthen the apostles for the scandal of the cross. Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets, both fulfilled in Him. Peter, not knowing what he said, wanted to build three tents and stay. The feast was kept in the East from early centuries. In 1457 Pope Callixtus III extended it to the whole Western Church, in thanksgiving for the relief of Belgrade the year before, news of which had reached Rome on 6 August.
The Transfiguration of the Lord · Prayer to

Lord Jesus, transfigured on the mountain, you showed your friends your glory before they saw you suffer. When my faith is tested by darkness and pain, let me remember the light of your face. Help me to listen to you, as the Father commands, and bring me at last to see you as you are. Amen.
The Transfiguration of the Lord · Prayer

O God, Who in the glorious Transfiguration of Your only-begotten Son strengthened the mysteries of faith by the testimony of the fathers, and, by the voice coming down in a shining cloud, miraculously betokened the complete adoption of Your children, mercifully grant that we be made co-heirs with that King of glory, and sharers in that same glory. Through the same Christ our Lord…
The Transfiguration of the Lord · Meditation
It is good for us to be here, said Peter. Jesus led them back down the mountain. Where is He asking you to carry the light of prayer into ordinary work today?

A nobleman of Vicenza and a lawyer in the papal court, Cajetan became a priest and gave his life to reforming the clergy from within. In 1524 he founded the Theatines, priests who lived in poverty and trusted in Providence alone, refusing even to beg. He served the sick and the poor, and is the patron of those seeking work.

Gaetano dei Conti di Thiene took his doctorate in law at Padua and went to Rome to serve Pope Julius II. There he joined the Oratory of Divine Love, a confraternity of priests and laymen devoted to prayer and to care for the incurable sick, and was ordained in 1516. Grieved by the worldliness of many clergy, in 1524 he founded with Gian Pietro Carafa, the future Pope Paul IV, the Clerks Regular, called Theatines. They lived in strict poverty, owned nothing, did not beg, and relied on what Providence sent, while preaching, celebrating the liturgy well and caring for the sick. During the Sack of Rome in 1527 Cajetan was beaten by soldiers who wanted money he did not have. In Naples he worked among the poor and helped found a lending house to rescue them from usurers. He died there in 1547 and was canonised in 1671.

Saint Cajetan, you trusted the Father to feed His children and gave your life to the poor and the sick. Pray for all who are out of work or anxious about money, that they may find honest work and daily bread. Free me from worry, and teach me to seek first the Kingdom of God. Amen.

O God, Who bestowed upon St. Cajetan, Your Confessor, the grace to follow the apostolic way of life; grant us by his intercession and example ever to trust in You and to long only for the things of heaven. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Cajetan would not let his priests beg, because he believed God already knew what they needed. What would change if you truly believed your Father knows what you need before you ask?

A Castilian canon who, travelling through southern France, saw how the Cathar heresy had won people from the Church, and how little the faith was being preached. He answered with poverty, study and preaching, and founded the Order of Preachers, approved in 1216. His friars spread quickly to the universities and cities of Europe.

Dominic de Guzmán was born at Caleruega in Castile and studied at Palencia, where in a time of famine he sold his precious books to feed the hungry. As a canon of Osma he travelled with his bishop, Diego, through Languedoc, where the Cathars taught that the material world was evil. Dominic saw that the people respected their preachers’ austere lives, and resolved to preach the Gospel in the same poverty, on foot and begging his bread. In 1206 he gathered converted women into a community at Prouille, the first of his nuns. In 1216 Pope Honorius III approved his order, and Dominic soon sent his small band of friars to Paris, Bologna and beyond, to study and to preach. Those who knew him said he spoke only with God or about God, and that he was cheerful by day and wept in prayer by night. He died at Bologna in 1221 and was canonised in 1234.

Saint Dominic, you gave your life to preach the truth with charity and joy. Pray that I may love the truth enough to study it and live it, and speak of God with gentleness to those who do not know Him. Win for the Church preachers who are poor, learned and holy. Amen.
Dominic’s friars were to contemplate and to hand on to others the fruits of contemplation. What have you received from God lately that you could share with someone else?
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross · Life

Edith Stein, a brilliant Jewish philosopher, found the truth she had long sought in reading the life of Saint Teresa of Ávila and was baptised in 1922. She became a Carmelite nun in Cologne. In 1942 she was arrested in the Netherlands and killed at Auschwitz. She is a co-patron of Europe.
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross · Life

Edith Stein was born in Breslau on the Day of Atonement, 1891, the youngest child of a devout Jewish family. As a young woman she lost her faith, studied philosophy and became the assistant of Edmund Husserl. In 1921, staying with friends, she read the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Ávila through the night and, closing it, knew that it was the truth. She was baptised on 1 January 1922. For years she taught at a Dominican school in Speyer, lectured widely and wrote on women and education. Barred from teaching by the Nazi laws of 1933, she entered the Carmel of Cologne that year. In 1938 she was moved to Echt in the Netherlands for safety. After the Dutch bishops publicly condemned the deportation of Jews, the Nazis arrested Catholics of Jewish origin, and on 2 August 1942 Edith and her sister Rosa were taken. She died in the gas chamber at Auschwitz on 9 August.
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross · Life
John Paul II canonised her in 1998.
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross · Prayer to

Saint Teresa Benedicta, you sought the truth with your whole mind and found it in Christ crucified. Pray for all who search, for the Jewish people you loved, and for Europe, whose patron you are. Help me to embrace the cross that comes to me and to stand with those who suffer. Amen.
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross · Meditation
As she was taken, Edith is remembered to have said to her sister, Come, we are going for our people. For whom is God asking you to stand today?

One of the seven deacons of Rome, Lawrence cared for the Church’s goods and its poor. He was martyred in 258 under the Emperor Valerian, a few days after his bishop, Pope Sixtus II. His courage made him one of the best-loved martyrs of Rome, and his name is said in the Roman Canon.

When Valerian ordered the execution of bishops, priests and deacons, Pope Sixtus II was beheaded on 6 August 258. Tradition, recorded by Saint Ambrose, says that Lawrence followed the pope to his death, asking why he should be left behind, and that Sixtus told him he would follow in three days. The prefect of Rome demanded the treasures of the Church. Lawrence asked for time, gathered the poor, the sick and the widows whom the Church supported, and presented them: these are the treasure of the Church. Tradition holds that he was roasted on a gridiron and, with astonishing calm, told his executioners to turn him over, for one side was done. He was buried on the Via Tiburtina, where the basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura now stands. The Perseid meteors of early August are called in Italy the tears of Saint Lawrence.

Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr, you saw the face of Christ in the poor and called them the treasure of the Church. Pray that I may serve them gladly and not be ashamed of them. Give me some of your courage and good humour when I suffer for what is right. Amen.
Grant us, we beseech You, almighty God, to extinguish the flames of our sins, as You granted St. Lawrence to overcome the fires of his tortures. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
These are the treasure of the Church. Who are the poor in your own street or parish, and do you see them as treasure or as a burden?

A young noblewoman of Assisi who, moved by the preaching of Saint Francis, left her family by night in 1212 to give herself to Christ in poverty. At San Damiano she founded the Poor Ladies, now the Poor Clares, and for over forty years guarded their poverty with great firmness. She wrote the first rule for women approved by a pope.

Clare Offreduccio heard Francis preach and resolved to follow Christ as he did. On the night after Palm Sunday 1212 she slipped out of her family’s house and went to the little church of the Portiuncula, where Francis cut her hair and received her vows. Her family tried to bring her back by force, but she held to the altar. Her sister Agnes soon joined her, and later her widowed mother. At San Damiano the sisters lived enclosed, in strict poverty, by prayer and the work of their hands. Clare fought for years for the privilege of owning nothing at all, and her own rule was approved by Innocent IV two days before she died. Tradition holds that when soldiers attacked the convent in 1240 she faced them with the Blessed Sacrament and they fled. Too ill to go to Mass one Christmas, she is said to have seen and heard it from her bed, and so is patron of television. She was canonised in 1255.

Saint Clare, you held fast to Christ poor and crucified and found in Him all your riches. Pray that I may be free of the things I cling to, and find my joy in God. Watch over the Poor Clares and all enclosed nuns, and make my own home a place of prayer and peace. Amen.
Clare urged Saint Agnes of Prague to gaze upon Christ, consider Him and contemplate Him. Spend a few minutes today simply looking at a crucifix or an image of Christ.
Saint Jane Frances de Chantal · Life

A Burgundian baroness, wife and mother, widowed at twenty-eight when her husband was killed in a hunting accident. Under the direction of Saint Francis de Sales she grew in holiness and in 1610 founded with him the Order of the Visitation at Annecy, open to women whose age or health kept them from stricter orders.
Saint Jane Frances de Chantal · Life

Jane Frémyot married Christophe de Rabutin, Baron de Chantal, in 1592, and they were happy together. Four of their children survived infancy. In 1601 Christophe was shot by accident while hunting and died, and Jane, grief-stricken, struggled for years to forgive the man responsible, until at last she stood godmother to his child. In 1604 she heard Francis de Sales preach in Dijon and placed herself under his direction. He taught her a gentle, steady holiness in place of anxiety. In 1610 they founded the Visitation at Annecy. Leaving home was hard; her teenage son, the story goes, lay across the threshold to stop her, and she stepped over him in tears. The order spread quickly, and by her death there were over eighty houses. After Francis died in 1622, Saint Vincent de Paul became her friend and counsellor. She died at Moulins in 1641 and was canonised in 1767.
Saint Jane Frances de Chantal · Prayer to

Saint Jane Frances, you knew the joys of marriage and the grief of losing your husband, and you learned to forgive. Pray for widows and for all who mourn, for those who cannot yet forgive, and for me, that I may serve God with a steady and gentle heart. Amen.
Saint Jane Frances de Chantal · Meditation
Francis de Sales taught her to do everything by love and nothing by force. Where are you trying to force holiness instead of letting God lead you gently?

Pontian was Bishop of Rome and Hippolytus a learned Roman priest who had set himself up as a rival bishop. In 235 the Emperor Maximinus sent them both to the mines of Sardinia, where they died. Tradition holds that they were reconciled there, and both are honoured as martyrs.

Hippolytus was the most important theologian of the Roman Church in the early third century, writing in Greek on Scripture and against the heresies of his time. He thought Pope Callistus too lenient towards repentant sinners and too unclear in his teaching, broke with him and was chosen bishop by a group of followers, the first antipope we know of. The schism lasted into the time of Pope Pontian. When Maximinus Thrax turned on the Church’s leaders in 235, he exiled both men to the mines of Sardinia, where few survived. Pontian resigned his office so that Rome could elect a successor, the first pope known to have done so. Hippolytus is believed to have returned to unity with the Church and urged his followers to do the same. Both died in exile, and Pope Fabian brought their bodies back to Rome to be buried with honour.
Saints Pontian and Hippolytus · Prayer to

Saints Pontian and Hippolytus, you were divided in life and united in suffering for Christ. Pray for all who are estranged within the Church and among Christians, that we may be reconciled before it is too late. Help me to put the unity of the Church above my own opinions. Amen.
A rival bishop and a pope died side by side in the mines. Is there a disagreement you are holding on to that you could lay down for the sake of peace?

A Polish Franciscan who spread devotion to the Immaculate Virgin through the press, founding a great friary and publishing house near Warsaw and a mission in Japan. Imprisoned at Auschwitz, he offered his life in place of a condemned man with a family and died in the starvation bunker. He is honoured as a martyr of charity.

Raymund Kolbe was born at Zduńska Wola. As a boy, he said, Our Lady showed him two crowns, one white for purity and one red for martyrdom, and he accepted both. He joined the Conventual Franciscans, taking the name Maximilian, and in Rome in 1917 founded the Militia of the Immaculata. Back in Poland, despite tuberculosis, he built Niepokalanów, the City of the Immaculata, where hundreds of friars printed magazines read across the country. From 1930 he founded a similar mission at Nagasaki. Arrested by the Gestapo in 1941, he was sent to Auschwitz. That summer, after a prisoner escaped, ten men were chosen to die by starvation. When one, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and children, Maximilian stepped forward and asked to take his place. He led the others in prayer and hymns for two weeks and was killed by lethal injection on 14 August.
Gajowniczek survived and was present when John Paul II canonised him in 1982.

Saint Maximilian, you gave your life for a stranger out of love for Christ and His Mother. Pray for all who suffer in prisons and camps, for families torn apart, and for me, that I may give myself in small ways each day, so that I am ready to give everything if God should ask. Amen.
Hatred is not a creative force; only love is creative, he is remembered as saying. Where is love asking you to take someone else’s place, even in a small thing?
The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

The Church teaches that the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Pope Pius XII defined this as a dogma of faith on 1 November 1950. It is one of the oldest feasts of Our Lady and a holy day of obligation.
The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

Scripture does not describe the end of Mary’s life, but the Church in both East and West has long believed that she who bore Christ was not left to the corruption of the grave. In the East the feast of the Dormition, the falling asleep of the Mother of God, was kept by the sixth century, and the Emperor Maurice fixed it on 15 August. Rome adopted it in the seventh century. Pius XII, after consulting the bishops of the whole world, defined the dogma in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus. The definition does not settle whether Mary died before she was assumed, though the long tradition of East and West speaks of her falling asleep. The feast proclaims what God has done for Mary and promises what He will do for all the faithful: the resurrection of the body and life with God in body and soul.
The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Prayer to

Holy Mary, taken up into heaven, you are the sign of hope for the pilgrim Church. Look on us who still struggle on earth. Keep our eyes on the glory to which God calls us, help us to honour our bodies as temples of the Holy Spirit, and bring us home to your Son. Amen.
The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Prayer

Almighty, everlasting God, Who took up, body and soul, the Immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of Your Son, into heavenly glory, grant, we beseech You, that, always devoting ourselves to heavenly things, we may be found worthy to share in her glory. Through the same Christ our Lord…
The Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Meditation
Where Mary has gone, the Church hopes to follow. How would you live today if you truly believed your body, too, is made for glory?

The first king of Hungary, crowned around the year 1000. Baptised as a boy, Stephen built the Church in his country, founded dioceses and monasteries, gave laws shaped by the Gospel and cared personally for the poor. Before he died he entrusted his kingdom to the Virgin Mary.

Stephen was born Vajk, son of Géza, chief prince of the Magyars, a people who had settled in the Carpathian basin a century before. He was baptised as a boy and married Gisela, sister of the future Emperor Saint Henry II. When Géza died, Stephen put down rebellion and in about the year 1000 was crowned king, by tradition with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II. He founded the archdiocese of Esztergom and other sees, built churches, supported the abbey of Pannonhalma and welcomed missionaries. His laws protected widows and orphans, and he was known to give alms in disguise. His deep grief was the death of his only surviving son, Saint Emeric, in a hunting accident in 1031. Having no heir, Stephen offered Hungary to Our Lady. He died on the feast of the Assumption in 1038 and was canonised in 1083. His right hand is venerated in Budapest.
Saint Stephen of Hungary · Prayer to

Saint Stephen, you ruled your people as a Christian king and entrusted your kingdom to the Mother of God. Pray for all who govern, that they may seek justice and protect the weak. Pray for parents who have lost children, and for me, that I may give God the first place in all I do. Amen.
In the counsels he wrote for his son, Stephen urged him to be patient and merciful, and to rule as a servant of Christ. Whom has God placed in your care, and how are you serving them?

A Polish Dominican who received the habit in the first years of the order and carried its preaching across Poland and far to the north and east. He founded houses of friars in Kraków and beyond and was called the apostle of the North. He died in Kraków on the feast of the Assumption, 1257.

Jacek Odrowąż was a priest of a noble Silesian family. Around 1220 he went to Rome with his bishop and there, tradition holds, received the habit of the Friars Preachers from Saint Dominic himself. Returning to Poland, he founded the Dominican house of the Holy Trinity in Kraków and others in Gdańsk and further afield. He preached in Poland, Prussia and among the peoples of the eastern lands, travelling enormous distances on foot. Many stories gathered around him. The best known says that when the Tatars attacked Kyiv he rescued the Blessed Sacrament from the church and, hearing Our Lady ask not to be left behind, carried off her heavy statue as well, which became light in his arms. He had a great love for the Mother of God and died, fittingly, on the day of her Assumption. He was canonised in 1594.

Saint Hyacinth, tireless preacher, you carried Christ and His Mother to people who had not heard of them. Pray for missionaries, for Poland, and for all who travel for the sake of the Gospel. When I am in danger, help me to keep hold of what matters most. Amen.

O God, Who, year by year, dost gladden us by the solemn feast-day of thy blessed confessor Hyacínthi, mercifully grant unto all who keep his birthday, grace to follow after the pattern of his godly conversation. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The story says the statue of Our Lady became light when he lifted it. Which burden might become lighter if you carried it with her?

A Norman priest and tireless preacher of parish missions who founded a congregation to train priests in seminaries and another to care for women leaving prostitution. He was the first to compose liturgical feasts in honour of the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the Heart of Mary.

John Eudes joined the French Oratory under Cardinal de Bérulle and was ordained in 1625. When plague struck Normandy he nursed the sick, and in one outbreak lived apart, it is said in a large cask in a field, so as not to carry the infection to his brothers. For more than fifty years he preached missions across Normandy and beyond, often with a team of confessors. Convinced that the reform of the Church depended on well-formed priests, he left the Oratory in 1643 and founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, the Eudists, to run seminaries. He also founded the Order of Our Lady of Charity for women who wished to leave prostitution, from which the Good Shepherd Sisters later grew. He wrote Masses and Offices for the Heart of Mary and the Heart of Jesus, and kept them in his communities long before the universal Church did. He died at Caen in 1680 and was canonised in 1925.

Saint John Eudes, you loved the Hearts of Jesus and Mary and spent your life for priests, for sinners and for the sick. Pray for seminarians and all who form them, for women caught in exploitation, and for me, that my heart may be made like the heart of Christ. Amen.

O God, Who wondrously enkindled St. John, Your Confessor, to promote the religious veneration of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary, and through him willed to found new religious families in the Church; grant, we beseech You, that we may honor his holy merits and may learn from the example of his virtues. Through the same Christ our Lord…
He taught that Christians should continue the life of Jesus in their own lives, as members of His body. In what one thing today could you let Christ live through you?

A young Burgundian noble who entered the struggling monastery of Cîteaux with about thirty relatives and friends, then became founding abbot of Clairvaux. Bernard was the most influential churchman of his age, a mystic, preacher and counsellor of popes. His sermons on the Song of Songs and on Our Lady earned him the title of the honey-sweet doctor.

Bernard arrived at Cîteaux in 1113, and his coming revived the new Cistercian reform. In 1115 he was sent to found Clairvaux, and from there some seventy monasteries were founded in his lifetime. He was drawn constantly into the affairs of the Church: he helped end the schism of 1130 on the side of Innocent II, advised his former monk, Pope Eugene III, and argued against Peter Abelard. At the pope’s request he preached the Second Crusade, whose failure grieved him deeply. When a wandering monk stirred up attacks on the Jews of the Rhineland, Bernard went there in person and stopped him. Yet his heart was in the cloister. He wrote of the love of God, of humility and of the Virgin Mary with great warmth, and Dante chose him as his last guide in Paradise. He died in 1153 and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1830.
Saint Bernard of Clairvaux · Prayer to

Saint Bernard, you loved Christ with all your heart and taught the Church to look to Mary in every danger. Pray that in temptation and confusion I may look to the star and call upon her. Help me to love God for His own sake, and to love Him without measure. Amen.

O God, who didst give blessed Bernard to be thy people’s minister in eternal salvation; grant, we pray, that we who have him for teacher of life here on earth, may also deserve now that he is in heaven, to have him for an advocate. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
In dangers, in difficulties, in doubts, think of Mary, call upon Mary, Bernard preached. What doubt or difficulty will you bring to her today?

Giuseppe Sarto, the son of a village postman, was a parish priest for years before becoming bishop of Mantua, Patriarch of Venice and, in 1903, pope. His motto was to restore all things in Christ. He encouraged frequent Communion, allowed children to receive it from the age of reason, and renewed sacred music.

Giuseppe Sarto was born at Riese in the Veneto, one of ten children of a poor family. After ordination in 1858 he served as a curate and then a parish priest, teaching the catechism himself and caring for the sick in a cholera outbreak. He became bishop of Mantua in 1884 and Patriarch of Venice in 1893, and remained simple in his habits. Elected pope in 1903, he took as his programme Saint Paul’s words, to restore all things in Christ. He urged the faithful to receive Communion often, even daily, and in 1910 ruled that children could make their First Communion once they reached the age of reason. He promoted Gregorian chant, reformed the breviary, began the first Code of Canon Law and defended the faith against the errors of his day. He died in August 1914, weeks after the outbreak of the First World War, which he had dreaded. Pius XII canonised him in 1954.

Saint Pius, you were a parish priest at heart and wished to bring everyone, even little children, close to Christ in the Eucharist. Pray for children preparing for their First Communion, for catechists and parents, and for me, that I may receive our Lord often and worthily. Amen.
Holy Communion, he taught, is the shortest and surest way to heaven. How do you prepare to receive it, and how do you give thanks afterwards?

Isabel Flores de Oliva, called Rose for her beauty as a baby, lived a hidden life of prayer and penance in her family’s garden in Lima, while caring for the sick and poor of the city. A Dominican tertiary, she died at thirty-one and was the first canonised saint of the Americas.

Rose was born in Lima, then the capital of Spain’s South American empire. Taking Saint Catherine of Siena as her model, she refused offers of marriage and in 1606 became a lay member of the Dominican order. She lived in a tiny hermitage in her parents’ garden and supported her struggling family by fine needlework and by growing flowers to sell. She took into her home sick and destitute people, among them Indians and African slaves, and nursed them herself. Her penances were severe, and her confessors and friends sometimes urged her to moderation. She also endured long years of spiritual darkness. Many in Lima, rich and poor, came to her for prayer and counsel, and when she died in 1617 the whole city mourned. Clement X canonised her in 1671. She is patron of Peru, of Latin America and of the Philippines.
Saint Rose of Lima · Prayer to

Saint Rose, you loved Christ in hiddenness and served Him in the poor of your city. Pray for the peoples of Latin America and for all who are poor and sick. Help me to find God in ordinary work, and to give Him my heart without holding anything back. Amen.
Rose is remembered to have said that apart from the cross there is no other ladder by which we may get to heaven. What cross is in front of you today, and will you climb it or walk around it?

One of the Twelve, generally identified with Nathanael of Cana, whom Philip brought to Jesus. Christ greeted him as an Israelite in whom there is no guile. Tradition holds that he carried the Gospel as far as India and Armenia, and that he was martyred by being flayed alive.

Bartholomew appears in each list of the apostles beside Philip, and since early times he has been identified with Nathanael in the Gospel of John. When Philip told him they had found the Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth, Nathanael replied, Can anything good come out of Nazareth? Philip simply said, Come and see. Jesus told him He had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him, and Nathanael answered, Rabbi, you are the Son of God. Later he was among the disciples to whom the risen Christ appeared by the Sea of Tiberias. Eusebius records a tradition that he took the Gospel of Matthew to India. Armenian tradition says he was martyred in Armenia, flayed and beheaded. Artists show him holding a knife, and in Michelangelo’s Last Judgment he holds his own skin. His relics are honoured in Rome on the island in the Tiber.
Saint Bartholomew the Apostle · Prayer to

Saint Bartholomew, you came and saw, and confessed Jesus as the Son of God. Pray that I may be without guile, honest with God and with others. When I doubt, bring me back to Christ, and give me courage to bear witness to Him whatever it costs. Amen.

Almighty, eternal God, Who bestowed on us the devout and holy joy of this day to celebrate the feast of Your blessed Apostle Bartholomew, grant unto Your Church, we beseech You, both to love what he believed and to preach what he taught. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Come and see. Philip did not argue with his friend; he brought him to Jesus. Whom could you invite to come and see?

Louis IX became King of France at twelve and reigned for over forty years as a just and devout king. He fed the poor at his own table, built the Sainte-Chapelle to house the Crown of Thorns, was loved for his fairness, and twice went on crusade. He died near Tunis in 1270 and was canonised in 1297.

Louis was crowned in 1226, and his mother, Blanche of Castile, ruled for him until he came of age. She told him she would rather see him dead than guilty of a mortal sin, and he never forgot it. He married Margaret of Provence, and they had eleven children. His friend and biographer Jean de Joinville describes him sitting under an oak at Vincennes to hear the complaints of anyone who came. He reformed the royal courts, forbade judicial duels, founded hospitals including the Quinze-Vingts for the blind, and served the poor with his own hands. In 1239 he acquired the Crown of Thorns and built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris for it. He led a crusade to Egypt in 1248, was captured and ransomed, and stayed four years in the Holy Land. On a second crusade in 1270 he fell sick at Tunis and died, praying for his people.

Saint Louis, king and servant of the poor, you ruled justly and kept your soul free of sin amid wealth and power. Pray for all who govern and judge, for husbands and fathers, and for me, that I may use whatever authority I have for the good of others and the glory of God. Amen.

O God, Who transported Your blessed Confessor Louis from an earthly throne to the glory of the heavenly kingdom, by his merits and intercession we beseech You to make us of the company of the King of kings, Jesus Christ Your Son. Who livest and reignest with God the Father…
Louis wrote to his son that he should have a tender heart for the poor and the suffering. Whose need have you been too busy to notice?

A Christian woman of North Africa, married to a hot-tempered pagan, whose patience won him to the faith before he died. For years she prayed and wept for her son Augustine, who had abandoned the faith, and followed him to Italy. She saw him baptised in Milan and died soon after at Ostia.

Almost all we know of Monica comes from her son’s Confessions. She was born at Thagaste in North Africa and married Patricius, a pagan official whose temper and infidelity she bore with patience; he was baptised shortly before his death. Of her children, Augustine caused her the deepest grief, living with a mistress and joining the Manichees. She prayed and wept for him for years, and a bishop she begged for help told her it was not possible that the son of so many tears should be lost. When Augustine left secretly for Rome she followed him there and on to Milan, where she came to love Saint Ambrose. At Easter 387 she saw her son baptised. Waiting to sail home, they stood at a window at Ostia and spoke together of eternal life. Days later she fell ill. She asked only that they remember her at the altar of the Lord, and died aged fifty-six.

Saint Monica, patient wife and faithful mother, you never stopped praying for your son. I bring you those I love who have fallen away from the faith. Pray that God will bring them home, and give me your patience, your hope and your perseverance in prayer. Amen.
It is not possible that the son of so many tears should be lost. For whom are you weeping and praying, and do you still hope?

A brilliant North African teacher of rhetoric who searched for truth through philosophy and the Manichees, and was converted in Milan in 386 through the prayers of his mother, the preaching of Ambrose and the letters of Saint Paul. As bishop of Hippo he wrote the Confessions and The City of God, and is one of the greatest Doctors of the Church.

Augustine was born at Thagaste and studied at Carthage, where he took a partner, with whom he had a son, Adeodatus. He joined the Manichees for nine years. Teaching rhetoric at Rome and then Milan, he went to hear Ambrose preach and was slowly won by his reading of the Scriptures. In the summer of 386, in a garden in Milan, he heard a child’s voice chanting, take and read, opened Saint Paul’s letter to the Romans, and his resistance gave way. Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387. Returning to Africa, he lived in community with friends until the people of Hippo pressed him to be ordained priest in 391; he became their bishop a few years later. For over thirty years he preached, judged disputes, cared for the poor and wrote on grace, the Trinity and the Church. He died in 430 as the Vandals besieged Hippo.
Saint Augustine of Hippo · Prayer to

Saint Augustine, you knew the restless heart and found its rest in God. Pray for all who search for meaning in the wrong places, and for me, that I may not delay any longer in loving God above all things. Help me to seek the truth humbly and to live it with charity. Amen.

Give heed to our humble prayers, almighty God, and through the intercession of blessed Augustine, Your Confessor and Bishop, kindly grant Your oft-given mercy to those upon whom You bestow great hope in Your forgiveness. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
You have made us for yourself, Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. What are you restless for, and have you brought it to God?
The Passion of Saint John the Baptist · Life

John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, told King Herod Antipas that it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife. Herod imprisoned him, and at a birthday feast, bound by a rash oath to the daughter of Herodias, had him beheaded. The Church honours his death as a martyrdom for truth and for Christ.
The Passion of Saint John the Baptist · Life

Saint Mark tells the story in full. Herod Antipas had married Herodias, the wife of his brother, and John rebuked him publicly. Herodias wanted John dead, but Herod feared him, knowing him to be a righteous and holy man, and liked to listen to him even when he was troubled by what he heard. At his birthday banquet her daughter danced for the guests, and Herod swore to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for the head of John the Baptist on a dish. Herod was grieved, but would not go back on his oath before his guests. John’s disciples came and laid his body in a tomb. The historian Josephus places his imprisonment in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. The feast is linked to a church at Sebaste in Samaria, where tradition placed his tomb.
The Passion of Saint John the Baptist · Prayer to

Saint John the Baptist, you prepared the way of the Lord and gave your life rather than keep silent about the truth. Pray that I may decrease so that Christ may increase in me. Give me courage to speak the truth with love, even when it is unwelcome, and to keep faith to the end. Amen.
The Passion of Saint John the Baptist · Meditation
He must increase, but I must decrease. Where is your own pride getting in the way of Christ today?

A Catalan friar of the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, founded to ransom Christians held captive in North Africa. Tradition holds that he gave himself as a hostage to free others. His name, meaning not born, recalls that he was delivered after his mother died in childbirth, and he is patron of mothers, midwives and the newborn.

Raymond was born in Catalonia, and tradition says that he was taken alive from his mother’s womb after she had died, hence the name Nonnatus. As a young man he joined the Mercedarians, founded by Saint Peter Nolasco in 1218, whose members vowed to give themselves as hostages, if need be, to free captives. Sent to North Africa with money for ransoms, he is said to have stayed behind as a hostage when the funds ran out, and to have preached to his fellow prisoners. Tradition holds that his captors pierced his lips and padlocked his mouth to stop him preaching. After his release he returned to Spain. The story goes that he was named a cardinal by Gregory IX and set out for Rome, but fell ill and died near Barcelona in 1240. Much of his life is known only through later tradition. His name was entered in the Roman Martyrology in 1657.

Saint Raymond, you were given life through your mother’s death and gave your own freedom for captives. Pray for expectant mothers and for all who help bring children into the world, for those held captive, and for me, that I may be willing to give something of myself so that others may be free. Amen.

O God, Who made blessed Raymund, Your Confessor, famous for delivering Your faithful from the captivity of the infidels, grant us by his intercession that, having been released from the bonds of our sins, we may with free minds do what is pleasing to You. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Mercedarians promised to take the place of captives if there was no other way. Who around you is held captive by debt, addiction or fear, and what could you do for them?

A Roman aristocrat and city prefect who gave away his wealth to become a monk, Gregory was elected pope in 590 in a time of plague, flood and invasion. He fed the hungry of Rome, ordered the liturgy, wrote the Pastoral Rule and sent Augustine to convert the English. He called himself the servant of the servants of God.

Gregory was born around 540 into a senatorial family. After serving as prefect of Rome he turned his family house on the Caelian Hill into the monastery of Saint Andrew and lived there as a monk. Pope Pelagius II made him a deacon and sent him as envoy to Constantinople. Elected pope in 590, he accepted reluctantly and led penitential processions through the plague-struck city. With the empire weak, he organised food for the poor, negotiated with the Lombards and cared for churches in every region. Bede tells how he once saw fair-haired English boys for sale in Rome and said they were not Angles but angels. In 596 he sent Augustine and some forty monks to Kent. His writings on Job, on the Gospels and on the life of Saint Benedict shaped the faith of the Middle Ages. He died in 604 and is honoured as a Doctor of the Church and the apostle of the English.
Saint Gregory the Great · Prayer to

Saint Gregory, apostle of the English, you sent missionaries to a far island and cared for the hungry at your door. Pray for the Church in this land, for our bishops and priests, and for me, that I may serve others humbly and bring to Christ those who do not yet know Him. Amen.
Gregory took the title servant of the servants of God, and every pope since has kept it. Whom are you called to serve today, rather than to be served by?
The Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

Nine months after the Immaculate Conception, the Church keeps the birthday of the Mother of God. A saint’s feast usually marks the day of death, the birthday into heaven, but the liturgy celebrates the earthly birth of only three: Christ, His Mother and Saint John the Baptist. The feast began in the East and was kept in Rome by the seventh century.
The Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Life

Scripture says nothing of Mary’s birth. The names of her parents, Joachim and Anne, come from the Protoevangelium of James, a second-century writing that the Church never received as Scripture but whose stories passed into art and devotion. The feast probably began in Jerusalem with the dedication of a church near the Pool of Bethesda, honoured as the site of her parents’ home, where the Crusader church of Saint Anne still stands. It spread through the East and was kept in Rome by the time of Pope Sergius I, at the end of the seventh century, who ordered a procession for it. Saint Andrew of Crete and Saint John Damascene preached on it. The liturgy sees in her birth the dawn before the sunrise: the child born today will bring forth the Saviour of the world.
The Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Prayer to

Holy Mary, the Church sings that your birth announced joy to the whole world, because from you would come Christ, the Sun of justice. Pray for every child born today, for mothers awaiting birth, and for me, that the grace God began in you may also be brought to completion in me. Amen.
The Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Prayer

Bestow upon Your servants, we beseech You, O Lord, the gift of heavenly grace, that, as the child-bearing of the Blessed Virgin stood for the beginning of our salvation, so may the solemn feast of her Nativity bring about an increase of peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
The Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary · Meditation
The liturgy compares Mary’s birth to the dawn before sunrise. Where in your life might God be preparing a dawn you cannot yet see?

A Catalan Jesuit who spent nearly forty years at Cartagena, in present-day Colombia, the chief slave port of Spanish America. He met each ship as it came in, going down into the holds with food, water and medicine, nursing the sick and teaching and baptising the enslaved. He called himself the slave of the Africans for ever.

Peter Claver was born at Verdú in Catalonia in 1580 and joined the Jesuits in 1602. At the college in Majorca the elderly porter, Saint Alphonsus Rodríguez, urged him to go to the Americas. He reached Cartagena in 1610, was ordained there in 1616, and signed his final vows as Peter Claver, slave of the Africans for ever. Thousands of captives arrived in the port each year, chained and starving after weeks at sea. Claver went aboard with interpreters, carried food and medicines, washed wounds and stayed with the dying. He taught the faith with pictures, baptised, by tradition, some three hundred thousand people, and visited the sick in the hospitals and the prisoners of the city. Struck by illness in 1650, he spent his last years largely forgotten in his room. He died on 8 September 1654, and Leo XIII canonised him in 1888, together with Alphonsus.

Saint Peter Claver, you went down into the darkness of the slave ships to bring bread, medicine and the love of Christ. Pray for all who are trafficked, exploited or held in forced labour today, and for me, that I may not look away from suffering but go out to meet it with practical love. Amen.
Claver taught that we must speak first with our hands and only then with our lips. What practical help could you give before you offer advice?

An Augustinian friar of the Italian Marche who spent thirty years preaching, hearing confessions and caring for the poor and sick of Tolentino. Known for his gentleness and his long hours of prayer, he prayed especially for the souls in purgatory and is honoured as their patron. In 1446 he became the first Augustinian to be canonised.

Nicholas was born around 1245 at Sant’Angelo in Pontano. His parents, childless for years, had made a pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Nicholas at Bari and named their son after him. As a youth, it is said, he heard an Augustinian friar preach on the words love not the world, and asked to join the order. After his ordination he moved between several friaries before settling at Tolentino around 1275, where he stayed until his death in 1305. The town was divided by the feuds of the age, and he preached peace in the streets, visited the sick and the poor, and spent long hours in the confessional. Tradition tells that a dead friar appeared to him asking for prayers, and that he offered Mass for the departed for a week. Blessed bread, known as Saint Nicholas bread, is still given out in his honour.
Saint Nicholas of Tolentino · Prayer to

Saint Nicholas, faithful friar and friend of the holy souls, you prayed for the dead as if they were your own family. Pray for all who have died with no one to remember them, and teach me to offer my prayers, my Masses and my small sufferings for them, trusting in the mercy of God. Amen.

Be mindful, O Lord, of our humble prayers in this commemoration of Blessed Nicholas, Your Confessor, so that we, who have no confidence in our own righteousness, may be helped by the merits of those who have been pleasing to You. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Nicholas spent long hours in prayer for those who had gone before him. Who among your own dead have you forgotten to pray for?

The greatest preacher of the early Church, called Chrysostom, golden-mouthed, for his eloquence. Priest at Antioch and then archbishop of Constantinople, he preached the Scriptures verse by verse, defended the poor and rebuked the luxury of the court. He died in exile in 407. Eastern Christians still celebrate the Divine Liturgy that bears his name.

John was born at Antioch around 347 and studied rhetoric under the famous pagan teacher Libanius. After his baptism he lived as a monk and hermit in the hills until his health gave way. Ordained priest in 386, he preached in Antioch for twelve years, and his homilies on Genesis, Matthew, John and the letters of Paul are still read. In 398 he was made archbishop of Constantinople, almost against his will. He cut the expenses of the bishop’s household, founded hospitals, called the clergy to holiness and spoke plainly against the wealth of the powerful while the poor went hungry. He made enemies, among them the Empress Eudoxia and Theophilus of Alexandria, and was deposed and exiled twice. Marched in harsh conditions toward the Black Sea, he died at Comana in 407. His last words are recorded as glory be to God for all things.

Saint John Chrysostom, you preached the word of God without fear and saw Christ in the poor at the church door. Pray for all preachers, that they may speak the truth with love, and for me, that I may honour Christ in the Eucharist and in those who are hungry, and give thanks to God for all things. Amen.
Chrysostom warned his people not to honour Christ in church with silks while neglecting Him naked and cold outside. Where is Christ waiting for you beyond the church door today?
The Exaltation of the Holy Cross · Life

The feast keeps the anniversary of the dedication of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem in 335, built by Constantine over the place of the crucifixion and the tomb. Tradition holds that his mother, Saint Helena, had found the wood of the true cross there. The cross, once a gallows, is lifted up as the throne of Christ’s victory.
The Exaltation of the Holy Cross · Life

Eusebius records the building of Constantine’s basilica at Golgotha and its dedication in September 335. Later in that century the pilgrim Egeria described the great crowds who came for the anniversary, and the faithful filing past one by one to kiss the relic of the cross on Good Friday. The story that Helena discovered the cross, around 326, is told by writers of the late fourth century, among them Saint Ambrose. In 614 the Persians sacked Jerusalem and carried the relic away; the Emperor Heraclius recovered it and restored it to the city around 630, and this too came to be remembered on the feast. Exaltation means lifting up: Christ said that when He was lifted up from the earth He would draw all people to Himself. Eastern Christians keep the day with fasting and a solemn veneration of the cross.
The Exaltation of the Holy Cross · Prayer to

Lord Jesus Christ, you were lifted up on the cross to draw all people to yourself. Through the prayers of Our Lady, who stood beside it, help me to embrace the crosses of my own life, to see in them a share in your love, and to glory in nothing but your cross, by which the world is redeemed. Amen.
The Exaltation of the Holy Cross · Prayer
We adore thee, O Christ, and we bless thee, because by thy holy cross thou hast redeemed the world.
The Exaltation of the Holy Cross · Meditation
When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself. Which cross in your life might be the place where Christ is drawing you closer?

The day after the Exaltation of the Cross, the Church stands with Mary beneath it. Simeon had told her that a sword would pierce her soul, and tradition counts seven sorrows, from his prophecy to the burial of her Son. Mary suffered with Christ, and her faith did not fail. The Servite friars did much to spread the devotion.

The seven sorrows traditionally honoured are the prophecy of Simeon, the flight into Egypt, the loss of the child Jesus in the Temple, the meeting with Jesus on the way to Calvary, the crucifixion, the taking down from the cross and the burial. Meditation on Mary’s compassion grew strongly in the Middle Ages, when the Stabat Mater was written, often attributed to the Franciscan Jacopone da Todi. The Order of Servants of Mary, founded in Florence in the thirteenth century by seven merchants, made the sorrows of Our Lady their particular devotion. Pius VII, on his return to Rome after captivity under Napoleon, extended the feast to the whole Church in 1814 in thanksgiving, and Pius X fixed it on 15 September. The Servite chaplet of the seven sorrows, seven groups of seven Hail Marys, is still widely prayed.
Our Lady of Sorrows · Prayer to

Holy Mother of Sorrows, you stood by the cross when others fled, and your faith held firm in the darkest hour. Stay beside all who keep watch at a deathbed, all parents who have lost a child, and all whose hearts are pierced. Pray for me, that I may stand by Christ in His suffering members. Amen.

O God, in Whose Passion the sword, according to the prophecy of blessed Simeon, pierced through the soul of Mary, the glorious Virgin and Mother, mercifully grant that we, who reverently commemorate her piercing through and her suffering, may, by the interceding glorious merits of all the saints faithfully standing by the Cross, obtain the abundant fruit of Your passion. Who livest…
Mary could not take away her Son’s suffering, but she stayed. Whose suffering are you being asked simply to stay beside?

A pope and a bishop of Carthage, allies in a time of persecution, both named in the Roman Canon. When Christians who had denied the faith under threat of death sought to return, Cornelius and Cyprian upheld both mercy and penance against a rigorist schism. Cornelius died in exile in 253; Cyprian was beheaded in 258.

Under the Emperor Decius in 250 many Christians gave way and offered sacrifice to the gods. When the persecution eased, the Church had to decide how to receive them back. Cornelius, elected Bishop of Rome in 251, held that the lapsed could be reconciled after penance. The priest Novatian, taking a harsher view, had himself made a rival bishop. Cyprian, a rhetorician who had become a Christian as a grown man and soon afterwards bishop of Carthage, stood by Cornelius and wrote his treatise On the Unity of the Catholic Church. Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae, on the coast north of Rome, where he died in 253. Under the Emperor Valerian, Cyprian was arrested and condemned. Hearing the sentence, he answered thanks be to God, and had twenty-five gold pieces given to his executioner.
Saints Cornelius and Cyprian · Prayer to

Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, shepherds in a time of trial, you held together mercy for the fallen and fidelity to Christ. Pray for the unity of the Church, for those who have drifted from the faith and long to return, and for me, that I may never be ashamed of Christ, whatever it may cost. Amen.
May the feast of the blessed Martyrs and Bishops Cornelius and Cyprian, protect us, O Lord, we beseech You, and may their holy prayer recommend us unto You. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Cyprian wrote that no one can have God for his Father who does not have the Church for his mother. How do you love the Church, with all her weakness?

A Jesuit theologian and cardinal from Montepulciano, the foremost defender of Catholic teaching in the controversies after the Reformation. His catechisms taught children for three centuries. He lived poorly, gave freely to the poor, and guided the young Aloysius Gonzaga. He was canonised in 1930 and named a Doctor of the Church a year later.

Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542, a nephew of Pope Marcellus II, and entered the Jesuits in 1560. Small, often unwell and quick-witted, he taught first at Louvain and then at the Roman College, where his lectures became the Controversies, a vast and careful statement of Catholic teaching on the questions disputed with the Reformers. He was known for setting out his opponents’ arguments fairly. Clement VIII made him a cardinal in 1599, and he served for three years as archbishop of Capua. In 1616 he was involved in the Church’s first inquiry into Galileo’s teaching. In Rome he kept a simple household, gave away most of his income, and wrote short spiritual books, among them The Art of Dying Well. He died in 1621, asking to be laid near Aloysius Gonzaga, whose confessor he had been; they now rest close together in Sant’Ignazio.

Saint Robert, you served the truth with learning, patience and courtesy, and lived simply among the riches of Rome. Pray for teachers of the faith and for all who seek the truth in good conscience, and for me, that I may know my faith well, speak of it with charity, and prepare each day to die well. Amen.
Bellarmine taught that the art of dying well is learned by living well. If today were your last, what would you want to put right?

A Franciscan friar of southern Italy, so slow at his books and clumsy at his work that he was sent away by one order and barely accepted by another. Ordained priest, he was caught up in ecstasy so often, and was seen by so many witnesses to rise from the ground in prayer, that he was kept away from crowds. He is a patron of students.

Joseph Desa was born in 1603 at Copertino in Apulia, in a shed, it is said, because his father’s debts had cost the family their home. A sickly, absent-minded boy, he was nicknamed Boccaperta, open-mouth. The Capuchins took him as a lay brother but sent him away after eight months for his clumsiness. The Conventual Franciscans at La Grottella accepted him to look after their mule, and his humility and prayer won him a place in the novitiate. He struggled with study, and tradition tells that at each examination he was questioned only on the one text he knew well; he was ordained in 1628. His ecstasies, in which he was seen to rise into the air, drew such crowds that the Inquisition examined him, and he was moved from friary to friary, ending at Osimo, where he died in 1663. He was canonised in 1767.
Saint Joseph of Cupertino · Prayer to

Saint Joseph of Cupertino, you were thought a fool and found your joy in God alone. Pray for all students, especially those who struggle and fear failure, and for me, that I may do my best with the gifts I have, accept my limits with humility, and let my heart be lifted to God in prayer. Amen.

O God, Who willed that all things be drawn unto Your Son when He was raised above the earth, mercifully grant, by the merits and example of Your seraphic Confessor Joseph, that, having been raised above all earthly desires, we may be found worthy to come unto Him. Who livest…
Joseph had little learning but a great love for God. Do you trust that God values your love more than your achievements?

Bishop of Benevento, martyred near Naples in the persecution of Diocletian around 305, and venerated as the patron of that city. A phial said to hold his blood is kept in Naples cathedral; on his feast and on other days each year the dried mass has repeatedly been seen to liquefy. The Church permits the devotion without pronouncing on its cause.

Little is certain about Januarius beyond his martyrdom, and the accounts of his death were written long afterwards. Tradition holds that he went to visit Christians imprisoned at Pozzuoli, was arrested himself, was thrown to wild beasts that would not touch him, and was beheaded near the Solfatara with several companions. His relics were moved more than once over the centuries and came back to Naples for good in 1497. The liquefaction of the blood was first recorded in 1389 and has been observed many times since, usually on the Saturday before the first Sunday of May, on 19 September and on 16 December, before crowds who pray for it. Neapolitans credit him with protecting their city, especially during the eruption of Vesuvius in 1631. Scientists have proposed explanations, and the Church has made no formal judgement: the devotion rests on faith and prayer, not on dogma.

Saint Januarius, bishop and martyr, you gave your life for Christ, and your people have trusted in your prayers for centuries. Pray for the city of Naples and for all who live in the shadow of danger, and for me, that my faith may not be dry and hard but warm and living. Amen.
Each year the people of Naples wait and pray for the blood to liquefy. Is there a hardened place in your heart that you could ask God to soften?
Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and Companions · Life

The Church in Korea was founded by lay people, scholars who found the faith in Christian books from China in the late eighteenth century. For decades it grew under persecution, often without priests, and thousands died. The 103 martyrs canonised in 1984 include Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean-born priest, and the lay leader Paul Chong Hasang.
Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and Companions · Life

In 1784 Yi Seung-hun, baptised in Beijing, came home to Korea and began baptising others. The young community spread the faith by itself for years and sent messengers again and again to beg for priests. Under a government that saw the new religion as a threat to the social order, it suffered waves of persecution. Paul Chong Hasang, whose father and brother had been martyred, travelled many times to Beijing to ask for clergy, and wrote a defence of the faith addressed to the authorities before his execution in 1839. Andrew Kim Taegon, son of a martyr, studied in Macau and was ordained in Shanghai in 1845. Back in Korea he served for barely a year before he was arrested and beheaded near Seoul in 1846, aged twenty-five. Among the 103 saints are French missionary bishops and priests, but most were lay men, women and children. John Paul II canonised them in Seoul in 1984.
Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and Companions · Prayer to

Holy martyrs of Korea, you received the faith from books and handed it on with your blood. Pray for the Church in Korea, for all who must practise their faith in secret, and for me, that I may treasure the faith I received so easily and share it with courage and joy. Amen.
Saints Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and Companions · Meditation
The first Korean Catholics found Christ in the pages of a book and kept the faith alone for years. What have you done with the faith that was handed to you?

A tax collector at Capernaum, despised as a collaborator with Rome, whom Jesus called from his booth with two words: follow me. He left everything, gave a feast for his old companions, and heard Christ say that He had come to call sinners. Tradition holds him to be the author of the first Gospel, written for Jewish Christians.

Mark and Luke call him Levi, son of Alphaeus; in the Gospel that bears his name he is Matthew the tax collector. Collecting customs by the Sea of Galilee, he would have been rich and unwelcome. When Jesus called him, he rose and followed, and soon invited Jesus to dine with tax collectors and sinners, which scandalised the Pharisees. Early writers, beginning with Papias, say that Matthew gathered the sayings of the Lord in the Hebrew language. His Gospel shows Jesus as the one in whom the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled, and gives us the visit of the Magi, the Sermon on the Mount, the Lord’s Prayer in the form we pray it and the command to make disciples of all nations. Traditions differ on where he preached and died, naming Ethiopia or Persia. His symbol is a winged man.
Saint Matthew the Apostle · Prayer to

Saint Matthew, you left your counting table at a word from Christ and opened your house to sinners. Pray for all whose work is with money, that they may be honest and generous, and for me, that I may hear the Lord’s call today, rise without delay, and follow Him. Amen.
May we be helped, O Lord, by the prayers of the blessed Apostle and Evangelist Matthew, that what we ourselves cannot obtain, may be granted by his intercession. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Jesus saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax office and said to him, follow me. What keeps you sitting at your table when Christ calls?

A Capuchin friar who for fifty years bore the wounds of Christ in his hands, feet and side. From the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo in southern Italy he heard confessions for many hours a day, drew pilgrims from all over the world, and founded a great hospital for the relief of suffering. He was canonised in 2002.

Francesco Forgione was born at Pietrelcina, near Benevento, in 1887, the son of farmers. He entered the Capuchin novitiate at fifteen, taking the name Pio, and was ordained in 1910. Poor health kept him at home for long periods, and in 1916 he was sent to San Giovanni Rotondo, where he spent the rest of his life. On 20 September 1918, praying before a crucifix, he received the visible stigmata. The wounds were examined by doctors and by the Holy See, and in the early 1930s, while the case was investigated, he was forbidden for a time to say Mass in public or to hear confessions. He obeyed. Crowds came to his Mass and to his confessional, where he could be gentle or severe. He encouraged prayer groups and built the hospital Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, opened in 1956. He died on 23 September 1968.
Saint Pio of Pietrelcina · Prayer to

Saint Pio, you shared the wounds of Christ and spent your days reconciling sinners to God. Pray for all who are sick and all who care for them, for priests in the confessional, and for me, that I may make a good confession, carry my cross without complaint, and learn to pray, hope and not worry. Amen.
Pray, hope and don’t worry, he told those who came to him. Which worry could you hand over to God in prayer today?

A Gascon farmer’s son who became a priest hoping for a comfortable living, and was converted to the service of the poor. He founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach to country people and, with Saint Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity. He is the patron of all works of charity.

Vincent was born in 1581 at Pouy, in south-west France, and ordained young, in 1600, hoping for a good benefice. His own letters tell of capture by pirates and slavery in Tunis, though historians debate the story. As chaplain to the powerful Gondi family he came to see the spiritual neglect of the peasants on their estates. In 1617 a dying man’s confession at Folleville, and a sick family in his parish at Châtillon, turned his life around: he preached missions and gathered wealthy women into Confraternities of Charity. In 1625 he founded the Congregation of the Mission, and in 1633, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity, sisters who served the sick in their homes and in the streets rather than behind a cloister. He cared for galley slaves, foundlings and refugees of war, and reformed the training of priests. He died in Paris in 1660.
Saint Vincent de Paul · Prayer to

Saint Vincent de Paul, you learned to see Christ in the poor and spent all your strength in serving them. Pray for all who work for the poor, the sick and the abandoned, and for me, that my charity may be practical and humble, and that I may love the poor as my masters in Christ. Amen.
Vincent told his sisters that to leave prayer to serve the poor is to leave God for God. Whose need might be God interrupting you today?

Duke of Bohemia, raised in the faith by his grandmother Saint Ludmila. He ruled justly, built churches and cared for the poor, but his Christian rule and his peace with the Germans made him enemies. He was murdered by his brother Boleslav on his way to Mass. He is the patron saint of the Czech people.

Wenceslaus was the son of Duke Vratislav. After his father’s death his grandmother Ludmila brought him up a Christian, and in 921 she was murdered by nobles loyal to his mother, Drahomíra, who resented her influence. When he came of age Wenceslaus took up the government himself. He favoured the Church, welcomed priests from Bavaria, founded the rotunda of Saint Vitus in Prague and, to spare his land war, accepted the overlordship of the German king Henry the Fowler. Early lives tell of his charity, of his gathering wood for the poor by night and of his care for the bread and wine of the Mass. In 935, or perhaps 929, he went to Stará Boleslav at his brother’s invitation for the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Next morning, on his way to Mass, he was struck down at the church door. The carol Good King Wenceslas is a Victorian invention, but true to his reputation.

Saint Wenceslaus, you ruled as a servant of Christ and met death on your way to Mass. Pray for all who hold power, that they may seek peace and justice, for families divided by envy and ambition, and for me, that I may love the Mass and be generous to the poor in their need. Amen.

O God, Who through the palm of martyrdom transported blessed Wenceslaus from an earthly dominion unto heavenly glory, keep us, by his prayers, from all harm and grant us to rejoice in his fellowship. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
Wenceslaus was killed by his own brother at the door of a church. Is there a brother or sister you need to forgive or be reconciled with?
Saints Michael, Gabriel and Raphael · Life

The three angels named in Scripture. Michael, whose name asks who is like God, leads the heavenly host against Satan. Gabriel, the strength of God, brought Mary the news of the Incarnation.
